title: GCSE Statistics
summary: The whole GCSE in sixteen short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Statistics specification.
subject: Statistics

title: The statistical enquiry cycle
words: Hypothesis — a statement you can test with data, such as "Year 11 students sleep less than Year 7 students"|Statistical enquiry cycle — plan, collect, process and represent, analyse and interpret, evaluate, then refine and go round again|Variable — a quantity or quality that can change from one person or item to the next|Constraint — a limit on the enquiry, such as time, cost or who you can reach|Evaluate — judge whether the data and the method really answered the question, and what to improve
points: Write the hypothesis first: every later choice, from what to collect to which chart to draw, should test it.|Hypothesis "taller people have longer arm spans": measure both on the same people, draw a scatter diagram, look for positive correlation.|A conclusion answers the hypothesis in words, using the numbers: "the Year 11 median is 40 minutes lower, so the data supports it."|An evaluation names a weakness and a fix: ten people from one class is small and may be biased, so sample fifty across the year.

title: Types of data
words: Qualitative data — described in words, such as eye colour; also called categorical data|Quantitative data — numbers that come from counting or measuring|Discrete data — can only take particular values, such as the number of brothers and sisters|Continuous data — can take any value in a range, such as height or time|Ordinal data — categories with a natural order, such as small, medium and large|Primary data — collected by you, for your own question|Secondary data — collected by somebody else, such as census results or a published table|Bivariate data — two variables measured on each item, such as the height and the mass of each person|Class boundaries — the true lower and upper limits of a group of continuous data
formulas: Class width — width = upper class boundary − lower class boundary|Class midpoint — midpoint = (lower boundary + upper boundary) / 2
points: Shoe size is discrete (there is no size 7.3), but the length of a foot is continuous.|Ages 10–14 in whole years have class boundaries 10 and 15, because somebody aged 14 years 11 months is still 14. Width = 5.|Lengths to the nearest cm grouped 20–24 have boundaries 19.5 and 24.5. Width = 5.|The midpoint of 10 ≤ t < 20 is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15.|Primary data fits your question but costs time; secondary data is quick but may be old or measured differently.

title: Populations and sampling
words: Population — everyone or everything the question is about|Census — data collected from every member of the population|Sample — the part of the population that data is collected from|Sampling frame — a list of every member of the population, which a sample is chosen from|Simple random sample — every member has the same chance of being picked, for example by numbering them and using random numbers|Systematic sample — every kth member of a list, after a random start|Stratified sample — the population is split into groups and each group is sampled in proportion to its size|Quota sample — people are picked until a set number from each group is reached; quick, but not random|Cluster sample — the population is split into clusters, some clusters are chosen at random, and everybody in them is sampled|Opportunity sample — whoever is easiest to reach; also called a convenience sample, and likely to be biased|Bias — a systematic error that makes the results unrepresentative
formulas: Stratified sample — number from a group = (group size) / (population size) × sample size|[H] Petersen capture–recapture — N = (M × n) / m, where M are marked first, n caught second, m of those marked
points: 600 students, 240 in Year 7, sample of 50: Year 7 gets 240 / 600 × 50 = 20.|Round each stratum to whole people, then check the numbers still add up to the sample size.|Systematic: 500 names, sample of 25, so k = 500 ÷ 25 = 20. Random start 7, then 7, 27, 47, …|[H] 40 fish marked; later 50 caught, 8 marked: N = (40 × 50) / 8 = 250. Assumes no births, deaths or moves in between.|A census gives complete information but takes time and money; a sample is quicker but may not represent everybody.

title: Collecting data
words: Questionnaire — a set of written questions that people answer themselves|Open question — any answer is allowed; rich, but hard to analyse|Closed question — the answer is chosen from given options; easy to analyse|Leading question — wording that pushes towards one answer, such as "Don't you agree that…?"|Pilot study — a small trial run that finds problems before the main survey|Explanatory variable — the variable that is changed or controlled; also called the independent variable|Response variable — the variable that is measured; also called the dependent variable|Extraneous variable — anything else that could affect the result, which should be kept the same|Control group — a group given no treatment, to compare against|Laboratory experiment — carried out under controlled conditions|Field experiment — carried out in a real setting, with some variables controlled|Natural experiment — the explanatory variable is not controlled by the researcher|Data cleaning — finding and fixing errors, gaps and impossible values before the analysis
points: Answer boxes must not overlap and must cover every answer: 0–1, 2–3, 4 or more, not 0–2, 2–4.|Not "How much TV do you watch?" but "How many hours of TV did you watch yesterday?" with tick boxes.|Does fertiliser help plants grow? Fertiliser is explanatory, height is response; keep water, light and soil the same.|A pilot study might show a question is misunderstood or an option is missing, so it is fixed before the real survey.|Cleaning: an age of 150 or a blank height is checked or removed before anything is calculated.

title: Tables
words: Tally — marks in groups of five, used to count while collecting|Frequency — how many times a value or a class occurs|Grouped frequency table — the data is counted in classes rather than single values|Class interval — the range of values in one class, such as 10 ≤ t < 20|Two-way table — frequencies for two variables at once, with row and column totals
points: 30 students, 18 of them girls: the table's missing entry is 30 − 18 = 12 boys.|Write classes as inequalities so they cannot overlap: 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20.|Grouping loses the exact values, so anything worked out from a grouped table is an estimate.|Check the grand total twice: it must equal the sum of the row totals and the sum of the column totals.

title: Charts for categories
words: Pictogram — symbols that each stand for a set number of items, with a key|Bar chart — bars of equal width with gaps between them; the height shows the frequency|Composite bar chart — each bar is split into parts showing the categories inside it|Comparative bar chart — bars for two or more groups drawn side by side|Pie chart — a circle split into sectors, each angle in proportion to its frequency|Population pyramid — a back-to-back bar chart of a population by age and sex|Choropleth map — a map shaded so that darker areas show higher values|Misleading diagram — a chart that gives a false impression, for example an axis that does not start at zero or an uneven scale
formulas: Pie chart angle — angle = frequency / (total frequency) × 360°|[H] Comparative pie charts — r₂ / r₁ = √(n₂ / n₁), because the area is in proportion to the total
points: 60 people, 15 chose blue: angle = 15 / 60 × 360° = 90°.|Reading back: a 72° sector of 200 people is 72 / 360 × 200 = 40 people.|[H] Totals 100 and 400: r₂ / r₁ = √(400 / 100) = 2, so a 3 cm pie becomes 6 cm.|A pie chart compares proportions; to compare actual numbers, use a bar chart.

title: Charts for numbers
topics: Stem & Leaf Diagrams, Frequency Polygons, Histograms
words: Stem-and-leaf diagram — every value shown, split into a stem and a leaf, with a key|Back-to-back stem-and-leaf — two data sets sharing one stem, for comparing|Frequency polygon — points at the midpoint of each class, joined by straight lines|Histogram — bars for continuous data, with no gaps between them|[H] Frequency density — the frequency per unit of class width; the height of a bar when the widths are unequal|[H] Bar area — in a histogram, the area of each bar is in proportion to its frequency
formulas: [H] Frequency density — frequency density = frequency / (class width)|[H] Frequency from a histogram — frequency = frequency density × class width
points: Key: stem 3, leaf 7 means 37. Leaves go in order, so stem 3 reads 1 4 4 8, never 4 1 8 4.|Class 20 ≤ x < 30 with frequency 6: plot the frequency polygon point at (25, 6).|[H] Class 10 ≤ t < 25, frequency 30: frequency density = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.|[H] A bar from 40 to 50 at height 1.6: frequency = 1.6 × 10 = 16.

title: Averages
topics: Mean, Median, Mode, Averages from a Table, Averages from Grouped Data
words: Mean — the total of the values divided by how many there are|Median — the middle value once the data is in order|Mode — the most common value|Modal class — the class with the highest frequency|Weighted mean — a mean in which some values count for more than others|[H] Geometric mean — the nth root of the product of n values; the average for growth rates
formulas: Mean — x̄ = Σx / n|Mean from a frequency table — x̄ = Σfx / Σf|Position of the median — (n + 1) / 2|Weighted mean — weighted mean = Σwx / Σw|[H] Geometric mean — geometric mean = (x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ)^(1/n)
points: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13: mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, median = 7, mode = 7.|x = 0, 1, 2 with f = 5, 8, 7: Σfx = 22 and Σf = 20, so the mean is 1.1.|From grouped data, use each class midpoint as x, so the mean is an estimate.|Coursework 60 with weight 1, exam 80 with weight 3: (60 + 240) ÷ 4 = 75.|[H] Growth of 10% then 21%: √(1.10 × 1.21) = √1.331 ≈ 1.154, so about 15.4% a year.

title: Measures of spread
topics: Range, Box Plots & Quartiles, Cumulative Frequency
words: Range — the largest value minus the smallest|Lower quartile — Q₁, a quarter of the way through the ordered data|Upper quartile — Q₃, three quarters of the way through the ordered data|Interquartile range — the spread of the middle half of the data|Percentile — the value below which a given percentage of the data lies; deciles split it into tenths|Cumulative frequency — a running total of the frequencies|Box plot — the minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃ and maximum drawn against a scale|Outlier — a value a long way from the rest of the data|[H] Variance — the mean of the squared distances from the mean|[H] Standard deviation — the square root of the variance; spread in the data's own units
formulas: Range — range = largest − smallest|Interquartile range — IQR = Q₃ − Q₁|Outliers — below Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR|[H] Standard deviation — σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)^2 / n)|[H] Standard deviation, quicker form — σ = √(Σx^2 / n − x̄^2)|[H] From a frequency table — σ = √(Σfx^2 / Σf − x̄^2)
points: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12: median = 7, Q₁ = 4, Q₃ = 10, IQR = 6.|Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 30, so IQR = 10 and the limits are 5 and 45: a value of 52 is an outlier.|Cumulative frequency is plotted at upper class boundaries; read the median at n / 2.|[H] 2, 4, 6: mean 4, Σx^2 = 56, σ = √(56 / 3 − 16) ≈ 1.63.

title: Comparing data and skewness
words: Skewness — how lopsided a distribution is|Positive skew — the tail is to the right; usually mode < median < mean|Negative skew — the tail is to the left; usually mean < median < mode|Symmetrical — the mean, median and mode are about equal|[H] Standardised score — how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean
formulas: [H] Skewness — skew = 3(mean − median) / (standard deviation)|[H] Standardised score — z = (value − mean) / (standard deviation)
points: Compare an average AND a spread, in context: "A's median, 62, is higher than B's, 55, so A did better on average; A's IQR is smaller, so A was more consistent."|From a box plot: if Q₃ − Q₂ is bigger than Q₂ − Q₁, the data is positively skewed.|[H] Mean 50, median 47, standard deviation 6: skew = 3 × 3 ÷ 6 = 1.5, positive.|[H] Maths 72 with mean 60 and SD 8 gives z = 1.5; English 70 with mean 64 and SD 3 gives z = 2, so English is relatively better.

title: Correlation
words: Scatter diagram — bivariate data plotted as points|Positive correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to increase|Negative correlation — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease|No correlation — no straight-line relationship between the two|Causation — a change in one variable directly causes a change in the other; correlation alone does not show it|Line of best fit — a straight line through the middle of the points, passing through the mean point (x̄, ȳ)|Interpolation — estimating inside the range of the data; fairly reliable|Extrapolation — estimating outside the range of the data; unreliable|[H] Spearman's rank correlation coefficient — how closely two rankings agree, from −1 to +1|[H] Product moment correlation coefficient — the strength of a straight-line correlation, from −1 to +1
formulas: [H] Line of best fit — y = a + bx, where b is the gradient and a the intercept|[H] Spearman's rank — rₛ = 1 − 6Σd^2 / (n(n^2 − 1))
points: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer: correlated, but hot weather causes both.|Draw the line through (x̄, ȳ) first, and use it only inside the range of the data.|[H] Marks y = 12 + 0.5x for x hours of revision: each extra hour is worth about half a mark.|[H] n = 5 and Σd^2 = 4: rₛ = 1 − (6 × 4) / (5 × 24) = 0.8, strong positive agreement.

title: Time series
words: Time series — data recorded at regular intervals over time|Trend — the general direction over a long time|Seasonal variation — a pattern that repeats every year, quarter or week|Moving average — the mean of a fixed number of consecutive values, moved along one at a time; it smooths out the seasons|Trend line — a line of best fit drawn through the moving averages|[H] Mean seasonal variation — the average gap between the actual values and the trend for one season
formulas: 4-point moving average — (sum of 4 consecutive values) / 4|Seasonal variation — seasonal variation = actual value − trend value|[H] Prediction — prediction = trend value + mean seasonal variation
points: Quarterly sales 20, 30, 40, 50, 60: the first 4-point moving average is 140 ÷ 4 = 35, the next 180 ÷ 4 = 45.|Plot each moving average at the middle of the values it uses.|Match the moving average to the cycle: 4 points for quarters, 12 for months.|[H] The trend line reads 80 next spring and spring's mean seasonal variation is −6, so predict 74.

title: Index numbers and rates
words: Index number — compares a value with the value in a base year, which is set at 100|Base year — the year all the others are compared with|[H] Chain base index — compares each year with the year before it|Weighted index — several index numbers combined, each weighted by how much it matters|RPI and CPI — official index numbers that track how prices change|Crude rate — the number of events for every 1000 people in the population|[H] Standardised rate — a rate adjusted to a standard population's age structure, so places can be compared fairly
formulas: Index number — index = value / (base year value) × 100|[H] Chain base index — index = (this year's value) / (last year's value) × 100|Weighted index — weighted index = Σ(index × weight) / Σweight|Crude rate — crude rate = (number of events) / population × 1000|[H] Standardised rate — standardised rate = Σ(rate for an age group × standard population fraction for that group)
points: £40 in the base year and £46 now: index = 46 / 40 × 100 = 115, a 15% rise.|An index of 120 is not £120; it means 20% more than in the base year.|60 births in a town of 4000: crude birth rate = 60 / 4000 × 1000 = 15 per 1000.|[H] Chain base 105 then 110: the second year rose 10%, and over both years 1.05 × 1.10 = 1.155, a 15.5% rise.|[H] A seaside town full of retired people has a high crude death rate; compare standardised rates instead.

title: Estimation and quality assurance
words: Estimate — a value for the population worked out from a sample|Sample mean — the mean of a sample, used to estimate the population mean|Sample proportion — the fraction of a sample with some property, used to estimate the population proportion|Reliability — bigger random samples give estimates that vary less|Control chart — sample results from a process plotted over time, with a target value and limits|Warning limits — a sample outside them means take another sample|Action limits — a sample outside them means stop and adjust the process
formulas: Estimating a population total — total ≈ sample proportion × population size|[H] Control limits — warning: target ± 2 standard deviations; action: target ± 3 standard deviations
points: 12 of a sample of 50 are left-handed: in a school of 1200, expect about 12 / 50 × 1200 = 288.|A machine fills 500 g bags; sample means 497 g, 502 g and 499 g stay inside the warning limits, so carry on.|One sample mean outside an action limit: stop the machine and reset it.|Two samples of the same size give different means; that is natural variation, and it shrinks as samples get bigger.

title: Probability
topics: Basic Probability, Listing Outcomes & Sample Space, Relative Frequency & Expectation, Venn Diagrams & Set Notation, Tree Diagrams, Conditional Probability
words: Outcome — one possible result of an experiment|Event — one or more outcomes, such as "an even number"|Sample space — the list of every possible outcome|Mutually exclusive — two events that cannot happen at the same time|Independent — the outcome of one event does not change the probability of the other|Relative frequency — how often an event happened, as a fraction of the trials; an estimate of the probability|Expected frequency — how many times an event should happen in a number of trials|Venn diagram — overlapping circles showing which outcomes are in which events|[H] Conditional probability — the probability of one event given that another has happened

title: GCSE English Language
summary: The whole GCSE in twelve short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE English Language (8700) papers, then Spoken Language and technical accuracy.
subject: English Language

title: Retrieving information
words: Paper 1 Question 1 — 4 marks: four things from a named part of the fiction source, one mark each|Retrieval — finding information in the text and writing it down, quoted or in your own words|Explicit information — stated directly in the text, so it can be found and copied|Implicit information — suggested rather than stated, so the reader has to work it out|Inference — a sensible conclusion drawn from clues in the text|Paraphrase — the writer's point put into your own words without changing its meaning|AO1 — finding and interpreting explicit and implicit information, and bringing together evidence from different texts
points: From "the kitchen was cold and a single bulb swung over the bare table": the kitchen is cold, it has one bulb, the bulb swings, the table is bare.|One point per line, each a short sentence: "The kitchen is cold." Four separate, correct points earn all 4 marks.|Quoting earns the mark too: "the old man's hands shook" is as good as "his hands are shaking".|Take all four from the lines named, and about the subject named: if the question asks about the boy, a fact about the weather will not do.

title: Analysing language
words: Paper 1 Question 2 — 8 marks: how the writer uses language in a named part of the source|Simile — a comparison using "like" or "as"|Metaphor — a comparison that says one thing is another|Personification — giving human qualities or actions to something that is not human|Pathetic fallacy — weather or surroundings that reflect a character's feelings or the mood|Connotation — an idea or feeling a word suggests beyond its literal meaning|Semantic field — a group of words linked by one topic, such as war or illness
points: The fog "crawled" through the streets: the verb personifies it as something alive and hunting, which makes the town feel under threat.|The metaphor "the sea was a sheet of grey iron" suggests it is hard, flat and cold, so the scene feels harsh and lifeless.|"Shattered" connotes something broken beyond repair, so her hopes seem gone for good, not just damaged.|The sky is "bruised", the sunset "bleeding" and the hills "scarred": a semantic field of injury makes the land itself seem hurt.|The minor sentence "Silence." stops the reader dead, just as the noise in the story stops.

title: Analysing structure
words: Paper 1 Question 3 — 8 marks: how the whole source is structured to interest the reader|Structure — how the whole text is ordered, and how its focus moves from beginning to end|Shift in focus — a move from one place, person, time or idea to another|Zooming in — the focus narrows from a wide view to one small detail, like a camera|Flashback — a scene from an earlier time that interrupts the present story|Foreshadowing — an early hint of something that happens later|Cyclical structure — the ending returns to a place, image or idea from the opening
points: The extract opens on a wide view of the empty beach, then zooms in on a single footprint, which raises a question the reader wants answered.|Halfway through, the focus shifts from the storm outside to her memory of her father, which slows the pace and builds sympathy.|A one-line paragraph, "Nobody came.", follows a long description, so the moment stands alone, just as she does.|Ending back at the station clock where it began creates a cyclical structure: nothing has changed for her, so she seems trapped.

title: Evaluating a text
words: Paper 1 Question 4 — 20 marks: how far you agree with a statement about a named part of the source, usually the second half|Evaluate — judge how successfully the writer creates an effect, backed by evidence|Statement — the view about the text given in the question, which you weigh up|Interpretation — your own reading of what a part of the text means or suggests|Writer's methods — the choices of language and structure that create an effect|Embedded quotation — a short quotation built into your own sentence|Reader response — the impression or feeling the text leaves the reader with
points: I largely agree the house feels threatening: "the windows stared" personifies it, as if it is watching her every move.|I only partly agree that the opening is calm: the word "waiting" hints at danger, so the peace feels uneasy.|The short sentences speed up the pace, which supports the view that the chase is exciting as well as frightening.|Embedded: the narrator feels "tiny" beside the mountains, which shows how powerless he is against nature.

title: Descriptive and narrative writing
words: Paper 1 Question 5 — 40 marks: one piece of descriptive or narrative writing, chosen from two tasks|Descriptive writing — creates a vivid picture of a place, person or moment, with little or no plot|Narrative writing — tells a story, with characters, events and a clear shape|Narrative perspective — who tells the story: first person uses I, third person uses he, she or they|Show, don't tell — revealing feelings through actions and details instead of naming them|Content and organisation — 24 of the 40 marks, for ideas, tone, style and how the writing is shaped and paragraphed|Technical accuracy — 16 of the 40 marks, for sentence variety, punctuation, spelling and range of vocabulary
points: Show, don't tell: not "Sam was nervous" but "Sam folded the ticket into smaller and smaller squares."|Open with a sense other than sight: "The smell of wet tarmac and diesel reached the platform before the train did."|Vary sentence openings: "Silently, the snow settled. Across the valley, a single light flickered on."|Plan a story in five steps: a calm opening, a problem, rising tension, a turning point, and an ending that echoes the start.|End a description where it began: the same café sign, now lit up in the dark, shows that time has passed.

title: True statements and summaries
words: Paper 2 Questions 1 and 2 — 4 marks for picking true statements, 8 marks for a summary using both sources|True statement — Question 1 lists eight statements about a named part of one source, and you choose the four that are true|Summary — the main points in brief; here, the differences or similarities between the two sources|Synthesise — bring together details from both sources into one answer|Comparative connective — a word or phrase that links or contrasts, such as "whereas", "similarly" or "however"|Literary non-fiction — true writing shaped with storytelling techniques, such as a memoir, diary or travel writing|19th-century source — Paper 2 pairs a source from the 19th century with one from the 20th or 21st century
points: A statement that adds a detail the named lines never give is false, however likely it sounds: check each one against the text.|In Source A the children are "eager" to reach school, whereas in Source B the boy dreads it, which suggests he feels trapped there.|Both writers cross the sea, but the 1880s traveller finds the voyage terrifying, whereas the modern one finds it dull.|The summary is about content: say what the details suggest about the people or places, not which techniques the writers use.

title: Non-fiction language and viewpoints
words: Paper 2 Questions 3 and 4 — 12 marks on language in one source, 16 marks comparing both writers' viewpoints and how they are conveyed|Viewpoint — the writer's opinion or attitude towards a topic|Perspective — the writer's way of seeing a topic, shaped by their time, place and experience|Tone — the writer's attitude shown in the voice of the text, such as angry, mocking or warm|Rhetorical question — a question asked for effect, with no answer expected|Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration for effect|Direct address — speaking to the reader as "you"
points: The writer calls the new road "a grey scar": the metaphor makes it an injury to the countryside and shows her anger at it.|Both writers dislike the city, but the Victorian writer is shocked by its dirt, whereas the modern writer mocks its noise with gentle humour.|Compare methods too: Source A piles up a list of horrors to shock, while Source B uses a calm personal anecdote to win the reader round.|Track the tone: writer B begins amused, turns serious, and ends hopeful, so her viewpoint develops as she writes.

title: Writing to present a viewpoint
words: Paper 2 Question 5 — 40 marks: writing in a set form to give your viewpoint on a statement|Audience — who the text is for, which decides how formal it should be|Form — the type of text asked for, such as a letter, article, speech, essay or leaflet|Counter-argument — an opposing view, raised so that it can be answered|Discourse markers — words that guide the reader through an argument, such as "firstly", "however" and "therefore"|Anecdote — a short personal story used to make a point|Rule of three — a list of three words or ideas, used for emphasis
points: Letter: "Dear Sir or Madam" ends "Yours faithfully"; a named person, "Dear Mr Hall", ends "Yours sincerely".|Counter-argument: "Some say cars give us freedom; however, there is little freedom in the same traffic jam every morning."|Rhetorical question and direct address: "Would you let a stranger read your diary? Then why let an app read your messages?"|Rule of three: "Our parks are free, green and open to everyone, so why are we selling them?"|Article: a headline, a strapline and subheadings. Speech: greet the audience at the start and thank them at the end.

title: Spoken Language
words: Spoken Language endorsement — a separate grade of Pass, Merit or Distinction, reported apart from the 9 to 1 grade|Presentation — a prepared talk on one topic, given to an audience in a formal setting|Questions and feedback — the audience's questions and comments after the talk, which the speaker listens and responds to|Standard English — the grammar and vocabulary accepted as correct in formal English, not tied to one region|Dialect — a regional or social variety of English with its own words and grammar|Non-verbal communication — eye contact, gesture and posture that support what is said
points: Standard English: "we were" not "we was"; "I did it" not "I done it"; "those books" not "them books".|Open with a hook: "Hands up if you checked your phone before you got out of bed this morning."|Signpost the talk: "I have three reasons. First, the cost. Second, the time it saves. Finally, the effect on wildlife."|Answer a question by showing you listened: "That's a fair point about the cost, but I still think it is worth it, because it pays for itself."

title: Sentences and grammar
words: Simple sentence — one main clause, with a subject and a verb|Compound sentence — two or more main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as "and", "but" or "so"|Complex sentence — a main clause with at least one subordinate clause|Subordinate clause — a clause that cannot stand alone, often starting with "because", "although" or "when"|Relative clause — a subordinate clause starting with a word such as "who", "which" or "that", adding detail about a noun|Passive voice — the subject has the action done to it, as in "The window was broken."|Tense — the form of a verb that shows when something happens
points: Simple: "The door opened." Compound: "The door opened and the cold rushed in." Complex: "As the door opened, the cold rushed in."|A relative clause adds detail mid-sentence: "My uncle, who never smiled, laughed until he cried."|Passive hides who did it: "Mistakes were made." Active names them: "The council made mistakes."|Keep the tense steady: not "She opens the door and saw him" but "She opened the door and saw him."|Agreement: "The box of apples is heavy", because the subject is box, not apples, so the verb is singular.

title: Punctuation
words: Comma — separates items in a list and marks off clauses and extra information|Semicolon — joins two closely linked main clauses, or separates long items in a list|Colon — after a complete main clause, introduces a list, an explanation or an example|Apostrophe — shows where letters are missed out, as in "don't", or possession, as in "the dog's lead"|Parenthesis — extra information in a pair of brackets, dashes or commas; the sentence still makes sense without it|Comma splice — two main clauses wrongly joined by a comma alone|Inverted commas — mark the exact words spoken, with the speech's own punctuation inside them
points: Comma splice fixed: "It was late, so we ran home." or "It was late; we ran home." or two separate sentences.|One girl's coat, two girls' coats, the children's coats. "Its" means belonging to it; "it's" means it is or it has.|Speech: "Wait," said Sam, "I'm coming too." A new speaker starts a new line.|Colon: "She had one aim: to win." Semicolon: "He trained every day; his brother never trained at all."|Parenthesis: "The house (empty for years) was finally sold." or "The house, empty for years, was finally sold."

title: Spelling and vocabulary
words: Homophones — words that sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning, such as "there", "their" and "they're"|Prefix — letters added to the start of a word to change its meaning, such as "un-" or "mis-"|Suffix — letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or word class, such as "-ful", "-ly" or "-tion"|Synonym — a word with the same or nearly the same meaning as another|Antonym — a word with the opposite meaning|Register — the level of formality, chosen to suit the audience and purpose|Precise vocabulary — the exact word for the meaning, such as "trudged" instead of "walked slowly"
points: Homophones in one line: "They're leaving their bags over there."|A prefix keeps every letter of the root: dis + satisfied = dissatisfied, mis + spell = misspell, un + necessary = unnecessary.|Affect is usually the verb and effect the noun: "The rain affected the match; the effect was a muddy pitch."|Formal register: not "loads of kids skip lunch" but "a large number of students miss lunch".|Often misspelt: definitely, separate, necessary, embarrass, accommodation, rhythm, government, beginning.

title: GCSE English Literature
summary: The GCSE in eleven short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each for the most-taught set texts and the Love and Relationships and Power and Conflict poems, in the order of the AQA GCSE English Literature (8702) specification.
subject: English Literature

title: How the exam works
words: AO1 — a personal, informed response to the text, argued clearly and backed by quotations and references|AO2 — how the writer's choices of words, form and structure shape meaning, explained with the right technical terms|AO3 — the links between the text and the context it was written in|AO4 — spelling, punctuation, grammar and a range of vocabulary; 4 marks each on the Shakespeare and modern text questions|Closed book — no copies of the texts are allowed in the exam, so quotations must be learned|Thesis — the one-line argument that answers the question, which every paragraph then supports|Context — the time, place and beliefs a text was written in, used to explain the writer's choices
points: Paper 1, 1 hour 45 minutes, 64 marks, 40%: Shakespeare, extract then whole play, 30 + 4 for AO4; the 19th-century novel, extract then whole novel, 30.|Paper 2, 2 hours 15 minutes, 96 marks, 60%: modern text, 30 + 4 for AO4; compare two anthology poems, 30; unseen poems, 24 + 8.|Thesis: "Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that destroys Macbeth's conscience, his marriage and finally his life."|Embed short quotations: Scrooge is a "squeezing, wrenching, grasping" old sinner, and the list of harsh words makes his greed feel violent.|Context explains a choice: Dickens, who worked in a factory at twelve, shows the Cratchits' poverty to shame readers like Scrooge.

title: Macbeth
words: Ambition — the drive for power that leads Macbeth to murder Duncan, then keep killing to stay king|Tragic hero — a noble figure brought down by a fatal flaw, here Macbeth's ambition|Regicide — killing a king, seen in Jacobean times as a sin against God and the natural order|Divine Right of Kings — the belief that a monarch is chosen by God and answers only to God|Equivocation — misleading by saying something with two meanings, as the witches' prophecies do|The supernatural — the witches, the dagger and Banquo's ghost, which a Jacobean audience took seriously
points: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair" (1.1): the witches' paradox warns that in this play appearances cannot be trusted.|"Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself" (1.7): Macbeth pictures a rider leaping too far and falling, which foreshadows his own fall.|Lady Macbeth's "unsex me here" (1.5) rejects the gentleness expected of a woman, which would have shocked a Jacobean audience.|"A little water clears us of this deed" (2.2) becomes "Out, damned spot!" (5.1): the guilt she brushed aside now drives her mad.|Written about 1606 for James I, who wrote a book on witchcraft and claimed descent from Banquo: the witches are evil and Banquo is noble.

title: Romeo and Juliet
words: Prologue — a sonnet spoken by the Chorus that tells the audience at the start that the lovers will die|Fate — the idea that events are fixed in advance; the lovers are "star-cross'd", doomed by the stars|Feud — the "ancient grudge" between the Montagues and the Capulets that drives the violence|Patriarchy — a society ruled by men; Capulet expects Juliet to obey him and marry Paris|Dramatic irony — the audience knows more than a character, as when Romeo believes Juliet is dead|Courtly love — worship of a distant, unreachable woman, as in Romeo's love for Rosaline
points: "A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life" (Prologue): the audience knows the ending, so every hopeful moment is full of dramatic irony.|Their first 14 lines together (1.5) form a shared sonnet, a traditional form for love poetry, so they seem made for each other from the start.|"Juliet is the sun" (2.2): the metaphor makes her the centre of Romeo's world, unlike the distant Rosaline.|"A plague o' both your houses!" (3.1): Mercutio's dying curse marks the turn from comedy to tragedy.|Capulet tells Juliet to "hang, beg, starve, die in the streets" (3.5) if she refuses Paris: a father's total power over his daughter.

title: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
words: Duality — the idea that every person has a good side and an evil side|Reputation — a gentleman's good name, which Jekyll, Utterson and Enfield all guard closely|Repression — hiding desires that society forbids; Jekyll creates Hyde to indulge his in secret|Gothic — a genre of mystery, horror and darkness, seen in the fog, the locked doors and the violence at night|Atavism — a throwback to a more primitive form; Hyde's ape-like behaviour reflects fears raised by Darwin|Epistolary — told through letters and documents, as the last two chapters are
points: Hyde "trampled calmly over the child's body" (Chapter 1): the adverb "calmly" shows he has no conscience at all.|Hyde kills Carew "with ape-like fury" (Chapter 4): the animal imagery suggests atavism, a fear sharpened by Darwin's theory of evolution.|Jekyll writes that "man is not truly one, but truly two" (Chapter 10): his own statement sums up the duality at the heart of the novella.|Hyde uses a shabby back door into Jekyll's laboratory, behind the grand house: the building mirrors a respectable front with a secret life at the back.|Published in 1886 and told mostly through Utterson, a reserved lawyer, so the truth is held back until Lanyon's and Jekyll's documents at the end.

title: A Christmas Carol
words: Stave — Dickens's name for each of the five chapters, like the verses of a carol|Redemption — being saved from sin; Scrooge changes from a miser into a generous man|Social responsibility — the duty to care for those less fortunate, the novella's central message|Ignorance and Want — two wretched children hidden under the robe of the Ghost of Christmas Present, a warning to society|Workhouse — where the poor were sent to live and work in harsh conditions under the Poor Law of 1834|Thomas Malthus — an economist who argued population would outgrow food; Scrooge echoes him on the "surplus population"
points: Scrooge is "solitary as an oyster" (Stave 1): hard and shut tight outside, though an oyster can hide a pearl, a hint that he can change.|Scrooge asks "Are there no prisons?" (Stave 1); in Stave 3 the Ghost of Christmas Present throws his own words back at him beside Ignorance and Want.|Scrooge says the poor should "decrease the surplus population"; in Stave 3 the Ghost says it of Tiny Tim, and Scrooge is ashamed.|"I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year" (Stave 4): his change is for life, not for one day.|He became "as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man" (Stave 5): the tricolon shows his redemption is complete.

title: An Inspector Calls
words: Social responsibility — the idea that we are all responsible for one another, the Inspector's message|Capitalism — an economic system run for private profit, which Mr Birling stands for|Socialism — the belief that wealth and welfare should be shared, which Priestley supported|Dramatic irony — the audience knows more than a character, as with Birling's confident predictions|Cyclical structure — the play ends with a phone call: a girl has died and an inspector is on his way, so the night will repeat|Generational divide — the older Birlings refuse to change, while Sheila and Eric accept their part in Eva's death
points: Birling calls the Titanic "unsinkable" and laughs off talk of war: a post-war audience knows he is wrong, so they doubt all he says.|The lighting is "pink and intimate" until the Inspector arrives, then harsher: the family's cosy comfort gives way to scrutiny.|Birling sacks Eva, Sheila gets her dismissed, Gerald keeps then leaves her, Eric gets her pregnant and Mrs Birling refuses her help.|Sheila and Eric accept the blame while their parents and Gerald do not: Priestley pins his hope for change on the young.|Written in 1945 and set in 1912: the Inspector's warning of "fire and blood" points to the two world wars the audience had lived through.

title: Blood Brothers
words: Social class — the main theme: twins get very different lives because one grows up rich and one poor|Nature versus nurture — the debate over whether birth or upbringing shapes a person; the twins share their genes but not their chances|Superstition — Mrs Lyons invents the belief that the twins will die if they learn the truth, and it comes true|Narrator — a figure who comments on the action, like a Greek chorus, and keeps fate in view|Foreshadowing — hints of what is to come; the play opens with the twins' deaths|Motif — a repeated image or idea, such as Marilyn Monroe, glamorous at first and tragic later
points: Twins separated at birth: Mickey grows up poor with Mrs Johnstone, Eddie rich with Mrs Lyons, so class, not character, shapes their futures.|The play opens on the twins' bodies, so the audience watches asking why it happens, not what happens: the tragedy feels inevitable.|At seven, Mickey and Eddie become blood brothers, not knowing they are already brothers by blood: dramatic irony.|Mickey loses his factory job and is drawn into crime while Eddie goes to university: the gap between them grows with their class.|The Narrator's closing lines ask whether superstition or class is to blame: Russell leaves the audience to answer, and points to class.

title: Love and Relationships poems
words: Romantic love — love between partners: Love's Philosophy, Sonnet 29, Winter Swans, Singh Song!|Family love — between parents, children and grandparents: Follower, Walking Away, Before You Were Mine, Eden Rock|Possessive love — wanting to own or control the person loved: Porphyria's Lover, The Farmer's Bride|Separation — love tested by distance or by its ending: When We Two Parted, Neutral Tones, Letters from Yorkshire|Sonnet — a 14-line poem, traditionally about love, as in Sonnet 29|Nostalgia — longing for the past, as in Eden Rock and Before You Were Mine
points: Shelley ends each stanza of Love's Philosophy with a question: if everything in nature mingles, why won't the one he loves?|"Three times her little throat around" (Porphyria's Lover): the steady rhythm and rhyme make the murder more chilling.|When We Two Parted begins "In silence and tears" (line 2) and ends "With silence and tears": the cyclical structure shows grief that has not moved on.|"the sun was white, as though chidden of God" (Neutral Tones): pathetic fallacy drains the scene of warmth, like the dead love.|Pairs: Porphyria's Lover with The Farmer's Bride (possession), Follower with Climbing My Grandfather (admiration), Walking Away with Mother, any distance.

title: Power and Conflict poems
words: Cluster — the 15 linked poems you study; one is printed in the exam and you choose a second to compare|Dramatic monologue — one speaker talks to a silent listener and reveals more than they intend, as in My Last Duchess|Hubris — excessive pride, like the boast in Ozymandias, which time destroys|Power of nature — nature as stronger than people: Storm on the Island, The Prelude, Exposure|Reality of war — the suffering behind the glory: Bayonet Charge, Remains, Exposure, War Photographer|Identity — who a person is and where they belong: Checking Out Me History, The Émigrée, Kamikaze|Comparison — linking the ideas and methods of both poems with words such as "whereas" and "similarly"
points: "Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" (Ozymandias): the boast is ironic, because nothing remains around the statue but empty sand.|"mind-forg'd manacles" (London): Blake's metaphor shows people chained by rules and their own fear, not by iron.|"Then all smiles stopped together" (My Last Duchess): the Duke hints he had his wife killed, in the same calm tone he uses for paintings.|Tennyson repeats "Rode the six hundred" to honour obedient soldiers; Hughes's Bayonet Charge shows one terrified soldier instead.|Pairs: Ozymandias with My Last Duchess (power), Exposure with Storm on the Island (nature), Remains with War Photographer (guilt and memory).

title: Unseen poetry
words: Unseen poem — a poem you have never studied, printed in the exam for you to analyse|First unseen question — 24 marks: how the poet presents an idea in one poem, marked for AO1 and AO2|Comparison question — 8 marks: compare the methods both poets use to present a similar idea, marked for AO2 only|Speaker — the voice in the poem, which may not be the poet|Tone — the attitude the voice shows, such as bitter, tender, playful or angry|Volta — a turn in a poem's argument or mood, often at a "But" or a new stanza
points: "The list of small daily tasks shows how much the mother does without being thanked." Name the method, quote it, give its effect.|"The short, end-stopped lines feel controlled, as if the speaker is holding back tears."|"Both poems show a child leaving home, but the first has calm, regular rhyme, whereas the second's broken lines feel anxious."|A sonnet about loss squeezes grief into a tight, ordered shape; free verse can suggest freedom, or a mind losing control.|The 8-mark answer compares methods, not ideas: one method from each poem, each quoted, and how their effects differ.

title: Literary and poetic terms
words: Iambic pentameter — ten syllables a line in five pairs, each unstressed then stressed|Blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter, spoken by most of Shakespeare's noble characters|Enjambment — a sentence running on past the end of a line without a pause|Caesura — a pause in the middle of a line, usually marked by punctuation|Juxtaposition — two contrasting ideas placed side by side to sharpen the difference|Oxymoron — two opposite words placed together, such as "loving hate"|Semantic field — a group of words linked by one topic, such as war, religion or nature
points: "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?" runs da-DUM five times: iambic pentameter, the rhythm of a heartbeat.|Romeo's oxymorons, "O brawling love! O loving hate!" (1.1), show how confused his feelings for Rosaline are.|Blake repeats "every" five times in one stanza of London: the repetition shows suffering is everywhere in the city.|Lady Macbeth sleepwalks in prose, not verse (5.1): losing the rhythm of verse shows her mind breaking down.|Enfield says Hyde behaved "like Satan" and Utterson sees "Satan's signature" on his face: a semantic field of hell around Hyde.

title: GCSE Biology
summary: The whole GCSE in twelve short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification, Foundation and Higher.
subject: Biology

title: Cells and microscopy
words: Eukaryotic cell — genetic material enclosed in a nucleus; animal and plant cells are eukaryotic|Prokaryotic cell — a bacterial cell: much smaller, no nucleus, DNA in a single loop plus small rings called plasmids|Organelle — a structure inside a cell with a specific job: nucleus (genetic material), mitochondria (aerobic respiration), ribosomes (proteins)|Plant cell extras — chloroplasts, a cellulose cell wall and a permanent vacuole of cell sap|Differentiation — a cell becoming specialised; animal cells mostly do it early, many plant cells throughout life|Resolution — the ability to tell two close points apart; electron microscopes give higher resolution and magnification than light ones|Aseptic technique — sterile working that keeps unwanted microorganisms out of a culture, such as flaming the loop
formulas: Magnification — magnification = (size of image) / (size of real object)|Units — 1 mm = 1000 µm, and 1 µm = 1000 nm|Bacteria after n divisions — number = (starting number) × 2^n|Area of a clear zone — area = π × r^2
points: Image 12 mm wide at ×400: real size = 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 mm = 30 µm.|Microscope practical: lowest-power objective first, coarse then fine focus; draw cells with clear, unshaded lines.|Dividing every 20 minutes for 2 hours is 6 divisions: one bacterium becomes 2^6 = 64.|Antiseptic practical: a clear zone of radius 6 mm has area π × 6^2 ≈ 113 mm²; the bigger the zone, the better the antiseptic.|School cultures are incubated at 25 °C at most, so pathogens harmful to humans are less likely to grow.

title: Cell division and transport
words: Chromosome — a long, coiled DNA molecule carrying many genes; human body cells have 23 pairs|Mitosis — division into two genetically identical cells, for growth and repair|Stem cell — an undifferentiated cell that can divide and become other cell types; in embryos, bone marrow and plant meristems|Diffusion — net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration; needs no energy from respiration|Osmosis — diffusion of water from a dilute to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane|Active transport — movement against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration|Exchange surface — large surface area, thin membrane; in animals also a good blood supply and ventilation
formulas: Percentage change in mass — % change = (final mass − starting mass) / (starting mass) × 100|Surface area to volume ratio — ratio = (surface area) / volume
points: Potato 2.50 g → 2.30 g in salt solution: (2.30 − 2.50) / 2.50 × 100 = −8%, so it lost water by osmosis.|Plot % change in mass against concentration: where the line crosses 0%, the solution matches the cell contents.|A 1 cm cube has SA : V of 6 : 1, a 2 cm cube only 3 : 1, so large organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems.|Cell cycle: the cell grows and copies its DNA; mitosis pulls one set of chromosomes to each end; the cytoplasm and membrane divide.|Therapeutic cloning: stem cells with the patient's own genes are not rejected, but there are ethical objections and a risk of viral infection.

title: Digestion and enzymes
words: Tissue — cells with a similar structure and function; tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems|Enzyme — a biological catalyst: a protein that speeds up a reaction without being used up|Active site — where the substrate fits, like a lock and key, so each enzyme is specific|Denatured — the active site has changed shape, by high temperature or the wrong pH, so the substrate no longer fits|Digestive enzymes — amylase: starch to sugars; proteases: proteins to amino acids; lipases: lipids to fatty acids and glycerol|Bile — made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder; alkaline, it neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat
formulas: Rate of reaction — rate = (amount of product formed) / time|Rate from the time taken — rate = 1 / time
points: Amylase practical: starch and amylase at a set pH; test a drop on iodine every 30 s until it stays orange-brown.|Starch gone in 60 s at pH 6 and 120 s at pH 8: rates 1/60 ≈ 0.017 and 1/120 ≈ 0.008 per second, so pH 6 is nearer the optimum.|Food tests: iodine goes blue-black with starch; Benedict's, heated, blue to brick red with sugar; biuret goes purple with protein.|Above the optimum, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits: the enzyme is denatured and the rate falls.

title: Heart, blood and health
words: Double circulatory system — the right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, the left to the rest of the body|Pacemaker — cells in the right atrium that set the resting heart rate; an artificial one corrects an irregular beat|Blood vessels — arteries: thick, muscular, elastic walls; veins: thin walls and valves; capillaries: one cell thick|Blood — plasma carrying red blood cells (oxygen), white blood cells (defence) and platelets (clotting)|Alveoli — air sacs in the lungs with a huge surface area and many capillaries, for gas exchange|Coronary heart disease — fatty material narrows the coronary arteries, so the heart muscle gets less oxygen|Risk factor — linked to a higher rate of a disease, such as smoking or obesity; not always a proven cause
formulas: Rate of blood flow — rate = (volume of blood) / time
points: Blood path: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.|3000 ml of blood through an organ in 4 minutes: rate = 3000 ÷ 4 = 750 ml per minute.|Stents hold a narrowed coronary artery open; statins lower blood cholesterol to slow fatty build-up, but can have side effects.|Smoking: lung disease and lung cancer. Obesity: Type 2 diabetes. Alcohol: liver and brain damage, and harm to an unborn baby.|Benign tumours stay in one place; malignant tumours are cancers that invade tissue and spread in the blood.

title: Plant tissues and transport
words: Palisade mesophyll — leaf tissue packed with chloroplasts, where most photosynthesis happens|Spongy mesophyll — loosely packed cells with air spaces for gas exchange|Stomata — pores, mostly under the leaf, for carbon dioxide in and water vapour out; guard cells open and close them|Xylem — hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, carrying water and mineral ions up from the roots|Phloem — elongated cells with pores in the end walls, carrying dissolved sugars|Transpiration — loss of water vapour from the leaves, drawing water up the xylem|Translocation — movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem to where they are used or stored
formulas: Rate of water uptake — rate = (volume of water taken up) / time|Volume from a potometer — volume = (distance the bubble moves) × π × r^2
points: Bubble moves 30 mm in 5 minutes in a tube of radius 0.5 mm: 30 × π × 0.5^2 ≈ 23.6 mm³, about 4.7 mm³ per minute.|Transpiration is faster when it is warmer, drier, windier or brighter: bright light opens more stomata.|A potometer measures water taken up, not lost: a little is used in photosynthesis or kept in the cells.|Root hair cells have a large surface area for taking in water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.|Meristems at shoot and root tips hold stem cells, so a plant can grow all its life.

title: Infection and response
words: Pathogen — a microorganism that causes infectious disease: a virus, bacterium, protist or fungus|Communicable disease — one that spreads between organisms, by air, water or direct contact|Non-specific defences — skin, nose hairs, mucus and cilia in the airways, and stomach acid|White blood cells — engulf pathogens (phagocytosis), make antibodies specific to one pathogen, and make antitoxins|Vaccination — a dead or inactive pathogen is injected; white blood cells make antibodies, so they respond fast to the live one|Antibiotic — a medicine such as penicillin that kills bacteria in the body, but not viruses; painkillers only ease symptoms|[H] Monoclonal antibodies — identical antibodies from a hybridoma: a mouse lymphocyte fused with a tumour cell
points: Viruses: measles, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus. Bacteria: salmonella, gonorrhoea. Fungus: rose black spot. Protist: malaria, spread by mosquitoes.|Spread is cut by hygiene, isolation, destroying vectors and vaccination; if most people are immune, a pathogen can hardly spread.|Drug testing: cells, tissues and animals first; then clinical trials, low doses on healthy volunteers, then patients, double-blind.|[H] Each monoclonal antibody binds one protein, so they are used in pregnancy tests and to carry drugs straight to cancer cells.|Plant defences: cellulose walls, waxy cuticle, bark; antibacterial chemicals and poisons; thorns, hairs and leaves that droop when touched.

title: Photosynthesis and respiration
words: Photosynthesis — endothermic: chloroplasts use light energy to make glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water|Limiting factor — the factor in shortest supply, which holds back the rate: light intensity, carbon dioxide, temperature or chlorophyll|Uses of glucose — respiration, starch, cellulose, fats and oils, and amino acids made with nitrate ions|Aerobic respiration — exothermic, in mitochondria: transfers energy from glucose using oxygen|Anaerobic respiration — no oxygen: muscles make lactic acid; plants and yeast make ethanol and carbon dioxide|Metabolism — the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body|[H] Oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with lactic acid and remove it from the cells
formulas: Photosynthesis — 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂|Aerobic respiration — C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O|Rate of photosynthesis — rate = (volume of oxygen) / time|[H] Inverse square law — light intensity ∝ 1 / d^2, where d is the distance from the lamp
points: Pondweed practical: lamp at 10, 20 and 30 cm; count oxygen bubbles per minute; a water tank in between keeps the temperature steady.|24 cm³ of oxygen in 4 minutes: rate = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm³ per minute.|[H] Lamp moved from 10 cm to 20 cm: the distance doubles, so the light intensity falls to 1/4.|In exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume rise; without enough oxygen, muscles respire anaerobically and tire.|[H] After exercise, blood carries lactic acid to the liver, which converts it back into glucose.

title: Nerves, brain and eye
words: Homeostasis — keeping internal conditions, such as temperature and blood glucose, at the best level for cells|Receptor — cells that detect a stimulus, a change in the environment|Effector — a muscle or gland that brings about a response|Synapse — the gap between two neurones, crossed by a chemical that diffuses over|Reflex — an automatic, rapid response that does not involve the conscious part of the brain|Accommodation — the ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens to focus near or far|Thermoregulatory centre — the part of the brain that monitors blood temperature and keeps it near 37 °C
formulas: Mean reaction time — mean = (sum of the results) / (number of results)
points: Reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response.|Ruler-drop practical: catches at 12, 10 and 11 cm give a mean of 33 ÷ 3 = 11 cm; a shorter catch is a faster reaction.|Cerebral cortex: memory, language, consciousness. Cerebellum: muscle coordination. Medulla: unconscious acts, such as breathing.|Short sight: the image forms in front of the retina; a concave lens corrects it. Long sight: behind the retina; a convex lens.|Too hot: sweating and vasodilation. Too cold: vasoconstriction and shivering, which releases heat by respiration.

title: Hormones
words: Endocrine system — glands that secrete hormones into the blood, to act on target organs; the pituitary is the master gland|Insulin — from the pancreas when blood glucose is high; glucose enters cells, and liver and muscle store it as glycogen|[H] Glucagon — from the pancreas when blood glucose is low; the liver turns glycogen back into glucose|Diabetes — Type 1: too little insulin is made, so it is injected; Type 2: body cells stop responding to it, so a carbohydrate-controlled diet and exercise|Kidneys — filter the blood and reabsorb what the body needs; excess water, ions and urea leave in the urine|Menstrual cycle — FSH matures an egg, LH releases it, oestrogen and progesterone build and keep the uterus lining|[H] Adrenaline and thyroxine — adrenaline raises heart rate for fight or flight; thyroxine raises metabolic rate, its level kept by negative feedback
points: [H] Dehydrated: more ADH from the pituitary, so the kidney tubules return more water to the blood and the urine is more concentrated.|Contraception: the pill's hormones stop FSH, so no egg matures; condoms and diaphragms block sperm, and condoms also protect against STIs.|[H] IVF: FSH and LH mature several eggs; they are fertilised in a lab and one or two embryos put in the uterus. Success rates are low.|Seedling practical: shoots lit from one side bend towards the light, as auxin gathers on the shaded side and speeds growth there.|[H] Auxins: weedkillers and rooting powders. Ethene: ripens stored fruit. Gibberellins: end seed dormancy, increase fruit size.

title: Reproduction and inheritance
words: Asexual reproduction — one parent and mitosis, no gametes, so the offspring are identical clones|Meiosis — division that makes four genetically different gametes, each with half the number of chromosomes|DNA — a polymer of two strands in a double helix; an organism's whole genetic material is its genome|Gene — a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein; each three bases code for one amino acid|Allele — a version of a gene; a dominant one shows with one copy, a recessive one only with two|Genotype — the alleles present, such as Bb; the phenotype is the characteristic they produce|Homozygous — two identical alleles, BB or bb; heterozygous means two different alleles, Bb
points: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb: a 3 : 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype, so P(bb) = 1/4.|Cystic fibrosis is recessive: carriers Ff × Ff have a 1/4 chance of an affected child. Polydactyly is dominant: one allele is enough.|Mother XX × father XY gives two XX and two XY, so each child has a 1/2 chance of being a boy.|Asexual: strawberry runners, daffodil bulbs. Fungi and the malaria parasite reproduce both ways. Sexual reproduction gives variation.|[H] A mutation changes the base sequence, so the amino acid order and the protein's shape change: an enzyme's active site may no longer fit.

title: Variation and evolution
words: Variation — differences between individuals, caused by genes, the environment or both|Mutation — a change in DNA; most have no effect on the phenotype, and very rarely one gives an advantage|Natural selection — the individuals best suited to their environment survive, breed and pass on their alleles|Selective breeding — humans breed parents with a wanted characteristic over many generations; it risks inbreeding|Genetic engineering — adding a gene from another organism, such as the human insulin gene into bacteria|Speciation — isolated populations change until they can no longer interbreed to give fertile offspring|Classification — kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; Woese added three domains: archaea, bacteria, eukaryota
points: A mutation lets one bacterium survive an antibiotic; it multiplies and the resistant strain spreads, as with MRSA.|Fossils: remains that did not decay, parts replaced by minerals, or traces like footprints. Soft bodies rarely fossilise, so there are gaps.|[H] Genetic engineering: enzymes cut out the gene; it is put into a vector, a bacterial plasmid or a virus, which carries it into the cells.|Adult cell cloning: an egg's nucleus is replaced by one from an adult body cell; an electric shock starts division; the embryo is implanted.|Darwin's theory was accepted slowly: it challenged the idea that God made all living things, and inheritance was not yet understood.

title: Ecology
words: Community — the populations of all the species in a habitat, which depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination|Abiotic and biotic factors — non-living: light, temperature, water, soil pH; living: food, predators, pathogens, competition|Adaptation — a structural, behavioural or functional feature that aids survival; extremophiles live in extreme heat, salt or pressure|Decomposer — bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter, returning carbon dioxide to the air and mineral ions to the soil|Biodiversity — the variety of species in an ecosystem or on Earth; high biodiversity makes an ecosystem stable|Trophic level — a feeding level in a food chain; only about 10% of the biomass passes to the next|Food security — enough food for a population; threatened by population growth, pests, climate change and conflict
formulas: Efficiency of biomass transfer — efficiency = (biomass at the higher level) / (biomass at the lower level) × 100|Population size — population ≈ (mean number per quadrat) × (total area) / (area of one quadrat)|Rate of decay — rate = (change in pH) / time
points: Ten 0.25 m² quadrats find 30 daisies, a mean of 3: a 100 m² field holds about 3 × 100 / 0.25 = 1200.|Grass 1000 kg, rabbits 100 kg: efficiency = 100 / 1000 × 100 = 10%; the rest is lost in faeces, urine and respiration.|Decay practical: lipase turns milk fat into fatty acids, so the pH falls; a fall of 2.0 in 10 minutes is 2.0 / 10 = 0.2 pH units per minute.|Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air; respiration, decay and burning return it. Deforestation cuts its uptake and biodiversity.|Fishing quotas and nets with a bigger mesh let young fish breed; mycoprotein, from the fungus Fusarium, is a protein-rich meat substitute.

title: GCSE Chemistry
summary: The whole GCSE in twelve short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE (9–1) Chemistry specification, Foundation and Higher.
subject: Chemistry

title: Atoms, isotopes and mixtures
topics: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table, Separating Mixtures
words: Element — a substance made of only one sort of atom|Compound — two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions|Mixture — substances not chemically combined, separated by physical methods such as filtration, distillation or chromatography|Atomic number — the number of protons in an atom; it decides the element|Mass number — the number of protons plus the number of neutrons in an atom|Isotopes — atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons|Nuclear model — a tiny, positive nucleus with electrons in shells around it; alpha scattering showed the plum pudding model was wrong
formulas: Neutrons — neutrons = mass number − atomic number|Relative atomic mass — Ar = Σ(isotope mass × percentage abundance) / 100
points: Sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23: 11 protons, 11 electrons and 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.|Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37: Ar = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) / 100 = 35.5.|Sodium's 11 electrons are arranged 2,8,1: one outer electron, so Group 1; three shells, so Period 3.|Relative charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1. Equal numbers of protons and electrons make an atom neutral.|Salt from rock salt: stir in water to dissolve the salt, filter off the sand, then heat the filtrate to crystallise the salt.

title: The periodic table
words: Group — a column of the periodic table; its elements have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways|Period — a row of the periodic table; its elements have the same number of electron shells|Metal — an element that forms positive ions; metals sit on the left and towards the bottom|Noble gases — Group 0; unreactive because the outer shell is full; boiling points rise down the group|Alkali metals — Group 1; one outer electron; react with water to give hydrogen; more reactive down the group|Halogens — Group 7; seven outer electrons; molecules of two atoms, such as Cl₂; less reactive and higher boiling points down the group|Transition metals — the central block; harder, denser and less reactive than Group 1; coloured compounds and useful catalysts
points: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂: sodium fizzes, melts into a ball and moves about; the solution left is alkaline.|Down Group 1 the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is attracted less strongly and lost more easily.|Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂: chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces it and the solution turns orange.|Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and swapped some pairs out of atomic weight order; isotopes later explained the swaps.|Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, as transition metal compounds are often coloured; iron is the catalyst in the Haber process.

title: Bonding and structure
words: Ionic bond — the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, made when a metal gives electrons to a non-metal|Covalent bond — a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms|Metallic bonding — positive metal ions held together by a sea of delocalised electrons|Giant ionic lattice — ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions; high melting point; conducts when melted or dissolved|Simple molecule — a few atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, with weak forces between molecules, so low melting and boiling points and no conduction|Giant covalent structure — every atom joined by strong covalent bonds, as in diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide; very high melting point|Nanoparticle — a particle 1 to 100 nm across, with a very large surface area to volume ratio
formulas: Surface area to volume ratio — ratio = (surface area) / volume
points: NaCl: sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron to chlorine (2,8,7), making Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8), both with full outer shells.|Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻ makes MgCl₂: two chloride ions balance each 2+ charge.|Diamond: four covalent bonds per carbon, so hard and no conduction. Graphite: three bonds and one delocalised electron per carbon, so it conducts.|Alloys are harder than pure metals: atoms of different sizes distort the layers, so they cannot slide over each other as easily.|A cube of side 10 nm: 600 ÷ 1000 = 0.6. Side 1 nm: 6 ÷ 1 = 6. Sides ten times smaller, ratio ten times bigger.

title: Quantitative chemistry
words: Conservation of mass — no atoms are lost or made in a reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants|Relative formula mass — Mr, the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula|[H] Mole — the amount of a substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant; its mass in grams equals its Mr|[H] Limiting reactant — the reactant that is used up first, so it decides how much product forms|Concentration — the mass or amount of solute in each dm³ of solution|Percentage yield — the mass of product actually made, as a percentage of the most that could be made|Atom economy — the percentage of the mass of the reactants that ends up in the product you want
formulas: [H] Moles — moles = mass / Mr|Concentration — concentration in g per dm³ = (mass of solute in g) / (volume in dm³)|[H] Concentration in moles — concentration in mol per dm³ = moles / (volume in dm³)|Percentage yield — percentage yield = (mass of product made) / (maximum theoretical mass) × 100|Atom economy — atom economy = (Mr of desired product) / (sum of Mr of all reactants) × 100|[H] Volume of a gas — volume in dm³ = moles × 24, at room temperature and pressure
points: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂: Mr 100 → 56 + 44, so mass is conserved. Wanting CaO, atom economy = 56 / 100 × 100 = 56%.|10 g of salt in 250 cm³, which is 0.25 dm³: concentration = 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40 g per dm³.|[H] 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: 4.8 g of Mg is 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2 mol, so it makes 0.2 mol of MgO = 0.2 × 40 = 8.0 g.|Expected 8.0 g but made 6.0 g: percentage yield = 6.0 / 8.0 × 100 = 75%.|[H] 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol per dm³ HCl neutralises 25.0 cm³ of NaOH: 0.0020 mol each, so NaOH is 0.0020 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.080 mol per dm³.

title: Metals, acids and salts
words: Reactivity series — metals in order of how easily they form positive ions: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper|Oxidation and reduction — oxidation is gain of oxygen and reduction is loss of oxygen|Salt — made when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal: hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates, nitric acid nitrates|Neutralisation — acid + alkali → salt + water; the ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O|pH scale — 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline; acids give H⁺ ions in water and alkalis give OH⁻ ions|[H] Strong acid — completely ionised in water, like hydrochloric acid; a weak acid, like ethanoic acid, is only partly ionised|[H] pH and H⁺ — each fall of one pH unit means ten times the concentration of hydrogen ions
points: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g): metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.|CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide, so it fizzes.|Copper sulfate crystals: add excess copper oxide to warm sulfuric acid, filter off the excess, then crystallise the filtrate.|2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂: carbon is more reactive than copper, so it reduces the oxide and is itself oxidised.|[H] Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu: zinc loses electrons, so it is oxidised; copper ions gain electrons, so they are reduced.

title: Electrolysis
words: Electrolysis — breaking down an ionic compound, molten or dissolved in water, using an electric current|Electrolyte — the molten or dissolved ionic compound, whose ions are free to move and carry the charge|Cathode — the negative electrode; positive ions move to it and gain electrons|Anode — the positive electrode; negative ions move to it and lose electrons|Inert electrode — an electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react with the products|[H] Half equation — shows the electrons gained or lost at one electrode, such as 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻|Cryolite — mixed with aluminium oxide so the electrolyte melts at a lower temperature, saving energy
points: Molten lead bromide: lead forms at the cathode and bromine at the anode.|In water, the cathode gives hydrogen unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, such as copper, which is deposited instead.|At the anode in water: oxygen, unless the solution contains halide ions, which give chlorine, bromine or iodine instead.|Brine, sodium chloride solution: hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide solution left behind.|Aluminium: oxygen forms at the carbon anodes and reacts with them to make carbon dioxide, so the anodes must be replaced.

title: Energy changes
words: Exothermic — transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises: combustion, neutralisation, many oxidation reactions|Endothermic — takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls: thermal decomposition, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate|Activation energy — the minimum energy that particles must have to react when they collide|Reaction profile — a diagram of energy against reaction progress, showing reactants, products and activation energy|[H] Bond energy — the energy needed to break a bond; breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases it|Chemical cell — two different metals in an electrolyte, giving a voltage until one of the reactants is used up|Fuel cell — hydrogen and oxygen react to give a voltage; the only product is water
formulas: [H] Overall energy change — energy change = energy taken in breaking bonds − energy given out making bonds
points: Neutralisation in a polystyrene cup: 19.0 °C to 25.5 °C is a rise of 6.5 °C, so the reaction is exothermic.|Exothermic profile: products below reactants. Endothermic: products above. Activation energy is the hump up from the reactants.|[H] H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl with H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432 kJ per mol: 679 in, 864 out, so −185 kJ per mol, exothermic.|The more two metals differ in reactivity, the bigger the cell's voltage; a non-rechargeable cell stops when a reactant runs out.|[H] Fuel cell, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O overall: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ at one electrode, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O at the other.

title: Rates and equilibrium
words: Rate of reaction — how fast a reactant is used up or a product is made|Collision theory — particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy|Catalyst — speeds up a reaction without being used up, by giving a different pathway with a lower activation energy|Reversible reaction — the products can react to make the reactants again, shown by ⇌|Equilibrium — in a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions go at the same rate, so the amounts stay the same|[H] Le Chatelier's principle — when the conditions change, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract the change
formulas: Mean rate — mean rate = (quantity of reactant used) / time|Mean rate from a product — mean rate = (quantity of product formed) / time|[H] Rate at one moment — rate = gradient of the tangent = (change in y) / (change in x)
points: 60 cm³ of gas in 30 s: mean rate = 60 / 30 = 2 cm³ per s.|Hotter: particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have the activation energy, so the rate increases.|Powder reacts faster than lumps: a larger surface area to volume ratio gives more frequent collisions.|Hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water: blue to white is endothermic; the reverse is exothermic by the same amount.|[H] N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, forward exothermic: higher pressure shifts it right, to fewer gas molecules; higher temperature shifts it left.

title: Organic chemistry
words: Crude oil — a finite mixture of hydrocarbons, compounds of hydrogen and carbon only, formed from ancient plankton buried in mud|Alkane — a saturated hydrocarbon, with only single bonds: methane, ethane, propane, butane|Fractional distillation — crude oil vapour condenses at different heights of a column, giving fractions with different boiling points|Cracking — breaking long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes, over a hot catalyst, or mixed with steam at a very high temperature|Alkene — a hydrocarbon with a C=C double bond; unsaturated, so it turns bromine water from orange to colourless|Functional group — the part of a molecule that decides how it reacts: C=C in alkenes, –OH in alcohols, –COOH in carboxylic acids|Addition polymer — a long chain made when many alkene monomers join as their double bonds open; ethene makes poly(ethene)
formulas: Alkanes — hydrogen atoms = 2 × carbon atoms + 2, as in C₃H₈|Alkenes — hydrogen atoms = 2 × carbon atoms, as in C₃H₆
points: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄: cracking gives a shorter alkane for petrol and ethene to make polymers.|Shorter chains have lower boiling points, are less viscous and catch fire more easily.|Ethanol + ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate + water, with an acid catalyst: an ester. Esters are used in perfumes and flavourings.|[H] Condensation polymer: two different monomers, each with two functional groups, join and usually lose a small molecule such as water at each link.|DNA is two polymer strands of four different nucleotides in a double helix; proteins are polymers of amino acids; starch and cellulose of glucose.

title: Chemical analysis
words: Pure substance — a single element or compound, which melts and boils at one fixed temperature|Formulation — a mixture designed as a useful product, each part in a measured amount, such as a medicine or paint|Chromatography — separates substances by how they spread between a stationary phase, the paper, and a mobile phase, the solvent|Rf value — how far a spot moves divided by how far the solvent moves; between 0 and 1|Flame test — lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green|Precipitate — an insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed|Flame emission spectroscopy — an instrument identifies metal ions from the light they give out and measures their concentration
formulas: Rf value — Rf = (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent)
points: Hydrogen pops with a lighted splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.|A spot moved 3.0 cm while the solvent moved 7.5 cm: Rf = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40.|Sodium hydroxide gives Cu²⁺ a blue precipitate, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ brown; Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ white, and only aluminium's dissolves in excess.|Dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: chloride white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. Dilute HCl then barium chloride: sulfate white.|Carbonate: add dilute acid; it fizzes, and the gas turns limewater milky.

title: The atmosphere
