words: Atmosphere today — about 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen, with small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases|Early atmosphere — mainly carbon dioxide from volcanoes, with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today|Photosynthesis — 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; algae and plants produced the oxygen in the atmosphere|Greenhouse gas — carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour, which absorb infrared radiation given off by the Earth and keep it warm|Carbon footprint — the total greenhouse gases given out over the whole life of a product, service or event|Acid rain — rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen from burning fuels|Global dimming — less sunlight reaching the ground because of solid particulates from burning fuels
points: Carbon dioxide fell as plants and algae photosynthesised, as it dissolved in the oceans, and as it was locked in carbonate rocks and fossil fuels.|Burning fossil fuels and deforestation add carbon dioxide; cattle farming, rice fields and landfill add methane.|2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O: incomplete combustion gives toxic carbon monoxide, which has no colour or smell; it can also give soot.|Effects of climate change: rising sea levels and flooding, more extreme weather, and changes to rainfall and where species live.|Cut a carbon footprint by using renewable energy, saving energy, capturing and storing carbon dioxide, and planting trees.

title: Using resources
words: Finite resource — one that will run out, such as crude oil; a renewable one, such as timber, can be replaced|Potable water — water that is safe to drink; it has low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, but it is not pure|Desalination — getting potable water from sea water by distillation or reverse osmosis; it needs a lot of energy|Life cycle assessment — the environmental impact of a product at every stage, from raw materials to disposal|[H] Phytomining and bioleaching — plants or bacteria extract metal compounds from low-grade copper ores|Alloy — a metal mixed with other elements to make it harder: bronze is copper and tin, brass copper and zinc, steel iron with carbon|Composite — a matrix holding fibres or fragments of a reinforcement, such as fibreglass or reinforced concrete
points: UK drinking water: choose a fresh water source, pass it through filter beds, then sterilise it with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.|N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: the Haber process uses an iron catalyst, about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres; unreacted gases are recycled.|[H] A lower temperature would give a higher yield of ammonia but too slowly, so 450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate.|Rusting needs air and water. Paint or oil keeps them out; zinc on galvanised iron is more reactive, so it corrodes instead.|Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate, a nitrogen fertiliser; NPK fertilisers supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

title: GCSE Physics
summary: The whole GCSE in twelve short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE (9–1) Physics specification, Foundation and Higher.
subject: Physics

title: Energy stores and resources
words: Energy stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear|Conservation of energy — energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated (wasted), but it cannot be created or destroyed|Specific heat capacity — the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius|Power — the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done; 1 watt is 1 joule per second|Thermal conductivity — how fast energy is transferred through a material by conduction; thick walls of low conductivity slow cooling|Renewable resource — one replenished as it is used: wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal or bio-fuel; fossil fuels and nuclear fuel are not
formulas: Kinetic energy — Ek = ½ × m × v^2|Gravitational potential energy — Ep = m × g × h|Elastic potential energy — Ee = ½ × k × e^2|Change in thermal energy — ΔE = m × c × Δθ|Power — P = E / t = W / t|Efficiency — efficiency = (useful energy output) / (total energy input) = (useful power output) / (total power input)
points: A 0.5 kg ball dropped from 5 m: Ep = 0.5 × 9.8 × 5 = 24.5 J, all kinetic just before landing if air resistance is ignored.|A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s: Ek = ½ × 1000 × 20^2 = 200 000 J.|Warming 2 kg of water by 10 °C, with c = 4200 J/kg °C: ΔE = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J.|A 60 W motor runs for 10 s, so it takes in 60 × 10 = 600 J; it gives a load 450 J of Ep, so efficiency = 450 / 600 = 0.75, or 75%.|Wind and solar are renewable and give off no CO₂ as they run, but are unreliable; gas and coal are reliable but release CO₂.

title: Electric circuits
words: Current — the rate of flow of electric charge, in amperes (A); measured with an ammeter in series|Potential difference — the energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points, in volts (V); measured with a voltmeter in parallel|Resistance — how much a component opposes the current, in ohms (Ω)|Series circuit — one loop: the same current through each component; the supply potential difference is shared, and the resistances add up|Parallel circuit — the same potential difference across each branch; the branch currents add up to the total; the total resistance is less than that of any single branch|Thermistor and LDR — a thermistor's resistance falls as its temperature rises; an LDR's resistance falls as the light on it gets brighter
formulas: Charge flow — Q = I × t|Potential difference — V = I × R|Resistors in series — R total = R₁ + R₂
points: A current of 2 A for 30 s: Q = 2 × 30 = 60 C.|2 Ω and 4 Ω in series on 12 V: total R = 6 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A, and V = I × R gives 4 V across one and 8 V across the other.|Two branches on a 6 V battery taking 1 A and 2 A: the battery supplies 1 + 2 = 3 A, and each branch has the full 6 V across it.|I–V graphs: an ohmic resistor at constant temperature is a straight line through the origin; a filament lamp curves as it heats; a diode conducts one way only.

title: Mains electricity and static
words: Direct current (dc) — current that flows in one direction only, as from a cell or a battery|Alternating current (ac) — current that keeps reversing direction; UK mains is ac at 50 Hz and about 230 V|Three-core cable — live (brown) at about 230 V; neutral (blue) at or near 0 V; earth (green and yellow) at 0 V, carrying current only in a fault|National Grid — links power stations to consumers; step-up transformers raise the potential difference for transmission, step-down ones lower it for homes|Static electricity — rubbing two insulators together moves electrons from one to the other; like charges repel and unlike charges attract|Electric field — the region round a charged object where another charge feels a force; strongest close to the object
formulas: Power from potential difference — P = V × I|Power from current and resistance — P = I^2 × R|Energy from power — E = P × t|Energy from charge — E = Q × V
points: A 2300 W kettle on 230 V mains: I = 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A, and in 180 s it transfers E = 2300 × 180 = 414 000 J.|A current of 3 A through a 4 Ω heater: P = 3^2 × 4 = 36 W.|The grid uses a very high potential difference so the current is low; a low current heats the cables less, so less energy is wasted.|Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth moves electrons onto the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth equally positive.

title: The particle model
words: Density — mass per unit volume; the particles are closest in a solid and furthest apart in a gas|Internal energy — the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system|Change of state — a physical change: mass is conserved, and reversing it gives back the original material|Specific latent heat — the energy to change the state of 1 kg of a substance with no change in temperature: of fusion for melting, of vaporisation for boiling|Gas pressure — particles in random motion hit the container walls, giving a force at right angles to them; heating a gas makes its particles move faster|[H] Work done on a gas — compressing a gas transfers energy to it, raising its internal energy and so its temperature
formulas: Density — ρ = m / V|Energy for a change of state — E = m × L|Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature — p × V = constant
points: Lowered into a eureka can, a 600 g stone pushes out 200 cm³ of water: ρ = 600 / 200 = 3 g/cm³.|Melting 0.5 kg of ice, with L = 334 000 J/kg: E = 0.5 × 334 000 = 167 000 J.|A heating curve is flat while ice melts and while water boils: the energy raises the potential energy of the particles, not the temperature.|A gas at 100 kPa in 3 m³ is squeezed slowly into 1.5 m³: p × V stays 300, so p = 300 ÷ 1.5 = 200 kPa.|[H] Pumping up a tyre warms the air in the pump: work is done on the air, raising its internal energy and so its temperature.

title: Atoms and radioactive decay
words: Isotopes — atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons|Radioactive decay — an unstable nucleus gives out radiation to become more stable; it is random: nobody can predict when a given nucleus will decay|Alpha particle (α) — two protons and two neutrons, a helium nucleus; the most ionising; stopped by paper or a few cm of air|Beta particle (β) — a fast electron from the nucleus, made as a neutron turns into a proton; stopped by a few mm of aluminium|Gamma ray (γ) — electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus; the least ionising; absorbed only by thick lead or concrete|Half-life — the time for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve, or for the activity, in becquerels (Bq), to fall to half
formulas: Alpha decay — ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He|Beta decay — ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e
points: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes: both have 6 protons, but they have 6 and 8 neutrons.|Alpha scattering: most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil and a few bounced back, so the plum pudding model gave way to a tiny, positive nucleus.|Bohr put the electrons in shells at set distances; Chadwick found the neutron about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.|Count rate 800 per minute, half-life 2 days: after 6 days, three half-lives, it falls 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 per minute.|[H] After three half-lives the activity is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8 of its start: start to now is a ratio of 8 : 1.

title: Radiation, fission and fusion
words: Irradiation — exposing an object to nuclear radiation; the object does not become radioactive|Radioactive contamination — unwanted radioactive atoms on or in a material; the hazard is from their decay, and depends on the radiation they give out|Background radiation — around us all the time: from rocks and cosmic rays, and from the fallout of weapons tests and nuclear accidents|Radiation dose — the risk of harm from radiation, in sieverts (Sv); 1000 millisieverts make 1 sievert|Nuclear fission — a large unstable nucleus, such as uranium or plutonium, absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing two or three neutrons, gamma rays and energy|Chain reaction — neutrons from one fission split more nuclei; controlled in a nuclear reactor, uncontrolled in a nuclear weapon|Nuclear fusion — two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus; some mass is converted into energy
points: Inside the body alpha is the most dangerous, because it is so strongly ionising; outside, it is the least, because skin stops it.|A medical tracer should give out gamma, so it is detected outside the body, and have a short half-life, so the patient is not exposed for long.|Gamma rays are used to treat cancer and to sterilise medical equipment, because they kill cells.|Workers keep their exposure low by using tongs, standing back, using lead shielding and spending as little time near the source as possible.

title: Forces, moments and pressure
words: Scalar and vector — a scalar has size only, such as speed; a vector has size and direction, such as velocity|Contact and non-contact forces — contact: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact; non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic|Weight — the force on an object due to gravity, acting at its centre of mass, in newtons (N)|Resultant force — the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together|Elastic deformation — the object goes back to its original shape when the force is removed|Moment — the turning effect of a force; an object is balanced when the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment|Pressure — the force normal to a surface per unit area, in pascals (Pa); air pressure falls with height, as there is less air above
formulas: Weight — W = m × g|Work done — W = F × s|Hooke's law — F = k × e|Moment of a force — M = F × d|Pressure — p = F / A|[H] Pressure in a liquid — p = h × ρ × g
points: A 60 kg student weighs W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N; climbing 3 m of stairs, the work done against gravity is 588 × 3 = 1764 J.|A spring with k = 40 N/m stretched by 0.05 m: F = 40 × 0.05 = 2 N. Past the limit of proportionality, F = k × e no longer applies.|A seesaw balances with 300 N at 2 m on one side and 400 N at 1.5 m on the other, since 300 × 2 = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m.|[H] 3 N east and 4 N north: a scale drawing, or Pythagoras, gives a resultant of 5 N, since 3^2 + 4^2 = 25.|[H] 10 m down in water of density 1000 kg/m³: p = 10 × 1000 × 9.8 = 98 000 Pa more than at the surface.

title: Motion and momentum
words: Acceleration — the rate of change of velocity, which is speed in a given direction; a deceleration is a negative acceleration|Newton's first law — with no resultant force, a still object stays still and a moving one keeps the same speed and direction|Newton's third law — when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction|Terminal velocity — the steady speed reached when the resistive forces on a falling object balance its weight|Stopping distance — the thinking distance plus the braking distance|[H] Conservation of momentum — in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it
formulas: Distance travelled — s = v × t|Acceleration — a = Δv / t|Uniform acceleration — v^2 − u^2 = 2 × a × s|Newton's second law — F = m × a|[H] Momentum — p = m × v|[H] Force and change in momentum — F = (m × Δv) / Δt
points: A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s: a = (25 − 5) / 4 = 5 m/s².|A ball dropped from rest falls 20 m: v^2 = 0 + 2 × 9.8 × 20 = 392, so v = √392 ≈ 19.8 m/s.|A 1200 kg car braking with a force of 6000 N: a = F ÷ m = 6000 ÷ 1200 = 5 m/s² deceleration.|Reaction times run from 0.2 s to 0.9 s. Tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions add thinking distance; wet or icy roads and worn tyres add braking distance.|[H] A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a still 1 kg trolley: 2 × 3 = 3 × v, so they move off at v = 2 m/s.

title: Waves and sound
words: Transverse wave — the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer, as in ripples on water|Longitudinal wave — the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions, as in sound|Amplitude — the maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed position|Wavelength — the distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave|Frequency — the number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz)|Reflection, absorption, transmission — what can happen to a wave at the boundary between two materials|[H] Ultrasound — sound above 20 kHz, beyond the 20 Hz to 20 kHz range of human hearing; partly reflected at each boundary, so used for imaging
formulas: Wave speed — v = f × λ|Period — T = 1 / f
points: Ripples at 4 Hz with a wavelength of 0.5 m: v = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m/s.|A wave of frequency 200 Hz has a period T = 1 / 200 = 0.005 s.|Clap 100 m from a wall and hear the echo 0.6 s later: the sound went 200 m, so v = 200 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 333 m/s.|[H] A sonar pulse returns after 0.8 s, and sound in sea water travels at 1500 m/s: depth = 1500 × 0.8 ÷ 2 = 600 m.|[H] Seismic P waves are longitudinal and cross solids and liquids; S waves are transverse and cannot cross liquids, evidence of a liquid outer core.

title: Electromagnetic waves and light
words: Electromagnetic spectrum — transverse waves that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum; by rising frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma|Refraction — a change of direction when a wave crosses a boundary at an angle, because its speed changes|Hazards — ultraviolet can age the skin early and raise the risk of skin cancer; X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can cause gene mutations and cancer|Convex and concave lenses — a convex lens focuses parallel rays and can form a real image, one a screen can show; a concave lens forms only virtual images|Colour — an opaque object looks the colour of the wavelengths it reflects most strongly; the others are absorbed|Perfect black body — an object that absorbs all the radiation falling on it; it is also the best possible emitter
formulas: Magnification — magnification = (image height) / (object height)
points: Uses: radio for TV, microwaves for satellites and cooking, infrared for heaters, visible light for fibre optics, X-rays for medical imaging.|An image 6 cm tall of an object 2 cm tall: magnification = 6 / 2 = 3, with no units.|[H] Refraction: the end of a wavefront that reaches the glass first slows down first, so the wave bends towards the normal.|A blue object under red light looks black: it reflects only blue, so it absorbs all the red light falling on it.|[H] A body stays at a constant temperature when it absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it; Earth warms if it absorbs faster.

title: Magnetism and electromagnetism
words: Permanent and induced magnets — a permanent magnet makes its own field; an induced magnet is magnetic only in a field, losing most or all of it when removed|Magnetic field — the region round a magnet where another magnet or a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel) feels a force; lines run north to south|Solenoid — a coil of wire carrying a current; the field inside is strong and uniform, and an iron core makes it an electromagnet|[H] Motor effect — a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force, greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field|[H] Fleming's left-hand rule — first finger for the field, second finger for the current, thumb for the motion|[H] Generator effect — a potential difference is induced across a wire moving relative to a magnetic field, or in a changing field|[H] Transformer — two coils on an iron core; alternating current in the primary induces an alternating potential difference in the secondary
formulas: [H] Force on a conductor — F = B × I × l|[H] Transformer turns — Vₚ / Vₛ = nₚ / nₛ|[H] Transformer power — Vₛ × Iₛ = Vₚ × Iₚ
points: The field round a straight wire is a set of circles; it is stronger with a bigger current and closer to the wire.|Make an electromagnet stronger with more turns on the coil, a bigger current, or an iron core.|[H] 0.5 m of wire carrying 2 A at right angles to a 0.2 T field: F = 0.2 × 2 × 0.5 = 0.2 N.|[H] 230 V on 1000 primary turns with 50 secondary turns: Vₛ = 230 × 50 ÷ 1000 = 11.5 V, a step-down transformer.|[H] An alternator uses slip rings to give ac; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator to give dc.

title: Space physics
words: Solar system — the Sun, the planets and dwarf planets orbiting it, and their moons (natural satellites); part of the Milky Way galaxy|Nebula — a cloud of dust and gas that gravity pulls together to form a protostar|Main sequence star — a stable star, because the outward pressure from fusion balances the inward pull of gravity|Supernova — the explosion of a star much bigger than the Sun; it makes elements heavier than iron and scatters them through space|Red-shift — the increase in the wavelength of light seen from a galaxy moving away from us|Big Bang theory — the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense, and has been expanding ever since
points: A star like the Sun: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.|A star much bigger than the Sun: main sequence → red super giant → supernova → neutron star, or a black hole if massive enough.|Fusion in stars makes the elements up to iron; elements heavier than iron are made in supernovae.|[H] A satellite in a circular orbit has a steady speed but a changing velocity, since gravity keeps turning it; a faster satellite needs a smaller orbit.|More distant galaxies show more red-shift, so they move away faster: evidence that the universe is expanding, which supports the Big Bang.

title: GCSE Geography
summary: The whole GCSE in fourteen short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each, with the formulas in the skills chapter, in the order of the AQA GCSE Geography (8035) specification, taking coasts, rivers, hot deserts and water as the options.
subject: Geography

title: Tectonic hazards
words: Natural hazard — a natural process or event that threatens people and property|Hazard risk — the chance of a hazard harming people; higher where more people live and where they are more vulnerable|Destructive margin — plates move together and the denser oceanic plate is subducted; strong earthquakes and explosive volcanoes|Constructive margin — plates move apart and magma rises to fill the gap; gentle volcanoes and small earthquakes|Conservative margin — plates slide past each other, stick, then slip in earthquakes; no volcanoes|Primary effect — caused directly by the hazard, such as collapsed buildings; secondary effects follow, such as fires, tsunamis and disease
points: Chile 2010, magnitude 8.8, about 500 died; Nepal 2015, magnitude 7.8, about 9000 died. Richer Chile had stronger buildings and a faster response.|Immediate responses: rescue, field hospitals, food, water, shelter. Long-term: rebuilding homes, roads and schools to stronger standards.|People stay near volcanoes for fertile soil, geothermal power and tourist jobs, or because they are too poor to move.|The four Ps: monitoring (tiltmeters, gas sensors), prediction, protection (earthquake-resistant buildings), planning (evacuation drills).

title: Weather hazards
words: Global atmospheric circulation — air moving between the equator and the poles in three cells each side: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar|Pressure belts — low pressure (rising air, cloud and rain) at the equator and 60°; high pressure (sinking air, clear skies) at 30° and the poles|Tropical storm — a huge, spinning low-pressure storm over warm tropical seas; a hurricane, cyclone or typhoon|Eye — the calm centre of a tropical storm, where air sinks, ringed by the eyewall's tall cloud and strongest winds|Storm surge — a rise in sea level as strong winds and low pressure push the sea onto the coast
points: Forms over seas above about 27°C, 5° to 30° from the equator: warm, moist air rises and condenses, releasing heat, and the Earth's spin turns it.|Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, 2013: a storm surge flooded Tacloban and over 6000 died; aid brought food, water and shelter.|Warmer seas may make storms stronger. Reduce the effects: satellite tracking, warnings, sea walls, storm shelters and evacuation plans.|Somerset Levels, winter 2013–14: weeks of rain flooded farmland and hundreds of homes and cut off villages; rivers were then dredged.|More extreme UK weather: 40°C was first recorded in July 2022, and the UK's ten warmest years on record are all this century.

title: Climate change
words: Climate change — a long-term change in the Earth's average temperatures and weather patterns|Quaternary period — the last 2.6 million years, swinging between cold glacials and warmer interglacials|Enhanced greenhouse effect — extra greenhouse gases from human activity, such as carbon dioxide and methane, trap more heat|Mitigation — reducing the causes of climate change, mainly by cutting greenhouse gas emissions|Adaptation — changing how people live and work to cope with the effects of climate change
points: Evidence: ice cores show past CO₂ and temperatures; tree rings and pollen show past climates; the Earth is over 1°C warmer than in the late 1800s.|Natural causes: changes in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles), sunspots changing the sun's output, and volcanic ash and gas blocking sunlight.|Human causes: burning fossil fuels releases CO₂; cattle and rice paddies give off methane; deforestation leaves fewer trees to absorb CO₂.|Effects: rising seas threaten low-lying Bangladesh and the Maldives; more extreme weather; habitats shift and some crops fail.|Mitigation: renewables, carbon capture, planting trees, the 2015 Paris Agreement. Adaptation: drought-resistant crops, saving water, sea walls.

title: Ecosystems and rainforests
words: Ecosystem — a community of plants and animals and the climate, soil and water they depend on|Producer — a plant that makes its own food from sunlight; consumers eat plants or other animals|Decomposer — a fungus or bacterium that breaks down dead material and returns its nutrients to the soil|Biome — a large global ecosystem, such as tropical rainforest, hot desert or tundra|Biodiversity — the variety of plants and animals in an area; higher in tropical rainforests than in any other land biome|Deforestation — cutting down and clearing forest
points: Pond: fertiliser runs in, algae bloom and block the light, plants die, and bacteria rotting them use up the oxygen, so fish die.|Rainforest: about 27°C all year, over 2000 mm of rain; poor soil, as heavy rain washes nutrients out and plants take them up fast.|Adaptations: drip-tip leaves shed heavy rain, buttress roots prop up tall trees in shallow soil, and lianas climb to the light.|Amazon: cleared mainly for cattle ranching, plus soya, logging, mining and roads; soil erodes, habitats are lost and CO₂ is released.|Worth keeping for medicines, timber and carbon storage; manage it with selective logging, replanting, ecotourism and protected areas.

title: Hot deserts
words: Hot desert — an area with less than 250 mm of rain a year and high daytime temperatures|Diurnal range — the difference between day and night temperatures; large in deserts, as clear skies let heat escape at night|Xerophyte — a plant adapted to very dry conditions, such as a cactus|Desertification — land on the edge of a desert turning into desert, through drought and human activity|Overgrazing — animals eat plants faster than they regrow, leaving bare soil; overcultivation farms the soil until its nutrients run out|Appropriate technology — simple, cheap methods that local people can build and maintain
points: Cactus: long or wide roots reach water, spines and a waxy skin cut water loss, a thick stem stores it. Camel: fat in the hump, wide feet.|Thar Desert: the Indira Gandhi Canal irrigates farms; mining, wind and solar power and tourism bring jobs. Challenges: heat, water, access.|Sahel: less rain, overgrazing, overcultivation, firewood cutting and population growth leave bare soil for the wind to erode.|Reduce it: plant trees (the Great Green Wall), manage water and soil, and lay lines of stones that slow rainwater so it soaks in.

title: Coastal landscapes
words: Constructive wave — low and long, with a strong swash and weak backwash, so it builds beaches|Destructive wave — tall and steep, with a weak swash and strong backwash, so it erodes|Weathering — rock broken down in place by freeze–thaw, salt or chemicals; mass movement moves it downhill by sliding, slumping or rock fall|Hydraulic power — waves force water and air into cracks, and the pressure breaks the rock apart|Abrasion — rocks hurled by the waves wear the cliff away; in attrition they knock each other smaller and rounder|Longshore drift — swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle and backwash drags it straight down, moving it along the coast
points: Soft rock erodes into bays and hard rock is left as headlands, whose cracks become caves, arches, stacks and stumps, as at Old Harry, Dorset.|Spit: where the coast changes direction, longshore drift keeps depositing sand out to sea, and changing winds curve the end. Spurn Head.|Hard: sea walls, rock armour, gabions, groynes. Soft: beach nourishment, dune regeneration. Managed retreat: letting low-value land flood.|Mappleton, 1991: rock armour and two rock groynes saved the village but starved beaches to the south, so cliffs at Cowden eroded faster.|UK uplands lie mostly north and west of a line from the Tees to the Exe, on harder, older rock; lowlands lie south and east, on softer rock.

title: River landscapes
words: Long profile — the gradient from source to mouth: steep upstream, with V-shaped valleys and interlocking spurs, gentle near the mouth|Vertical erosion — deepens the channel in the upper course; lateral erosion widens it further down|Transportation — traction (rolling), saltation (bouncing), suspension (carried in the flow) and solution (dissolved)|Levée — a raised bank beside the river, built up as floods drop their heaviest sediment first|Discharge — the volume of water passing a point each second, in cumecs|Lag time — the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
points: Waterfall: soft rock under hard rock erodes faster, the hard overhang collapses, and the fall retreats, leaving a gorge. High Force, River Tees.|Meander: fast flow outside the bend erodes a river cliff; slow flow inside deposits a slip-off slope. A flood cuts the neck; the bend becomes an ox-bow lake.|River Tees: High Force and its gorge upstream, meanders lower down, then mudflats and a wide estuary at Teesside.|Short lag time and high peak after heavy rain on steep, impermeable or urban land; forest and permeable rock give a lower, later peak.|Hard: dams, straightening, embankments, relief channels such as the Jubilee River, Maidenhead. Soft: flood warnings, flood plain zoning, trees.

title: Cities in LICs and NEEs
words: Urbanisation — an increase in the proportion of people living in towns and cities|Rural–urban migration — moving from the countryside to a city, pushed by drought or poverty and pulled by jobs, schools and hospitals|Natural increase — more births than deaths, so the population grows|Megacity — an urban area of more than 10 million people|Squatter settlement — homes built illegally on land the people do not own, often without clean water or sanitation|Informal economy — work that is not taxed or regulated, such as street selling
points: Urbanisation is fastest in LICs and NEEs, especially in Africa and Asia; in HICs most people already live in cities.|Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (NEE): a port, tourist city and oil centre, grown by migration from the poorer north-east and by natural increase.|Opportunities: better schools, health care, water and electricity than in the countryside, and jobs in services, industry and tourism.|Challenges: favelas on steep slopes prone to landslides, poor water and sanitation, unemployment, crime, traffic congestion and pollution.|Favela Bairro Project: paved roads, water and sewage pipes, rubbish collection, day care and job training, upgrading favelas, not clearing them.

title: UK cities
words: Brownfield site — land that has been built on before and can be redeveloped|Greenfield site — land never built on, usually farmland at a city's edge|Urban sprawl — a city spreading into the rural–urban fringe, where town meets countryside|Commuter settlement — a town or village whose residents travel into a city to work|Deprivation — lacking what most people have, such as a decent income, housing, health or education|Urban regeneration — new investment, homes and jobs brought to a run-down area
points: Most of the UK's people live in English cities, especially London and the South East; the Scottish Highlands and mid-Wales have few people.|Migration brings a cultural mix of food, music and festivals and a younger workforce, but adds pressure on housing and school places.|Brownfield sites reuse land and save countryside but can be costly to clean up; greenfield sites are cheaper to build on but destroy habitats.|London 2012: polluted, derelict land at Stratford was regenerated as the Olympic Park, with new homes, shops, sports venues and transport links.|Sustainable city: solar panels, recycling, parks, green roofs, cycle hire, trams, park-and-ride; London's congestion charge began in 2003.

title: The development gap
words: Development gap — the difference in standards of living between the richest and poorest countries|HIC, NEE and LIC — high-income country, newly emerging economy (developing fast) and low-income country|GNI per head — a country's gross national income divided by its population|Human Development Index — life expectancy, years of schooling and income combined into one score from 0 to 1|Infant mortality rate — the number of babies per 1000 live births who die before their first birthday|Intermediate technology — simple, affordable tools and machines that local people can use and repair
points: GNI per head is an average, so it hides the gap between rich and poor in a country; HDI is more useful because it combines several measures.|DTM: stage 1 high birth and death rates; 2 deaths fall, population soars; 3 births fall; 4 both low; 5 births below deaths, population falls.|Causes: physical (landlocked, hazards, disease), economic (cheap raw materials, debt), historical (colonialism). Results: wealth and health gaps, migration.|Closing the gap: investment, industry, tourism, aid, intermediate technology, Fairtrade, debt relief and microfinance loans.|Tourism in Jamaica brings jobs, foreign money and better roads and airports, but much of the profit leaves with foreign-owned hotels.

title: Nigeria and the UK economy
words: Employment sectors — primary (raw materials), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services), quaternary (research and IT)|Transnational corporation — a company that operates in more than one country, such as Shell|Globalisation — the growing links between countries through trade, investment and communication|Deindustrialisation — the decline of manufacturing industry|Science park — offices and laboratories for high-tech firms, usually beside a university|North–south divide — the gap in wealth, health and jobs between the South East of England and much of the north
points: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is an NEE: oil is most of its exports, and manufacturing and services such as Nollywood films are growing.|Shell's oil wells in the Niger Delta brought jobs, taxes and investment, but oil spills and gas flaring polluted farmland, rivers and air.|Nigeria belongs to OPEC and the African Union and trades more with China; aid such as mosquito nets cuts malaria and improves quality of life.|UK deindustrialisation: coal, steel and shipbuilding declined as cheaper goods came from abroad and machines replaced workers.|Post-industrial UK: services employ most people, from finance in London to research at Cambridge Science Park.

title: Resources and water
words: Food miles — the distance food travels from where it is grown to where it is eaten|Agribusiness — farming run as a large, intensive commercial business|Energy mix — the sources a country uses for its energy, such as gas, wind and nuclear|Water deficit — demand for water is greater than supply; a surplus is the opposite|Water insecurity — not enough safe, reliable water, bringing disease such as cholera, poor harvests and even conflict|Over-abstraction — taking more water from rivers or aquifers than is naturally replaced|Desalination — removing salt from sea water to make fresh water
points: UK food: year-round imports of high-value foods such as exotic fruit, and more organic food, raise food miles and the carbon footprint.|UK water: the north and west get most rain, but the South East has most people and a deficit; transfers could move water south.|UK energy: the last coal power station closed in 2024 and North Sea oil and gas are running down, while wind and solar give a growing share.|China's South–North Water Transfer Project takes Yangtze water to the dry north, including Beijing, but people were moved and ecosystems changed.|Sustainable water: a sand dam in Kenya traps sand that stores rainwater safe from evaporation; at home, reuse grey water and fix leaks.

title: Issue evaluation and fieldwork
words: Pre-release resources — a booklet on an issue, released before Paper 3 to study; a clean copy comes in the exam|Hypothesis — a statement fieldwork can test, such as "pebbles get smaller downstream"|Primary data — data you collect yourself in the field; secondary data was collected by others, such as census figures|Systematic sampling — measuring at regular intervals, such as every 50 m along a street|Risk assessment — spotting the dangers at a site, such as deep water or traffic, and how to reduce them|Evaluation — judging how reliable the data and conclusions are, and how the enquiry could be improved
points: Six stages: ask a question, collect data, present it, analyse and explain it, reach a conclusion, then evaluate the whole enquiry.|Two enquiries in contrasting places, one physical and one human: how a river changes downstream; how quality of life varies across a town.|Issue evaluation: pick an option, back it with facts and figures from the booklet, weigh it against another option, and justify your choice.|"Only 10 people were asked, on one weekday, so the results may not be representative; asking 50 across a week would be more reliable."

title: Geographical skills
words: Four-figure grid reference — locates a square: the easting along the bottom first, then the northing up the side|Six-figure grid reference — locates a point, splitting each side of the square into tenths|Contour line — joins points of equal height; the closer together, the steeper the slope|Scale — map distance compared with ground distance; at 1:50 000, 2 cm on the map is 1 km|Choropleth map — areas shaded darker for higher values, such as population density|Isoline — a line joining places of equal value, such as rainfall or air pressure
formulas: Mean — mean = (total of the values) / (number of values)|Position of the median — (n + 1) / 2|Interquartile range — IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile|Percentage change — percentage change = (new value − old value) / (old value) × 100|Gradient — gradient = (difference in height) / (horizontal distance)|River discharge — discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity
points: Grid reference 456 723: 45 and 6 tenths along, then 72 and 3 tenths up. Along the corridor, then up the stairs.|On a 1:50 000 map 1 cm is 500 m, so 4.2 cm on the map is 4.2 × 500 = 2100 m, or 2.1 km.|Rainfall 12, 15, 18, 20 and 35 mm: mean = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 mm, median = 18 mm, range = 35 − 12 = 23 mm.|Pebbles 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11 cm: median 6 cm, lower quartile 3 cm, upper quartile 9 cm, so IQR = 9 − 3 = 6 cm.|A town grows from 40 000 to 50 000 people: percentage change = 10 000 ÷ 40 000 × 100 = 25%.

title: GCSE History
summary: The GCSE in ten short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each for the exam skills and the most-taught options (Germany, 1890–1945: Democracy and dictatorship; Conflict and tension, 1918–1939; Britain: Health and the people, c1000 to the present day; Elizabethan England, c1568–1603), in the order of the AQA GCSE History (8145) specification.
subject: History

title: Skills and question types
words: Source — something made at the time, such as a letter, diary, cartoon or photograph; asked about in Conflict and tension and in Health|Interpretation — a later view of the past by a historian or other writer; asked about in Germany and in Elizabethan England|Provenance — who made a source or interpretation, when and why, which decides how far it can be trusted|Contextual knowledge — what you know about the period, used to explain, test and judge a source or interpretation|Significance — how far an event, person or idea mattered: how many it affected, how deeply and for how long|Causation — why something happened, linking factors such as war, government, ideas, chance and individuals|Change and continuity — what was different afterwards, and what stayed the same
points: Paper 1, 2 hours, 50%: Germany, 1890–1945, then Conflict and tension, 1918–1939. Paper 2, 2 hours, 50%: Health and the people, then Elizabethan England.|How useful is an 1858 Punch cartoon of the filthy Thames? It shows what Londoners feared in the Great Stink, but it was drawn to mock, so it exaggerates.|Why do two interpretations differ? Ask who wrote each, when and why: a Nazi writer in 1934 and a historian in 1990 had different aims and evidence.|Significance: Jenner's vaccine saved lives at the time, and vaccination went on to wipe out smallpox, declared gone by the World Health Organization in 1980.|A 16-mark essay weighs the named factor against others, then judges; one essay on each paper earns 4 more marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

title: Kaiser and Weimar, 1890–1929
words: Kaiser Wilhelm II — emperor of Germany from 1888 to 1918, who chose the chancellor and commanded the army|Weltpolitik — the Kaiser's "world policy" of winning colonies and building a navy to make Germany a world power|Weimar Constitution — the 1919 democracy: a president elected every seven years and a Reichstag elected by proportional representation|Article 48 — let the president rule by decree in an emergency, without the Reichstag|November Criminals — the politicians who signed the armistice, blamed by nationalists for a "stab in the back"|Hyperinflation — prices rising so fast in 1923 that German money became almost worthless|Golden Years — 1924 to 1929, when Stresemann's policies brought steadier money, American loans and a new culture
points: By 1912 the socialist SPD was the largest party in the Reichstag. War and the British blockade brought hunger, and the Kaiser abdicated on 9 November 1918.|Risings: the Spartacists (left) in Berlin, January 1919, crushed by the Freikorps; the Kapp Putsch (right), March 1920, beaten by a general strike.|January 1923: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr; strikers were paid with printed money, and by November 1923 one US dollar was worth 4.2 trillion marks.|November 1923: Hitler's Munich Putsch failed; he was sentenced to five years in prison, served only nine months, and wrote Mein Kampf there.|Stresemann's recovery: the Rentenmark (1923), the Dawes Plan's American loans (1924), Locarno (1925), the League of Nations (1926), the Young Plan (1929).

title: Hitler's rise to power
words: Wall Street Crash — the collapse of the American stock market in October 1929, after which US loans to Germany were called in|Depression — the slump that followed; German unemployment reached about six million by 1932|SA — the Nazi stormtroopers or Brownshirts, led by Ernst Röhm, who broke up opponents' meetings|Propaganda — information spread to persuade, which Goebbels used to sell the Nazis as the answer to Germany's problems|Reichstag Fire — the burning of the parliament building on 27 February 1933, blamed on the communists|Enabling Act — the law of March 1933 that let Hitler make laws without the Reichstag for four years|Führer — leader; Hitler's title from August 1934, when he joined the posts of chancellor and president
points: Nazi seats in the Reichstag: 12 (1928), 107 (1930), 230 (July 1932, the largest party), 196 (November 1932), 288 (March 1933).|30 January 1933: Papen persuaded Hindenburg to make Hitler chancellor, believing that with only two other Nazis in the cabinet he could be controlled.|The Enabling Act passed by 444 votes to 94 on 23 March 1933, with the communists kept out and only the SPD voting against.|Night of the Long Knives, 30 June 1934: the SS killed Röhm and other SA leaders, removing a rival and winning the army's support.|2 August 1934: Hindenburg died, Hitler became Führer, and the army swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.

title: Life under the Nazis
words: Gestapo — the secret state police, who could arrest and imprison people without trial|SS — the Nazi elite guard led by Himmler, which ran the police and the concentration camps|Propaganda Ministry — run by Joseph Goebbels, it controlled newspapers, radio, films and rallies|Kinder, Küche, Kirche — children, kitchen, church: the Nazi idea of a woman's role|Hitler Youth — the Nazi organisation for boys; girls joined the League of German Maidens|Confessing Church — Protestants, among them Pastor Martin Niemöller, who refused to join the Nazi Reich Church|Nuremberg Laws — the 1935 laws that took away Jews' German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans
points: Work: public works, the Labour Service and rearmament cut unemployment from about six million in 1932 to under half a million by 1939.|Women: a marriage loan of 1,000 marks, with a quarter written off for each child born; the Mother's Cross in bronze, silver or gold for 4, 6 or 8 children.|Opposition: Niemöller, arrested in 1937 and held in camps until 1945; the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth; the White Rose students, executed in 1943.|Persecution grew: the boycott of Jewish shops (1933), the Nuremberg Laws (1935), Kristallnacht (November 1938), the Final Solution planned at Wannsee (1942).|War: rationing from 1939, Goebbels's "total war" from 1943, the bombing of cities such as Hamburg (1943) and Dresden (1945), and refugees fleeing west.

title: Peace treaties and the League
words: Fourteen Points — Woodrow Wilson's plan for peace, including self-determination and a League of Nations|Big Three — Wilson (USA), Clemenceau (France) and Lloyd George (Britain), who drew up the Treaty of Versailles|War guilt clause — Article 231, which made Germany accept the blame for the war|Reparations — payments for war damage; Germany's were set at £6,600 million in 1921|League of Nations — set up in 1920 to keep the peace; the USA never joined and it had no army of its own|Collective security — League members acting together to stop an aggressor|Sanctions — punishments such as a ban on trade, meant to make an aggressor back down
points: Versailles, 28 June 1919: army cut to 100,000, no air force or submarines, six battleships, Rhineland demilitarised, colonies lost, Alsace-Lorraine to France.|Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled; Wilson wanted a fair peace and a League; Lloyd George wanted Germany punished but able to trade with Britain again.|The other treaties: St Germain with Austria (1919), Neuilly with Bulgaria (1919), Trianon with Hungary (1920), Sèvres with Turkey (1920).|The 1920s: the League settled the Aaland Islands (1921) and Bulgaria (1925), but Vilna (1920) and Corfu (1923) showed it could be ignored.|The 1930s: Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and left the League (1933); Italy invaded Abyssinia (1935), and oil was never added to the sanctions.

title: The road to war
words: Lebensraum — living space; Hitler's aim to win land for Germans in eastern Europe|Rearmament — building up the armed forces; Hitler announced conscription and an air force in 1935, breaking Versailles|Anschluss — the union of Germany and Austria, banned at Versailles and carried out in March 1938|Sudetenland — the border area of Czechoslovakia where about three million German speakers lived|Appeasement — giving in to demands to avoid war, the policy of Britain and France and above all of Neville Chamberlain|Nazi–Soviet Pact — the August 1939 agreement not to fight each other, with a secret plan to divide Poland
points: Step by step: the Saar voted to rejoin Germany (January 1935); troops entered the Rhineland (March 1936), breaking Versailles, and nobody stopped them.|Munich, 29–30 September 1938: Hitler, Chamberlain, Daladier and Mussolini agreed Germany would take the Sudetenland; Czechoslovakia was not invited.|March 1939: Germany took the rest of Czechoslovakia, where most people were Czech or Slovak, so Britain gave up appeasement and promised to defend Poland.|Why appease? Britain was not ready to fight, many thought Versailles too harsh, and the memory of 1914–1918 made another war seem unthinkable.|1 September 1939: Germany invaded Poland; on 3 September Britain and France declared war.

title: Medicine, c1000 to c1800
words: Four Humours — the idea from Hippocrates and Galen that illness comes from too much or too little blood, phlegm, yellow bile or black bile|Galen — a Greek doctor in Rome whose books, backed by the Church, were followed for over 1,000 years|Miasma — the belief that disease is caused by bad air from rotting matter|Black Death — the plague that reached England in 1348 and killed perhaps a third to a half of the people|Dissection — cutting up a body to study it, which showed Vesalius that Galen was sometimes wrong|Vaccination — giving a mild or weakened form of a germ to protect against a deadly disease; Jenner used cowpox against smallpox in 1796
points: Medieval treatments aimed to restore balance: bleeding and purging, herbal remedies, and prayer or pilgrimage when illness was seen as God's punishment.|Vesalius, On the Fabric of the Human Body (1543): he dissected humans and showed the jaw is one bone, not two as Galen said.|Harvey (1628) showed that the heart pumps blood round the body in a circulation; doctors still bled patients, so treatment barely changed.|Great Plague, London, 1665: perhaps 100,000 died; infected houses were shut up and marked with a red cross, and cats and dogs were killed.|Jenner, 1796: cowpox from a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, given to James Phipps, then smallpox, which did not make him ill; vaccination became compulsory in 1853.

title: Medicine since 1800
words: Germ theory — Pasteur's proof, published in 1861, that microbes in the air cause decay; Koch then linked microbes to particular diseases|Anaesthetic — a drug that stops pain during surgery; Simpson used chloroform in 1847|Antiseptic — a chemical that kills germs; Lister published his results with carbolic acid in 1867|Nursing — made a trained profession by Florence Nightingale after the Crimean War; her training school opened in 1860|Public health — action by government to keep people healthy, such as clean water, sewers and vaccination|Antibiotic — a drug, such as penicillin, that kills bacteria or stops them growing|NHS — the National Health Service, free at the point of use, set up in 1948 by Aneurin Bevan after the 1942 Beveridge Report
points: Koch found the bacteria that cause TB (1882) and cholera (1883); Pasteur used weakened germs to make vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies.|Snow, Broad Street, London, 1854: he mapped cholera deaths round one water pump, had its handle removed, and showed cholera spread in water, not by miasma.|Public Health Acts: 1848 let towns set up boards of health but did not force them; 1875 made councils provide clean water and sewers.|Penicillin: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in 1928; Florey and Chain purified and tested it from 1940; US factories mass-produced it for D-Day in 1944.|Government: Liberal reforms (school meals 1906, pensions 1908, National Insurance 1911), the NHS (1948) and the Clean Air Act (1956).

title: Elizabeth, court and society
words: Privy Council — the queen's chief advisers, such as William Cecil and Francis Walsingham|Patronage — the queen's power to give titles, land and jobs, which kept nobles loyal|Succession — who would rule next, a worry because Elizabeth never married and had no child|Golden Age — a time of success in exploration, theatre and building, as Elizabeth's reign is often seen|Vagabond — a wandering beggar, feared as a threat to order and punished by law|Poor Law — the 1601 Act that made each parish collect a poor rate to help those who could not work and find work for those who could|Circumnavigation — sailing all the way round the world, as Drake did from 1577 to 1580
points: Elizabeth: born 1533, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, queen from 1558 to 1603; she never married, so the Tudor line ended with her.|Essex, once a favourite, led a failed rising in London in February 1601 after losing royal favour, and was executed for treason.|Causes of poverty: a rising population, rising prices, enclosure and bad harvests in the 1590s; the 1572 Act had vagabonds whipped and burned through the ear.|Theatre: the Theatre opened in Shoreditch in 1576 and the Globe in 1599; Puritans attacked plays as sinful, but Elizabeth enjoyed them at court.|Drake sailed round the world in the Golden Hind (1577–1580), raiding Spanish treasure, and was knighted in 1581; Raleigh's Roanoke colony in Virginia failed.

title: Troubles at home and abroad
words: Religious Settlement — the 1559 laws making Elizabeth Supreme Governor of a Protestant Church of England that kept some Catholic features|Recusant — a Catholic who refused to attend Church of England services; fined a shilling for each Sunday missed, then £20 a month from 1581|Puritan — a strict Protestant who wanted the Church cleared of Catholic ceremony|Excommunication — expulsion from the Catholic Church; the Pope excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570|Jesuits — Catholic priests of the Society of Jesus, sent secretly to England from 1580, such as Edmund Campion, executed in 1581|Armada — the Spanish fleet sent by Philip II in 1588 to invade England|Historic environment — the site AQA names for each year's exam, studied in its Elizabethan setting
points: Northern Rebellion, 1569: the Catholic earls of Northumberland and Westmorland rose to free Mary, Queen of Scots and restore Catholicism; it was crushed.|Mary fled to England in 1568 and was held for nearly 19 years as the focus of Catholic plots: Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583), Babington (1586).|Walsingham's agents read Mary's coded letters approving the Babington Plot; she was executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587.|Causes of the Armada: English help for the Dutch rebels (Treaty of Nonsuch, 1585), Drake's raids on Spanish treasure, religion, and Mary's execution.|Armada defeat, 1588: fireships broke the Spanish formation at Calais, the English won at Gravelines, and storms wrecked ships round Scotland and Ireland.

title: GCSE Religious Studies
summary: The GCSE in eleven short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each for the question types, the two most-taught religions, Christianity and Islam, and Themes A, B, D and E (relationships and families, religion and life, peace and conflict, crime and punishment), in the order of the AQA GCSE Religious Studies A (8062) specification.
subject: Religious Studies

title: Answering the question types
words: AO1 — knowledge and understanding of beliefs, practices and sources of authority, and their influence; half the marks|AO2 — analysing and evaluating religion and belief to reach a reasoned judgement; the other half of the marks|Source of authority — a scripture, hadith, creed or church teaching that a belief comes from|Contrasting beliefs — two different views on the same issue, such as Catholic and Church of England views on contraception|Evaluate — weigh up arguments for and against a statement, then reach a justified conclusion|Humanist — a non-religious person who makes moral choices by reason, evidence and care for human welfare|Atheist — a person who believes there is no God
points: Two papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes and 50%: four 24-mark questions plus 6 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Paper 1 religions, Paper 2 themes.|Every 24-mark question runs 1, 2, 4, 5, 12: a multiple choice, give two, explain two, explain two with a source, then evaluate a statement.|4 marks, one way developed: "Belief in the resurrection gives Christians hope when someone dies, because they trust the dead will rise to eternal life."|5 marks: "Muslims believe God is One, so worshipping anything beside him is shirk, the gravest sin; Surah 112 says God is One." The source earns a mark.|12 marks end in a justified conclusion: "Both sides value life, but a court can be wrong and an execution cannot be undone, so the case against it is stronger."

title: Christian beliefs
words: Omnipotent — all-powerful; nothing is impossible for God|Benevolent — all-loving; God cares for everything he has made|Just — fair; God treats people rightly and will judge them fairly|Trinity — one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit|Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus, who is fully God and fully human|Original sin — the tendency to do wrong that all people are born with, which began with Adam and Eve's disobedience|Atonement — the restoring of the relationship between God and humans through Jesus' death and resurrection
points: Creation: in Genesis 1 God makes the world in six days, with his Spirit over the waters; John 1 says all things were made through the Word, the Son.|Answers to evil: people misuse the free will God gave them; suffering can build courage and compassion; Christians fight it, as Jesus healed the sick.|Jesus was crucified on Good Friday, rose on the third day, leaving an empty tomb (Mark 16), and ascended to heaven forty days later (Acts 1).|Salvation through law, by keeping the commandments; through grace, a free gift of God received by faith; through the Spirit, who helps believers live well.|Matthew 25: the sheep, who fed the hungry and welcomed the stranger, go to eternal life, and the goats to punishment. Catholics also believe in purgatory.

title: Christian worship and festivals
words: Liturgical worship — a service with a set order and set words, such as the Catholic Mass|Non-liturgical worship — a service with no fixed order, often built round Bible readings, hymns and a sermon|Informal worship — spontaneous worship with open prayer and praise, often in a house church|Sacrament — an outward sign of an inward grace from God; Catholics and Orthodox Christians have seven, most Protestants two|Infant baptism — baptising a baby to welcome it into the Church; Catholics believe it frees the child from original sin|Eucharist — the service that remembers the Last Supper with bread and wine; also called Holy Communion or Mass|Pilgrimage — a journey to a holy place, made to pray, to seek healing or to grow closer to God
points: The Lord's Prayer, taught by Jesus (Matthew 6), is a set prayer said in most services; informal prayer is in a person's own words.|Believers' baptism: Baptists and Pentecostals fully immerse people old enough to declare their faith, as Jesus was baptised as an adult in the Jordan.|Eucharist: Catholics believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation); many Protestants share them as a memorial.|Lourdes, France: Bernadette saw visions of Mary there in 1858, and the sick come to bathe in its spring. Iona, Scotland: St Columba's island, for quiet prayer.|Christmas celebrates the incarnation, after Advent; Easter, the most important festival, celebrates the resurrection, after Lent, Holy Week and Good Friday.

title: The Church in the world
words: Mission — the Church's calling to spread the gospel and to serve others, at home and abroad|Evangelism — preaching the Christian message to bring people to faith|Church growth — more people coming to faith and new churches being started|Agape — selfless, unconditional love, the kind Jesus taught and showed|Food bank — a place giving free food to people in crisis; many are run by churches|Reconciliation — restoring friendship and peace between people or groups after a conflict|Persecution — hostility and ill-treatment because of a person's faith
points: The Great Commission: the risen Jesus sent his followers to make disciples of all nations and baptise them (Matthew 28:19), the root of mission.|Street Pastors: trained volunteers from local churches help vulnerable people in town centres at night, like the Good Samaritan (Luke 10).|Coventry Cathedral, bombed in 1940, became a centre for reconciliation; the Corrymeela Community brings Catholics and Protestants together in Northern Ireland.|Persecution: Christians pray for those who suffer and for their persecutors, following "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44).|Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic) and Tearfund give emergency relief after disasters and fund long-term work, such as clean water projects.

title: Muslim beliefs
words: Tawhid — the oneness of God, who has no partners and nothing like him; the most important belief in Islam|Six articles of faith — Sunni beliefs in God, angels, holy books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and predestination|Usul ad-Din — the five roots of Shi'a faith: Tawhid, justice (Adalat), prophethood, the Imamate and the Day of Judgement|Al-Qadr — predestination: God knows and decides all that happens, yet humans make real choices and are judged on them|Akhirah — everlasting life after death, which for each person is decided on the Day of Judgement|Risalah — prophethood: God's guidance brought to people by prophets|Imamate — the Shi'a belief that God chose Imams from Muhammad's family to lead after him, the first being Ali
points: God is transcendent, beyond the universe, and immanent, nearer to us than our jugular vein (Surah 50:16). All surahs but one open by calling him merciful.|Angels are made of light and obey God: Jibril brought the Qur'an to Muhammad; Mika'il brings rain and nourishment to the earth.|Judgement: everyone's deeds are recorded in a book and judged; the righteous enter Jannah, a garden of paradise, and the wicked Jahannam, a place of fire.|Prophets: Adam the first; Ibrahim, who rejected idols and built the Ka'aba with Isma'il; Muhammad the last, the Seal of the Prophets (Surah 33:40).|Holy books: the Qur'an, God's final word, revealed to Muhammad; the Tawrat (Torah) to Musa, the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud and the Injil (Gospel) to Isa.

title: Muslim worship
words: Five Pillars — the five key duties of Sunni Islam: Shahadah, Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj|Ten Obligatory Acts — the duties of Shi'a Islam, including Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Khums, Hajj and jihad|Shahadah — the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God|Salah — the compulsory prayer, five times a day|Wudu — ritual washing before prayer, so the worshipper is clean and ready to stand before God|Qiblah — the direction of the Ka'aba in Makkah, which Muslims face to pray; a niche called the mihrab shows it|Rak'ah — one set sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitations
points: The five daily prayers: Fajr (dawn), Zuhr (after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night). Many Shi'a pray them in three sessions.|Shi'a Muslims often add "and Ali is the friend of God" to the Shahadah. Saying it sincerely, usually before witnesses, is how a person becomes a Muslim.|Jummah: the Friday midday prayer, said together at the mosque after a sermon (khutbah). Each prayer time is announced by the adhan, the call to prayer.|Du'a: personal prayer in a Muslim's own words, at any time, alongside the set Salah.|Many Shi'a Muslims rest the forehead on a small clay tablet (turbah), often of earth from Karbala, when they prostrate.

title: Muslim duties and festivals
words: Sawm — fasting from food, drink and sexual relations between dawn and sunset in the month of Ramadan|Zakah — giving 2.5% of savings above a minimum amount (nisab) to those in need, once a year|Khums — a Shi'a duty to give a fifth of surplus yearly income, shared between religious leaders and those in need|Hajj — pilgrimage to Makkah in the month of Dhul-Hijjah, a duty once in a lifetime for those healthy and able to afford it|Ihram — the state of holiness for Hajj; men wear two plain white sheets, so all are equal before God|Greater jihad — the inner struggle to live as God wants; the most important kind|Lesser jihad — the outward struggle to defend Islam, which may be military but only under strict conditions
points: Excused from Sawm: children, the sick, the elderly, travellers and pregnant women. Those who can make up the missed days later do so.|Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan and remembers the first revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad in 610 CE.|Hajj: circling the Ka'aba seven times; walking between Safa and Marwah, as Hajar did looking for water; standing at Arafat; stoning the pillars at Mina.|Id-ul-Fitr celebrates the end of Ramadan; Id-ul-Adha, during Hajj, recalls Ibrahim's readiness to sacrifice his son, and an animal is sacrificed.|Ashura, 10 Muharram: Shi'a mourn Husayn, Muhammad's grandson, killed at Karbala in 680 CE; many Sunnis fast to remember Musa being saved from Pharaoh.

title: Relationships and families
words: Cohabitation — living together as a couple without being married; Islam and traditional Christian teaching say sex belongs within marriage|Procreation — having children; a main purpose of marriage in Christianity and Islam|Contraception — methods used to prevent pregnancy, such as the pill or condoms|Annulment — a Catholic ruling that a marriage was never valid, which leaves both people free to marry|Nuclear family — two parents and their children; an extended family also includes grandparents, aunts and uncles|Polygamy — being married to more than one person at the same time; bigamy is a crime in the UK|Gender discrimination — treating someone unfairly because of their sex; the Equality Act 2010 makes it illegal at work and in services
points: Mark 10:9, "what God has joined together": the Catholic Church does not recognise divorce; the Church of England may remarry divorced people in church.|Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2014; the Church of England does not conduct it, but Quakers do, and humanists support it.|Contraception: the Catholic Church teaches that only natural methods are acceptable; the Church of England and many Muslims accept it within marriage.|Islam allows divorce as a last resort, with a waiting time (iddah) for reconciliation; a man may have up to four wives if he treats them equally (Surah 4:3).|Galatians 3:28 says all are "one in Christ"; the Church of England has ordained women as priests since 1994, but the Catholic Church ordains only men.

title: Religion and life
words: Big Bang theory — the theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a hot, dense point, and is still expanding|Evolution — the theory that living things, humans included, developed from earlier forms over millions of years by natural selection|Stewardship — the duty to look after the world for God; in Islam humans are khalifah, trustees of the earth|Sanctity of life — life is holy because God created it, so only God should end it|Quality of life — how good a life is, judged by health, comfort and the ability to live it fully|Abortion — the deliberate ending of a pregnancy so that the foetus does not survive|Euthanasia — ending a life to relieve suffering; voluntary if the person asks, non-voluntary if they cannot
points: Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, first proposed the Big Bang; many Christians see it as how God created, while creationists read Genesis literally.|Genesis 1:28 gives humans dominion over the earth and Genesis 2:15 puts Adam in the garden to work it and take care of it: stewardship, not exploitation.|The Abortion Act 1967, amended in 1990, allows abortion up to 24 weeks if two doctors agree; later only in rare cases, such as a risk to the mother's life.|Abortion: Catholics teach life begins at conception, so it is always wrong; most Muslims allow it to save the mother's life; humanists stress her choice.|Euthanasia: most Christians and Muslims oppose it because of the sanctity of life and support hospice care; many humanists support it for quality of life.

title: Peace and conflict
words: Pacifism — the belief that war and violence are always wrong; Quakers are a pacifist Christian group|Just war theory — the conditions a war must meet to be morally right, such as a just cause and being a last resort|Holy war — a war fought for God or a religion and declared by a religious leader, such as the Crusades|Terrorism — the use of violence, often against civilians, to cause fear and force political change|Weapons of mass destruction — nuclear, chemical and biological weapons that kill huge numbers of people without discriminating|Retaliation — deliberately harming someone in return for a harm they caused|Justice — fairness, where people are treated equally and wrongs are put right; injustice is a common cause of conflict
points: Just war conditions: a just cause, declared by proper authority, with the right intention, as a last resort, with a chance of success and proportionate force.|Lesser jihad must be declared by a religious authority, be in self-defence or against oppression, spare civilians, and stop when the enemy seeks peace.|Christian pacifists quote "blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9) and Jesus telling his follower to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52).|Nuclear weapons have been used in war only on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in 1945; many Christians and Muslims say they can never be just, as they kill civilians.|Christian Aid, CAFOD and Islamic Relief give food, shelter and medical care to people caught up in war and to refugees, whatever their religion.

title: Crime and punishment
words: Retribution — an aim of punishment: making criminals pay for what they did|Deterrence — an aim of punishment: putting the criminal and others off committing crime|Reformation — an aim of punishment: helping the criminal change and become law-abiding|Corporal punishment — punishment that causes physical pain, such as caning; illegal in all UK schools|Death penalty — capital punishment: the state putting someone to death for a crime|Forgiveness — letting go of anger and blame towards someone who has done wrong, while they may still be punished|Principle of utility — the right action is the one that brings the greatest good for the greatest number
points: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (Exodus 21:24) is used to support retribution; Jesus taught "turn the other cheek" instead (Matthew 5:39).|Peter asked whether to forgive seven times; Jesus said seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), meaning without limit.|Stealing food because of poverty is still theft, but many Christians and Muslims say the cause matters, so they run food banks and give to the poor.|Britain suspended hanging for murder in 1965, abolished 1969; Catholics call it inadmissible; Islam allows it, but the family may forgive (Surah 2:178).|Utility: if executions deter murder, they save more lives than they take; against: an innocent person may be executed, and the sanctity of life forbids it.

Je joue means I play or I am playing.|choisir → je choisis, tu choisis, il choisit, nous choisissons, vous choisissez, ils choisissent.|entendre → j'entends, tu entends, il entend, nous entendons, vous entendez, ils entendent.|Je dois faire mes devoirs, mais je veux sortir. — I have to do my homework, but I want to go out.|Je me lève à sept heures et je m'habille. — I get up at seven o'clock and get dressed.

title: Memory
words: Encoding, storage and retrieval — putting information into memory, holding it there over time, and getting it back out when it is needed|Episodic, semantic and procedural memory — memories of personal events, of facts and meanings, and of how to do things such as riding a bike|Multi-store model — Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968): information passes from the sensory store to short-term memory and, if rehearsed, to long-term memory|Primacy and recency effects — the first and the last items in a list are recalled better than the items in the middle|Reconstructive memory — Bartlett (1932): a memory is rebuilt from schemas each time it is recalled, not replayed like a recording, so it can be distorted|Interference — proactive when old learning disrupts new learning; retroactive when new learning disrupts old|Context and false memories — recall is better in the same setting as learning; a false memory is recall of something that did not happen
points: STM: coded mainly by sound, holds about 7 ± 2 items for about 18–30 seconds unrehearsed. LTM: coded mainly by meaning, unlimited, can last a lifetime.|Murdock (1962): lists of words recalled in any order gave a serial position curve; early words had been rehearsed into LTM, the last were still in STM.|Bartlett (1932): English participants retold the Native American tale War of the Ghosts; it became shorter and more familiar, and canoes became boats.|Godden and Baddeley (1975): divers recalled words better when they learned and recalled in the same place, both underwater or both on land.

title: Perception
words: Sensation and perception — sensation is detecting information with the sense organs; perception is the brain organising it and making sense of it|Monocular depth cues — cues that need only one eye: height in plane, relative size, occlusion and linear perspective|Binocular depth cues — retinal disparity (each eye sees a slightly different image) and convergence (the eyes turn inwards more for near objects)|Size constancy — seeing an object as the same size even though its image on the retina shrinks as it moves away|Direct theory — Gibson: perception comes straight from the information in light, such as motion parallax, with no need for past experience; nature|Constructivist theory — Gregory: perception is built from inferences, using visual cues and past experience to construct a model of reality; nurture|Perceptual set — a readiness to perceive something in a certain way, shaped by culture, motivation, emotion and expectation
points: Motion parallax: from a moving train, nearby fences rush past while distant hills seem to drift slowly, which shows how far away each is.|Müller-Lyer: the line with outward fins looks like the far corner of a room, so it is judged further away and therefore longer — misread depth cues.|Ambiguity: the Necker cube and Rubin's vase. Fiction: the Kanizsa triangle. Misread depth cues: the Ponzo illusion. Size constancy: the Ames room.|Gilchrist and Nesberg (1952): hungry participants judged pictures of food to be brighter than participants who were not hungry did — motivation.|Bruner and Minturn (1955): the same broken figure was drawn as B after a list of letters and as 13 after a list of numbers — expectation.

title: Development
words: Brain development — the brainstem and thalamus form first, then the more complex cerebellum and cortex; shaped by both nature and nurture|Schema — a mental framework of knowledge about something, built up from experience|Assimilation and accommodation — fitting new information into an existing schema; changing the schema when the information does not fit|Conservation — knowing that a quantity stays the same when only its appearance changes, such as a row of counters being spread out|Egocentrism — seeing the world only from your own point of view; typical of the pre-operational stage|Fixed and growth mindset — Dweck: believing that ability is set and cannot change, or that it grows with effort and practice|Self-efficacy — a person's belief in their own ability to succeed at a task
points: Piaget's stages: sensorimotor 0–2 (object permanence), pre-operational 2–7, concrete operational 7–11 (conservation), formal operational 11+ (abstract thought).|Piaget in school: teach a child when they are ready, set tasks that suit their stage, and let them learn by discovery.|McGarrigle and Donaldson (1974): when a "naughty teddy" spread the counters, 62% of 4–6 year olds conserved, against 16% when the adult did it.|Hughes (1975): hiding a boy doll from two policeman dolls, 90% of children aged 3½ to 5 succeeded, so they were less egocentric than Piaget claimed.|Dweck: praise effort, as in "you worked hard on that", not ability. Willingham: no good evidence that teaching to a visual or verbal learning style helps.

title: Research methods
words: Null and alternate hypotheses — the alternate hypothesis predicts a difference or a relationship; the null hypothesis predicts there will be none|Variables — the independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured, and extraneous variables are kept the same|Sampling — random, opportunity, systematic (every nth name on a list) or stratified (each subgroup in proportion), from a target population|Experimental designs — independent groups (different people in each condition), repeated measures (the same people in all) or matched pairs|Experiments — laboratory (a controlled setting), field (a real-life setting, IV still changed) natural (the IV changes on its own) or quasi (the IV is a difference between people, such as age)|Other methods — interviews and questionnaires (open or closed questions), case studies, correlations, and observations (naturalistic or controlled)|Ethical issues — informed consent, deception, confidentiality, the right to withdraw, protection from harm and debriefing
formulas: Mean — mean = Σx / n|Median position — (n + 1) / 2|Range — range = highest − lowest|Percentage — percentage = part / total × 100|Percentage change — percentage change = (new − old) / old × 100|Stratified sample — number from a subgroup = (subgroup size) / (population size) × sample size
points: Scores 4, 6, 6, 9, 15: mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, median = 6, mode = 6, range = 15 − 4 = 11.|18 of 24 participants conformed: 18 / 24 × 100 = 75%. Conformers to non-conformers is 18 : 6, which simplifies to 3 : 1.|300 students, 120 of them in Year 10, sample of 20: Year 10 gets 120 / 300 × 20 = 8 places.|Counterbalancing: half do condition A then B, half B then A, so order effects cancel out. Random allocation spreads participant variables evenly.|Normal distribution: bell-shaped and symmetrical, with the mean, median and mode equal at the peak. 45 000 in standard form is 4.5 × 10^4.

title: Social influence
words: Conformity — changing behaviour or beliefs to fit in with a group|Obedience — following a direct order from a person in authority|Agentic and autonomous states — acting for an authority and so not feeling responsible; or acting on your own free will and feeling responsible|Legitimacy of authority — the belief that the person giving orders has the right to, often shown by a uniform or the setting|Authoritarian personality — Adorno (1950): rigid, respectful of authority and hostile to those seen as inferior, from a strict upbringing; more obedient|Bystander intervention — onlookers help less with more people present or a high cost of helping, and more with expertise or similarity to the victim|Deindividuation and social loafing — losing your sense of personal identity in a crowd; putting in less effort as part of a group
points: Asch (1951): judging line lengths beside confederates who gave wrong answers, participants conformed on 32% of critical trials; 75% conformed at least once.|Asch's variations: conformity rose with up to three confederates and with a harder task; it fell if one confederate gave the right answer.|Milgram (1963): 40 men gave a "learner" shocks they believed were real; all went to 300 volts and 65% to the full 450 volts — the agentic state.|Piliavin (1969): on the New York subway a man with a cane who collapsed was helped on 95% of trials, one who seemed drunk on about 50% — cost of helping.|Zimbardo (1969): women in hoods and baggy lab coats gave "shocks" for about twice as long as women wearing name tags — deindividuation.

title: Language, thought and communication
