words: Piaget's view — language depends on thought: a child must understand an idea before using the words for it|Sapir–Whorf hypothesis — thought depends on language: the words a language has shape how its speakers think about and see the world|Displacement — talking about things that are not here and now, such as the past or plans for the future; a feature of human language that most animal communication lacks|Non-verbal communication — passing on messages without words, through eye contact, body language, touch and personal space|Body language — open or closed posture, postural echo (copying another person's posture, a sign of rapport) and touch|Personal space — the area around a person that they treat as their own; its size varies with culture, status and gender|Darwin's evolutionary theory — non-verbal signals such as baring the teeth in anger evolved because they helped survival, so they are innate and adaptive
points: Von Frisch: a round dance means food is near the hive; in the waggle dance the angle gives its direction from the sun and the waggle's length its distance.|Animal communication serves survival, reproduction, territory and food. Humans can also plan ahead, discuss the past and make up new sentences.|Brown and Lenneberg (1954): Zuni speakers have one word for yellow and orange, and confused them more than English speakers did — language shaping thought.|Eye contact regulates conversation: a speaker looks away when starting to talk and back at the listener when finishing. Pupils widen with attraction.|Innate: babies born blind still smile. Learned: Yuki (2007) found Japanese people read emotion from the eyes and Americans from the mouth.

title: Brain and neuropsychology
words: Central and peripheral nervous systems — the CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS is every other nerve, split into somatic and autonomic|Autonomic nervous system — controls automatic functions; the sympathetic branch arouses the body for fight or flight, the parasympathetic calms it|Neurons — sensory neurons carry messages to the CNS, relay neurons pass them on inside it, motor neurons carry them to muscles and glands|Synaptic transmission — an impulse reaches the end of a neuron and releases neurotransmitters across the synapse, which excite or inhibit the next neuron|Lobes — frontal (motor area, Broca's area), parietal (somatosensory area), occipital (visual area), temporal (auditory area, Wernicke's area)|Cerebellum — at the back of the brain, below the cortex; controls balance and coordinates movement|Brain scans — CT uses X-rays to show structure; PET uses a radioactive tracer to show activity; fMRI shows activity from changes in blood oxygen
points: Fight or flight: heart rate and breathing rise, pupils widen, digestion slows. James–Lange: the body's arousal comes first and the emotion follows.|Hebb (1949): learning strengthens the connections between neurons that fire together, forming cell assemblies; practice makes a pathway efficient.|Penfield: stimulating the temporal lobes of awake patients during surgery for epilepsy made some relive past experiences — the interpretive cortex.|Tulving (1989): scans using radioactive gold showed more blood flow at the front of the brain for episodic memories and at the back for semantic ones.|A stroke in Broca's area makes speech slow and effortful; one in the motor area of the left hemisphere weakens the right side of the body.

title: Psychological problems
words: Mental health — emotional and psychological wellbeing; beliefs about its problems vary between cultures, and stigma can stop people seeking help|Unipolar and bipolar depression — unipolar is low mood alone; bipolar swings between depression and mania|Neurotransmitter explanation — the biological explanation of depression: too little serotonin activity, which affects mood, sleep and appetite|Negative schema — a pessimistic set of beliefs about yourself, the world and the future, which shapes how events are interpreted|Attributional style — how a person explains events; a depressive style blames failure on causes that are internal, stable and global|Addiction — a compulsion to keep taking a substance or doing an activity despite harm; dependence adds tolerance and withdrawal symptoms|Peer influence — the psychological explanation of addiction: friends who use a substance make it seem normal, offer it and reward joining in
points: The ICD diagnoses depression from symptoms such as low mood, loss of interest or enjoyment and tiredness, lasting at least two weeks.|SSRI antidepressants stop serotonin being reabsorbed, so more stays in the synapse. CBT challenges negative thoughts and replaces them with realistic ones.|Wiles (2013): of patients not helped by antidepressants alone, 46% improved when CBT was added, against 22% with usual care.|Kaij (1960): Swedish twins and alcohol abuse — concordance about 54% for identical twins against 28% for non-identical twins: genetic vulnerability.|Aversion therapy pairs alcohol with a drug that causes sickness, so drinking becomes unpleasant. Self-management includes twelve-step self-help groups.

title: GCSE Sociology
summary: The whole GCSE in eight short chapters: the key words, the key sociologists and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Sociology (8192) specification.
subject: Sociology

title: Sociological perspectives
words: Functionalism — a consensus approach: each part of society, such as the family or school, has a function that helps society run smoothly|Marxism — a conflict approach: the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, exploit the proletariat, who sell their labour|Feminism — a conflict approach: society is patriarchal, organised by and for men, and women's inequality must be challenged|Interactionism — a social action approach: society is built up from small-scale interactions and the meanings people give them, such as labels|Consensus — broad agreement on shared norms and values, which holds society together|Conflict — groups with opposing interests, such as classes or genders, competing for wealth and power|Structure and action — whether society shapes people from above (structural theories) or people create society through their choices (action theories)
points: Durkheim: shared values bind society together in social solidarity; when they weaken the result is anomie, a state of normlessness.|Marx: capitalism splits society into the bourgeoisie and the exploited proletariat, who he predicted would one day overthrow it in a revolution.|Weber: inequality comes from class, status and party, not ownership alone, and sociologists must understand the meanings behind people's actions.|Liberal feminists seek equality through laws such as the Equal Pay Act 1970; radical feminists see patriarchy as the root of inequality and want deeper change.|The family four ways: it meets society's needs (functionalist), serves capitalism (Marxist), oppresses women (feminist), is negotiated daily (interactionist).

title: Socialisation and social control
words: Culture — the whole way of life of a group: its shared norms, values, beliefs, language and customs|Norms — unwritten rules of expected behaviour in a situation, such as queuing|Values — general beliefs about what is right and worth striving for, such as honesty or respect for life|Primary socialisation — learning the basic norms and values of a society in early childhood, mainly from the family|Secondary socialisation — learning that continues through life from agencies such as school, peer groups, the media, religion and work|Formal social control — control by written rules and laws, enforced by agencies such as the police, the courts and prisons|Informal social control — control through other people's reactions, such as praise, gossip or disapproval from family and friends
points: Value: respect for older people. A norm that follows from it: giving up your seat on the bus to an older passenger.|Oakley on gender socialisation: canalisation steers girls to dolls and boys to toy cars; manipulation encourages behaviour seen as fitting their sex.|Sanctions: a merit certificate is a positive sanction; a detention, a fine or a disapproving look is a negative one.|Nature or nurture: what counts as polite, from greeting with a kiss to bowing, differs between cultures, so much behaviour is learned rather than inborn.|Peer group control: a teenager wears the same trainers as friends to fit in, and risks being mocked or left out if not.

title: Family forms and roles
words: Nuclear family — two parents and their dependent children living in one household|Extended family — a nuclear family plus other relatives such as grandparents; a beanpole family has many generations but few aunts, uncles or cousins|Reconstituted family — a stepfamily, in which at least one partner has children from an earlier relationship|Lone-parent family — one parent living with their dependent children|Conjugal roles — a couple's roles in the home: segregated when tasks are split by gender, joint when they are shared|Family diversity — the variety of family types today; Rapoport and Rapoport named five kinds: organisational, cultural, class, life course and cohort|Polygamy — marriage to more than one spouse at a time; polygyny is one husband with several wives, polyandry one wife with several husbands
points: Parsons (functionalist): the family's two basic functions are primary socialisation and stabilising adult personalities; men instrumental, women expressive.|Zaretsky (Marxist): the family serves capitalism as a unit of consumption and a private refuge. Delphy and Leonard (feminist): men exploit women's family work.|Young and Willmott: families moved in stages to the symmetrical family, home-centred, with joint conjugal roles and both partners often working.|Oakley: interviews with 40 London housewives found few husbands did much housework, so symmetry was exaggerated; the "conventional family" ideal stays strong.|Divorce rose after the Divorce Reform Act 1969 made irretrievable breakdown the ground; no-fault divorce began in 2022. Secularisation also played a part.

title: Education and achievement
words: Hidden curriculum — the norms and values taught by the way school is run rather than in lessons, such as punctuality and obedience|Meritocracy — a system in which rewards go to ability and effort, not to background|Streaming — grouping pupils by ability for all lessons; setting groups them subject by subject; banding puts them in broad ability bands|Self-fulfilling prophecy — a label such as "bright" or "thick" changes how a pupil is treated and so comes true|Counter-school culture — a group of pupils who reject the school's values and win status by breaking its rules|Material deprivation — lacking money for things that help at school, such as books, a computer, a quiet room or trips|Marketisation — competition between schools through league tables and parental choice; Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz found it favours middle-class parents
points: Parsons (functionalist): school is the bridge between family and society, judging everyone by the same standards, so success rests on merit.|Bowles and Gintis (Marxist): the correspondence principle; school mirrors work, its hidden curriculum teaches obedience, and meritocracy is a myth.|Willis: 12 working-class "lads" rejected school and so drifted into manual jobs. Ball: lower-band pupils were labelled and formed an anti-school culture.|Douglas: middle-class parents showed more interest in schooling. Halsey, Heath and Ridge: service-class boys were far likelier to reach university.|Girls outperform boys at GCSE, and Chinese and Indian pupils have the highest average results; explanations include labelling, parental support and racism.

title: Crime and deviance
words: Crime — an act that breaks the law and can be punished by the state|Deviance — behaviour that goes against a group's norms; it may or may not be illegal|Dark figure of crime — crime that is never reported to or recorded by the police, so it is missing from official statistics|Victim survey — asking people which crimes they have suffered, as the Crime Survey for England and Wales does|Self-report study — an anonymous questionnaire asking people which crimes they have committed|Moral panic — an exaggerated reaction by the media and public to a group seen as a threat, as Stanley Cohen showed with the mods and rockers|White-collar crime — crime by people in high-status jobs, such as fraud or tax evasion, which is often hidden and less often prosecuted
points: Merton (functionalist): strain between the goal of wealth and the means to reach it leads some to innovate, through crime, or to retreat and drop out.|Albert Cohen: working-class boys who fail at school feel status frustration and join delinquent subcultures that give status for acts such as vandalism.|Becker (interactionist): deviance is behaviour that people so label; a youth labelled a "troublemaker" may find the label becomes his master status.|Heidensohn: women offend less as they are more controlled at home, in public and at work. Carlen: poor women offended when the class and gender deals failed.|Social construction: sex between men was a crime in England and Wales until 1967, while smoking in pubs was legal until 2007.

title: Social stratification
words: Social stratification — the division of society into layers that are unequal in wealth, income, status and power|Life chances — the chances of good things in life, such as health, education and housing, which vary with class|Social mobility — moving up or down between classes, within one lifetime (intragenerational) or between generations (intergenerational)|Absolute poverty — lacking the minimum needed to survive, such as food, clean water and shelter|Relative poverty — being poor compared with the usual living standards of a society; Townsend called it relative deprivation|Ascribed and achieved status — ascribed status is fixed at birth, such as a royal title; achieved status is earned, such as qualifying as a doctor|Authority — power that people accept as legitimate; Weber's three types are traditional, charismatic and rational-legal
points: Davis and Moore (functionalist): high rewards draw the most able into the most important jobs. Tumin: importance is hard to judge, and talent is wasted.|Marx: class is about owning the means of production or not. Weber: class rests on market position, such as skills, and status and party divide people too.|Walby: patriarchy works through six structures: paid work, the household, the state, male violence, sexuality and culture.|Murray (New Right): an underclass living on benefits, outside work, passes its values on to its children; critics say this blames the poor for poverty.|Life chances: people in the richest areas of England live several years longer than those in the poorest, so class shapes even how long you live.

title: Research methods
words: Quantitative data — numbers and statistics, such as the percentage of couples who share the housework|Qualitative data — words and meanings, giving rich detail about people's feelings and experiences|Primary and secondary data — primary is collected by the researcher; secondary already exists, such as official statistics or diaries|Reliability — the method can be repeated and gives the same results|Validity — the data gives a true picture of what is being studied|Representative sample — a sample with the same characteristics as the population, so the findings can be generalised|Ethics — the moral rules of research: informed consent, confidentiality, protection from harm and no deception
points: Structured interviews and questionnaires give reliable quantitative data, easy to compare; unstructured interviews give rich, valid data but are hard to repeat.|Participant observation, as Willis used with the lads, shows meanings first hand; done covertly, it raises the ethical problems of deception and no consent.|Sampling: random gives everyone an equal chance; stratified mirrors the population's groups; snowball follows contacts, useful for hidden groups such as gangs.|Official crime statistics are cheap and cover the whole country, but they miss the dark figure of crime, so they may lack validity.|A pilot study, a trial run on a few people, finds confusing questions before the main study. A longitudinal study follows the same group over years.

title: Answering the question types
words: AO1 — knowledge: showing you know and understand the theories, concepts, studies and methods|AO2 — application: using that knowledge on the question, the item or a research situation|AO3 — analysis and evaluation: weighing theories, studies and methods to argue, judge and conclude|Item — a short source printed in the paper, often describing a study, which some questions ask you to use|Identify and explain — name one point, then develop it with how or why, backed by a study or an example|Discuss how far — the 12-mark question: weigh the view against others, using named sociologists, then reach a judgement
points: Two papers, each 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks and half the GCSE: Paper 1 families and education, Paper 2 crime and deviance and social stratification.|Each section mixes multiple choice, short answers and questions on an item about a study with longer 12-mark "discuss how far" answers.|Identify and explain: "One function is primary socialisation. Parsons argues the family teaches children society's norms and values, shaping who they become."|Methods, applied: "Questionnaires suit a study of housework: they reach many couples and are easy to compare, but people may exaggerate their share."|12 marks end in a judgement: "Bowles and Gintis show school also teaches obedience to authority, so the functionalist view is only partly true."

title: GCSE Business
summary: The whole GCSE in ten short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Business specification.
subject: Business

title: Enterprise and entrepreneurship
words: Entrepreneur — a person who organises resources, makes business decisions and takes risks to start or run a business|Enterprise — using initiative and taking risks to spot an opportunity and turn it into a business|Risk — what an entrepreneur could lose: the business may fail, savings may be lost and there is no steady wage|Reward — what an entrepreneur hopes to gain: business success, profit and independence|Added value — the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the materials bought in to make it|Unique selling point (USP) — a feature that makes a product different from its competitors and gives customers a reason to choose it|Obsolete — out of date and no longer wanted, often because newer technology has replaced it
formulas: Added value — added value = selling price − cost of bought-in materials
points: A café spends 60p on the coffee, milk and cup and sells the drink for £2.80: added value = £2.80 − £0.60 = £2.20.|New ideas come from new technology (streaming replaced DVD rental), changing wants (plant-based food) and products becoming obsolete.|Not every idea is original: a bakery that adds a home delivery service has adapted an existing service.|Ways to add value: convenience, branding, quality, design and a USP — a branded hoodie sells for more than a plain one made of the same cotton.|Model sentence: "Sam risks £5000 of savings, but if the shop succeeds she gains profit and the independence of being her own boss."

title: Spotting an opportunity
words: Customer needs — what customers want from a product: the right price, quality, choice and convenience|Primary research — new data collected first-hand for the business's own purpose: surveys, questionnaires, focus groups and observation|Secondary research — data that already exists, collected by someone else: the internet, market reports and government reports|Quantitative and qualitative data — quantitative data is numerical and can be measured; qualitative data is opinions, feelings and reasons given in words|Market segmentation — dividing a market into groups of customers with similar features: location, demographics, lifestyle, income or age|Market map — a diagram placing products on two axes, such as price and quality, to show the competition and any gaps|Gap in the market — a customer need that no existing product meets
points: Market research identifies customer needs and gaps in the market, reduces risk and informs decisions before money is spent.|A survey of 200 local people finds 50 would buy vegan cakes: 50 / 200 × 100 = 25%, quantitative data that supports the idea.|Asking only friends and family gives unreliable data: the sample is small and does not represent the target market.|Social media polls and comments collect research cheaply and quickly, but the people who answer may not be typical customers.|A new gym near a cheap chain competes on customer service and quality rather than price — judge rivals on price, quality, location, range and service.

title: Putting the idea into practice
words: Aims and objectives — an aim is a long-term goal; objectives are measurable targets, financial (survival, profit, market share) or non-financial (independence, challenge)|Fixed costs — costs that stay the same whatever the output, such as rent and salaries|Variable costs — costs that rise and fall with output, such as raw materials and packaging|Break-even point — the output at which total revenue equals total costs, so there is neither a profit nor a loss|Margin of safety — how far actual sales are above the break-even level of output|Cash-flow forecast — a prediction of the cash coming into and going out of a business each month|Sources of finance — short term: overdraft and trade credit; long term: personal savings, loans, share capital, venture capital, retained profit and crowdfunding
formulas: Total revenue — total revenue = price × quantity sold|Total costs — total costs = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit × quantity)|Profit — profit = total revenue − total costs|Interest on a loan — interest (%) = (total repayment − amount borrowed) / (amount borrowed) × 100|Break-even output — break-even = (fixed costs) / (selling price per unit − variable cost per unit); margin of safety = actual sales − break-even sales|Cash flow — net cash flow = cash inflows − cash outflows; closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow
points: Price £4, variable cost £1.50 a unit, fixed costs £2000 a month: break-even = 2000 ÷ (4 − 1.50) = 800 units a month.|Selling 1000 a month: revenue £4000, total costs £2000 + £1500 = £3500, profit £500; margin of safety = 1000 − 800 = 200 units.|Borrow £8000 and repay £9200 in total: interest = 1200 ÷ 8000 × 100 = 15%.|Opening balance £500, inflows £3000, outflows £3400: net cash flow −£400, closing balance £100, which is next month's opening balance.|Profit is not cash: a business that gives customers 60 days to pay can be profitable yet unable to pay its suppliers and staff, and become insolvent.

title: Making the business effective
words: Limited liability — owners can lose only the money they put into the business; with unlimited liability, their personal possessions can be taken to pay its debts|Sole trader — a business owned by one person, who keeps all the profit and has unlimited liability|Partnership — two or more owners who share the decisions and the profits, and in an ordinary partnership have unlimited liability|Private limited company (Ltd) — owned by shareholders who have limited liability; its shares cannot be offered to the general public|Franchise — a franchisee pays to trade under a franchisor's brand, selling its products and following its methods|Marketing mix — the 4Ps: product, price, promotion and place, balanced to meet customer needs|Business plan — a document setting out the idea, objectives, target market, forecasts, finance, location and marketing mix
points: A sole trader with £20 000 of business debts could have to sell her car to pay them; a shareholder in a private limited company loses only what she invested.|A franchisee pays a start-up fee and a royalty from revenue, but gets a known brand, training and support, so the risk is lower and the control less.|Location: a café goes where its customers pass; a factory near materials or labour; an online shop needs only a warehouse with good transport links.|E-commerce lets a small business sell across the country, and social media is a cheap way to promote it.|A bank reads the cash-flow forecast and break-even in a business plan before lending; writing the plan makes the owner think through the risks.

title: External influences
words: Stakeholder — anyone with an interest in a business: owners, employees, customers, managers, suppliers, the local community, pressure groups and the government|Consumer law — goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described, or the customer is entitled to a repair, replacement or refund|Employment law — rules on recruitment, pay (the National Minimum Wage), discrimination, and health and safety at work|Inflation — a rise in the general level of prices over time|Interest rate — the cost of borrowing money and the reward for saving it|Exchange rate — the price of one currency in terms of another, such as £1 = $1.25|Unemployment — people who are able and willing to work but cannot find a job
formulas: Pounds to a foreign currency — foreign price = price in pounds × (foreign currency per £1)|A foreign currency to pounds — price in pounds = (foreign price) / (foreign currency per £1)
points: The pound falls from $1.25 to $1.20: a $120 import rises from £96 to £100, and a £50 export falls from $62.50 to $60.|Interest rates rise: loans and overdrafts cost more. Income tax rises: households have less to spend. Either way, sales of luxuries tend to fall.|Shareholders want higher profit and employees want higher pay: a pay rise satisfies one group at the cost of the other.|Obeying the law costs money (safety training, paying at least the minimum wage), but breaking it risks fines, legal action and a damaged reputation.|Technology: e-commerce, social media and contactless payment can raise sales and cut costs, but cost money to set up and keep secure.

title: Growing the business
words: Organic growth — growing from within, through new products (innovation, research and development) or new markets|Merger — two businesses agree to join together as one|Takeover — one business buys enough of another's shares, more than half, to take control of it|Public limited company (plc) — a company whose shares can be sold to the general public; first selling them on the stock market is a flotation|Globalisation — the world's economies becoming more connected, so businesses buy, sell and locate across borders|Multinational — a business that operates in more than one country|Tariff — a tax on imported goods; a trade bloc is a group of countries that remove or reduce such barriers between themselves
points: Finance for growth: retained profit and selling assets are internal; loans and share capital, including floating as a plc, are external.|Objectives change as a business evolves: from survival to growth, entering new markets, widening the product range, or cutting staff when sales fall.|A 10% tariff on a £200 import adds £20, so it costs £220 and goods made at home look cheaper.|To compete abroad a business may sell through e-commerce and adapt its marketing mix: a new product name, price or promotion for each country.|Fairtrade cocoa or recycled packaging raises costs and cuts profit, but can attract customers and head off a pressure group campaign.

title: Marketing decisions
words: Design mix — the balance of function, aesthetics (how it looks) and cost in a product's design|Product life cycle — the stages of a product's sales over time: introduction, growth, maturity and decline|Extension strategy — a way to delay decline, such as new packaging, new features, a new market or a lower price|Product differentiation — making a product different from its rivals' so that customers choose it|Price skimming — a high price at launch, while the product is new, lowered later|Penetration pricing — a low price at launch to win market share quickly, raised later|E-tailer — a retailer that sells only online, through e-commerce
points: Cost-plus pricing: a cost of £8 a unit plus a 25% mark-up gives a price of 8 × 1.25 = £10.|A soft drink in maturity is relaunched in a sugar-free version with a new can design: an extension strategy.|Promotion fits the segment: targeted online adverts, viral videos on social media and e-newsletters for young buyers, sponsorship for a wide audience.|A shop lets customers see and try the product; an e-tailer reaches more people with lower costs, but customers cannot try before buying.|Each P affects the others: a premium price needs a high-quality product, upmarket promotion and selective outlets, which together build competitive advantage.

title: Operational decisions
words: Job production — one-off products made to each customer's order, such as a wedding dress|Batch production — a set number of identical products made together before switching to the next batch, such as loaves of bread|Flow production — identical products made continuously on a production line, such as cans of drink|Just in time (JIT) — stock arrives exactly when it is needed, so little or no stock is held|Procurement — finding and buying supplies, choosing suppliers on quality, cost, delivery speed and reliability, availability and trust|Quality control — inspecting products, usually at the end of production, to find and remove faulty ones|Quality assurance — checking quality at every stage of production so that faults are prevented rather than found
formulas: Labour productivity — productivity = (output in a period) / (number of workers)
points: Bar gate graph: 50 units used a day, lead time 2 days, buffer stock 100: reorder at 100 + 50 × 2 = 200 units, so the delivery arrives as stock hits the buffer.|10 workers make 400 units a day: productivity = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 units per worker a day. New machinery may raise this but costs money.|JIT cuts storage costs and waste, but relies on reliable suppliers: one late delivery can stop production.|Fewer faults mean less waste and fewer returns, which cuts costs and gives a competitive advantage through a reputation for quality.|The sales process: product knowledge, fast service, engaging customers, acting on feedback and after-sales service bring repeat custom.

title: Financial decisions
words: Cost of sales — the direct cost of making or buying in the goods that were sold|Gross profit — the profit left after the cost of sales, before any other costs|Net profit — the profit left after all costs, including operating expenses and interest|Profit margin — profit as a percentage of sales revenue: how much of each £1 of sales is kept as profit|Average rate of return (ARR) — the average yearly profit from an investment as a percentage of what it cost|Quantitative data — figures from graphs, charts, accounts and market research, used to support and justify decisions|Limitations of financial data — it shows what happened rather than why, can be out of date, and leaves out qualitative factors such as staff morale
formulas: Gross profit — gross profit = sales revenue − cost of sales|Net profit — net profit = gross profit − (other operating expenses + interest)|Gross profit margin — gross profit margin (%) = (gross profit) / (sales revenue) × 100|Net profit margin — net profit margin (%) = (net profit) / (sales revenue) × 100|Average annual profit — average annual profit = (total profit) / (number of years), where total profit = total returns − cost of investment|Average rate of return — ARR (%) = (average annual profit) / (cost of investment) × 100
points: Revenue £200 000, cost of sales £120 000: gross profit £80 000, gross profit margin = 80 000 ÷ 200 000 × 100 = 40%.|Expenses and interest of £50 000: net profit £30 000, net profit margin = 30 000 ÷ 200 000 × 100 = 15%.|A £40 000 machine returns £60 000 over 4 years: total profit £20 000, £5000 a year, ARR = 5000 ÷ 40 000 × 100 = 12.5%.|An ARR of 12.5% beats a loan at 8% interest, but the returns are only a forecast.|A steady gross profit margin with a falling net profit margin points to rising overheads, such as rent or salaries.

title: Human resource decisions
words: Hierarchical structure — many layers of management, each manager with few people below; a flat structure has few layers and wider spans of control|Centralised — the main decisions are made at the top by senior managers; decentralised businesses delegate them to branches or lower managers|Job roles — directors set the strategy, senior managers run departments, supervisors lead teams, and operational and support staff do the daily work|Job description — the job's title, duties and responsibilities|Person specification — the qualifications, skills, experience and qualities needed by the person who does the job|Financial motivation — pay (remuneration), bonuses, commission on sales, promotion and fringe benefits such as a staff discount|Non-financial motivation — job rotation (moving between tasks), job enrichment (more challenging work) and autonomy (freedom to decide how to work)
points: A sales assistant on £1500 a month plus 5% commission who sells £20 000 of goods earns 1500 + 1000 = £2500.|Internal recruitment is quicker and cheaper and the person knows the business; external brings new ideas and skills but costs more.|Temporary staff for the Christmas rush and a freelance designer for one project cost less than permanent staff; technology lets people work remotely.|Formal training is a course; informal training is learning from a colleague on the job. Trained staff are more productive and motivated, so fewer leave.|Too little communication leaves staff unsure and demotivated; too much wastes time. Jargon and long chains of command are barriers.

title: GCSE Computer Science
summary: The whole GCSE in twelve short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the OCR GCSE (9–1) Computer Science specification.
subject: Computer Science

title: Systems architecture
words: CPU — the central processing unit: it fetches, decodes and executes the instructions of a program, one after another|Von Neumann architecture — a program's instructions and its data are stored together in the same memory|ALU — the arithmetic logic unit: carries out calculations and logical comparisons|Control unit — decodes each instruction and sends signals that control the other parts of the CPU|Cache — very fast memory in the CPU for frequently used instructions and data, so they need not come from slower RAM|Registers — program counter: address of the next instruction; MAR: address to read from or write to; MDR: the data or instruction fetched or to be stored; accumulator: ALU results|Embedded system — a computer built into a larger device to do one dedicated job, such as the controller in a washing machine
points: Fetch: the address in the program counter is copied to the MAR, the program counter goes up by 1, and the instruction at that address is copied into the MDR.|Decode: the control unit works out what the instruction means. Execute: it is carried out, any result going to the accumulator.|3.5 GHz is 3.5 billion clock cycles a second, so more instructions are fetched and executed each second than at 2 GHz.|A bigger cache holds more of the data the CPU needs close by, so it waits less often for slower RAM and performance improves.|Four cores can each process instructions at once, but a program that cannot be split into separate tasks gains little.

title: Memory, storage and units
words: RAM — random access memory: volatile primary storage holding the programs and data currently in use|ROM — read-only memory: non-volatile primary storage holding the instructions that start the computer, such as the BIOS|Volatile — loses its contents when the power is switched off; RAM is volatile, ROM and secondary storage are not|Virtual memory — part of secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full; much slower than real RAM|Secondary storage — non-volatile storage for files and programs not in use: magnetic, optical or solid state|Bit — one binary digit, 0 or 1, as a circuit is off or on; 4 bits make a nibble and 8 a byte|Units — 1 kilobyte (KB) is 1000 bytes, and each step up is 1000 times bigger: megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte, petabyte
formulas: Bits to bytes — bytes = bits / 8|Bytes to kilobytes — KB = bytes / 1000|Each unit up — MB = KB / 1000, GB = MB / 1000, TB = GB / 1000|Storage needed — total = file size × number of files
points: 24 000 bits ÷ 8 = 3000 bytes, and 3000 ÷ 1000 = 3 KB.|How many 5 MB photos fit on a 64 GB card? 64 × 1000 = 64 000 MB, and 64 000 ÷ 5 = 12 800 photos.|With many programs open, RAM fills and data is moved to virtual memory; swapping it back is slow, so adding RAM speeds the computer up.|Choose storage by capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost: an SSD suits a laptop, being fast with no moving parts.|A magnetic hard disk gives large capacity cheaply, so it suits backups; an optical disc is cheap and portable but holds little.

title: Data representation
words: Binary — base 2, using only 0 and 1; the 8 place values are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, so 8 bits hold 0 to 255|Hexadecimal — base 16: 0 to 9, then A to F for 10 to 15; one hex digit is one nibble, so it is shorter and easier for people to read|Overflow — a result needs more bits than are available, such as a sum over 255 in 8 bits|Character set — the characters a computer can represent, each with a binary code; ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters, Unicode more bits for the world's alphabets|Bitmap image — made of pixels; colour depth is the bits for each pixel, resolution the number of pixels; metadata such as width and height is stored with it|Sound sampling — the wave's amplitude is measured at regular intervals; sample rate is samples per second (hertz), bit depth the bits for each sample|Compression — lossy removes data for good, making files much smaller (MP3, JPEG); lossless loses nothing, so the original is rebuilt exactly (ZIP, PNG)
formulas: Image file size — size in bits = colour depth × image width (px) × image height (px)|Sound file size — size in bits = sample rate (Hz) × duration (s) × bit depth|Text file size — size in bits = bits per character × number of characters|Number of colours — colours = 2^n, where n is the colour depth|Binary shift — n places left multiplies by 2^n; n places right divides by 2^n, losing any remainder
points: 77 = 64 + 8 + 4 + 1, so in binary 01001101. Split into nibbles 0100 and 1101, which are 4 and 13, so in hex 4D.|11001000 + 01010000 = 1 00011000: 200 + 80 = 280 needs a 9th bit, so in 8 bits this is overflow.|00001100 (12) shifted 2 places left is 00110000 (48), which is × 4; shifted 1 place right it is 00000110 (6).|Image 100 × 50 pixels with 8-bit colour: 8 × 100 × 50 = 40 000 bits; ÷ 8 = 5000 bytes = 5 KB.|10 s of sound at 44 100 Hz and 16-bit: 44 100 × 16 × 10 = 7 056 000 bits; ÷ 8 = 882 000 bytes = 882 KB.

title: Binary
html: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1

title: Networks and protocols
words: LAN and WAN — a LAN covers a small area, such as one school, on its owner's hardware; a WAN covers a large area, often on rented lines; the internet is the largest WAN|Client–server network — clients request files and services from a central server, which also manages security and backups|Peer-to-peer network — every computer has equal status and shares its files directly with the others, with no central server|Star and mesh topologies — in a star every device links to a central switch; in a mesh devices link to each other, so data has more than one route|Protocol — an agreed set of rules for sending data between devices; protocols are grouped into layers, each doing one job|DNS — the domain name system, which looks up the IP address that belongs to a domain name, such as a website's|The cloud — storage, services and software on remote servers, reached over the internet
points: Hardware for a LAN: a NIC in each device, a switch to join them, a wireless access point for Wi-Fi, and a router to reach the internet.|TCP and IP split data into packets and route them; HTTP fetches web pages, HTTPS encrypts them; FTP moves files; SMTP sends email; POP and IMAP fetch it.|An IP address such as 192.168.1.20 identifies a device on a network and can change; a MAC address is fixed in its NIC when it is made.|Ethernet cable is faster and more reliable; Wi-Fi and Bluetooth let devices move around, but suffer interference and need encryption.|Performance drops with lower bandwidth, more users at once, wireless rather than cable, a high error rate and high latency.

title: Network security
words: Malware — software written to harm a computer or steal data, such as a virus, worm, trojan, spyware or ransomware|Social engineering — manipulating people, the weakest point of any system, into giving away data or access|Phishing — an email or message pretending to come from a trusted organisation, to trick people into giving away passwords or bank details|Brute-force attack — trying every possible password, usually automatically, until one works|Denial of service attack — flooding a server with so many requests that genuine users cannot reach it|Data interception — data is captured as it travels across a network, for example with a packet sniffer|SQL injection — typing SQL code into a website's input box so the database runs it, revealing or changing data
points: Penetration testing: an organisation pays experts to attack its own network, with permission, to find weaknesses before criminals do.|Anti-malware compares files with a database of known malware and quarantines matches; a firewall blocks traffic that breaks its rules.|Long passwords mixing letters, numbers and symbols, and locking the account after a few wrong tries, defeat a brute-force attack.|Access levels: staff can edit the shared drive but students can only read it, so one stolen student login does less damage.|Encryption means intercepted data cannot be understood without the key; locks, swipe cards and CCTV give the server room physical security.

title: Systems software
words: Operating system — software that manages the computer's hardware and lets applications run|User interface — how the user and computer communicate, such as a graphical one of windows, icons, menus and a pointer, or a command line|Memory management — the OS moves programs and data in and out of RAM, each in its own area, and shares CPU time between them for multitasking|Device driver — software that lets the OS communicate with one particular piece of hardware, such as a printer|User management — the OS keeps an account for each user, with a password and access rights|File management — the OS organises files into folders and lets users name, move, copy and delete them and set who may open them|Utility software — small programs that keep the computer working well, such as encryption, defragmentation and data compression
points: Defragmentation moves the scattered parts of each file on a hard disk next to each other, so the read head moves less; an SSD does not need it.|Compression makes files smaller, so they take less storage and send faster, such as zipping a folder before emailing it.|Encryption software scrambles files with a key, so the data on a stolen laptop cannot be read.|Plugging in a new printer: the OS uses its driver to talk to it, then manages the queue of documents sent to it.|With music and a browser open, the OS gives each its own area of RAM and switches the CPU between them so fast both seem to run at once.

title: Ethics, law and the environment
words: Data Protection Act 2018 — personal data must be used fairly and lawfully, only for its stated purpose, kept accurate and secure, and no longer than needed|Computer Misuse Act 1990 — makes it illegal to access a computer without permission, to do so to commit a further crime, or to change or damage data without permission|Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 — protects original work, including software, music and images, from being copied, shared or sold without permission|Open source licence — the source code is free to see, change and share, but there may be little official support|Proprietary licence — the source code is kept secret; users usually pay to use the software and may not change or copy it|Digital divide — the gap between people who have easy access to computers and the internet and people who do not|E-waste — thrown-away electronic devices; toxic metals such as lead and mercury can leak from landfill
points: Logging into a friend's account without permission is an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, even if nothing is changed.|A gym must keep members' details secure, accurate and only as long as needed (Data Protection Act 2018); members can ask to see them.|Sharing a copied film or game online breaks the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.|Ethical and cultural: self-service tills save money but can cut jobs, and people without the internet are left out as services move online.|Privacy: apps can collect a user's location and browsing history. Environmental: data centres use a lot of electricity, and old devices become e-waste.

title: Algorithms
words: Abstraction — removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters, such as a train map that shows the stations but not the real distances|Decomposition — breaking a problem into smaller problems that are each easier to solve|Linear search — checks each item in turn from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end; the data need not be sorted|Binary search — on sorted data only: check the middle item, discard the half the target cannot be in, and repeat|Bubble sort — compares each pair of neighbouring items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order; passes repeat until one makes no swaps|Merge sort — splits the list in half again and again until every list holds one item, then merges the lists back together in order|Insertion sort — takes each item in turn and inserts it into its correct place among the items already sorted
points: Trace: total = 0, then for i = 1 to 3, total = total + i. i takes 1, 2, 3 and total goes 0, 1, 3, 6, so the output is 6.|Binary search for 23 in 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27: middle 15 is too small, so keep 19, 23, 27; middle 23, found. Linear search takes 6 checks.|Bubble sort, first pass of 5, 1, 4, 2: swap 5 and 1, swap 5 and 4, swap 5 and 2, giving 1, 4, 2, 5. The largest is now at the end.|Merge sort of 6, 2, 8, 1: split to 6, 2 and 8, 1, then to single items; merge to 2, 6 and 1, 8; merge again to 1, 2, 6, 8.|Flowchart shapes: rounded box for start or end, parallelogram for input or output, rectangle for a process, diamond for a decision.

title: Sorting
html: sorting

title: Programming fundamentals
words: Variable and constant — a variable is a named memory location whose value can change as the program runs; a constant's value cannot change|Sequence, selection and iteration — the three constructs: steps in order, a choice with if or switch, and repetition with a loop|Count-controlled loop — repeats a set number of times (for); a condition-controlled loop (while, do until) repeats depending on a condition|Data types — integer (whole number), real (number with a decimal part), Boolean (True or False), character (one symbol) and string (text)|Array — several items of the same data type under one name, each found by its index, which starts at 0; a 2D array is like a table|Record — related fields stored together under one name, which can be of different data types, such as a pupil's name and age|Sub program — a named block of code that can be called; a function returns a value and a procedure does not
formulas: Remainder — 17 MOD 5 = 2|Whole-number division — 17 DIV 5 = 3|Power — 2^3 = 8|Even test — n MOD 2 == 0 is True when n is even|Comparison operators — == equal, != not equal, < less than, <= less than or equal, > greater than, >= greater than or equal
points: input always returns a string, so age = int(input("Age: ")) casts it to an integer before any maths; str(5) turns 5 into "5".|word = "Computer": word.length is 8, word.upper is "COMPUTER", word.left(3) is "Com"; scores = [12, 7, 9], so scores[2] is 9.|f = open("scores.txt"); f.readLine() reads a line, f.writeLine("Sam") writes one, f.close() closes it. random(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 to 6.|SELECT name, score FROM Results WHERE score > 50 returns the name and score of everyone who scored over 50; SELECT * returns every field.|function double(n) return n * 2 endfunction, so double(4) returns 8; a procedure does its job but returns nothing.

title: Producing robust programs
words: Defensive design — planning for misuse and mistakes, so a program keeps working and stays secure whatever the user enters|Authentication — confirming a user is who they claim to be, such as with a username and password|Input validation — checking input is sensible before it is used: range, type, length, presence and format checks|Maintainability — code that others can read and change: sub programs, clear names, indentation and comments|Iterative testing — testing each part as it is written, fixing it and testing again; final testing checks the whole program at the end|Syntax error — code that breaks the rules of the language, such as a missing bracket, so the program will not run|Logic error — the program runs but does the wrong thing, such as using < where <= was needed
points: Test data for a whole-number age from 11 to 16: normal 13; boundary 11 and 16; invalid 25 (right type, out of range); erroneous "ten" (wrong type).|Range check: while age < 11 OR age > 16, print an error and ask again, so only 11 to 16 gets through.|if mark > 50 when 50 is a pass is a logic error: a mark of exactly 50 fails. Fix it with mark >= 50.|Refining: the average of 0 numbers crashes with a divide by zero, so check the count is above 0 before dividing.|Maintainable code: totalScore, not t; indent inside every loop and if; a comment above each sub program saying what it does.

title: Boolean logic
words: AND gate — the output is 1 only when both inputs are 1|OR gate — the output is 1 when either input, or both, is 1|NOT gate — one input; the output is the opposite of the input|Truth table — every combination of inputs with the output for each: 2 inputs give 4 rows, 3 inputs give 8|Logic diagram — gates joined together to show how the inputs combine to give the output|Gate symbols — AND is a D shape; OR has a curved back and a pointed front; NOT is a triangle with a small circle at its tip
points: P = (A AND B) OR C with A = 1, B = 0, C = 1: A AND B = 0, then 0 OR 1 = 1, so P = 1.|A AND NOT B for inputs 00, 01, 10, 11 gives 0, 0, 1, 0: it is 1 only when A is 1 and B is 0.|NOT (A OR B) is 1 only when A and B are both 0.|A heater comes on if it is cold AND either the switch or the timer is on: H = C AND (S OR T).|With three inputs, list the rows in binary order, 000 to 111, so no combination is missed.

title: Languages and IDEs
words: High-level language — written with English-like words that people can read, such as Python; it works on many types of processor but must be translated|Low-level language — close to the hardware: machine code (binary) and assembly language (mnemonics such as ADD); written for one type of processor|Translator — converts source code into machine code that the CPU can execute|Compiler — translates the whole program in one go into an executable file, and reports the errors at the end|Interpreter — translates and runs the program one line at a time, and stops at the first error|Assembler — translates assembly language into machine code, one instruction for each mnemonic|IDE — integrated development environment: one program with an editor, error diagnostics, a run-time environment and a translator
points: Compile a finished game: the executable runs fast without the compiler and hides the source code, but each change means compiling again.|Interpret while developing: it stops at the line with the error, so bugs are easier to find, but it runs slower and needs the interpreter every time.|Low-level code suits an embedded system or a device driver, where speed and small memory use matter and the hardware is controlled directly.|IDE tools: line numbers and colour coding in the editor, breakpoints and stepping to find logic errors, and error messages naming the line.|One line of Python, total = a + b, becomes several machine code instructions: load a, add b, store the result in total.

title: GCSE Design and Technology
summary: The whole GCSE in ten short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Design and Technology (8552) specification, ending with making principles and the non-exam assessment.
subject: Design and Technology

title: New and emerging technologies
words: Automation — robots and computer-controlled machines doing work that people used to do, quickly and with few errors|Lean manufacturing — cutting waste of materials, time and energy at every stage; just in time (JIT) means parts arrive only as they are needed|Crowdfunding — raising money for a new product from many people who each give a small amount, usually online|Technology push and market pull — a new technology or material leads to a new product; customer demand leads to a new or better product|Finite resource — one that will run out, such as crude oil and metal ores; non-finite resources, such as timber from managed forests, can be replaced|Planned obsolescence — designing a product to go out of date or stop working after a time, so that it is replaced|Life cycle assessment (LCA) — measuring a product's impact on the environment from raw material, through making and use, to disposal
points: Automation: robots weld car bodies fast, accurately and around the clock, but they cost a lot to set up and replace some jobs.|Just in time: a car factory receives seats hours before they are fitted, so no stock is stored, but one late lorry can stop the line.|Technology push: light lithium-ion batteries made e-bikes practical. Market pull: demand for less plastic packaging led shops to sell refills.|A phone with a glued-in battery is often replaced when the battery fails; design for maintenance uses screws so the battery can be swapped.|Inclusive design: a kettle with a large easy-grip handle and a raised switch suits older users with weaker hands.

title: Energy generation and storage
words: Fossil fuel — coal, oil or natural gas, burnt in power stations to drive turbines and generators; finite, and burning it releases carbon dioxide|Nuclear power — uranium nuclei split (fission) to release heat; no carbon dioxide while running, but radioactive waste must be stored safely, some for thousands of years|Renewable energy — from a source that will not run out: wind, solar, tidal, hydro-electric and biomass|Photovoltaic (PV) cell — a solar cell that turns light directly into electricity|Biomass — plant material or animal waste used as a fuel to generate electricity; renewable because new crops can be grown|Pumped storage — spare electricity pumps water up to a high reservoir; at times of peak demand it flows back down through turbines|Alkaline and rechargeable batteries — both store energy chemically; an alkaline battery is used once and thrown away, a rechargeable one such as lithium-ion can be recharged many times
points: Wind: free fuel and no carbon dioxide while the blades turn, but no wind means no power, so it needs storage or a backup.|Tidal power is predictable, because tides are known years ahead, but a barrage is costly to build and changes the habitats around it.|Pumped storage gives back less energy than it used for pumping, but it can meet a sudden rise in demand very quickly.|Choosing a power source: mains for a kettle, which needs high power; batteries for a portable torch; a PV cell for a garden light.|Solar garden light: a PV cell charges a rechargeable battery by day; at dusk a light sensor switches the LED on.

title: New and smart materials
words: Graphene — a sheet of carbon one atom thick; very strong, light and flexible, and it conducts electricity|Metal foam — a metal, usually aluminium, full of gas pockets; light and stiff, and good at absorbing impact|Titanium — a strong, light metal that resists corrosion and is not rejected by the human body|Smart material — changes a property in response to a change in its surroundings, such as heat, light or force, and changes back when it is removed|Shape memory alloy — such as nitinol, a nickel and titanium alloy; returns to a shape it has been set to when it is heated|Thermochromic and photochromic pigments — change colour with temperature, and with light, then change back|Composite — two or more materials combined to give better properties than either alone, such as glass or carbon fibres set in resin
points: Thermochromic: a baby's feeding spoon changes colour if the food is too hot to eat.|Photochromic: glasses lenses darken in bright sunlight and clear again indoors.|Shape memory alloy: a nitinol stent opens up when it warms to body temperature, holding a blood vessel open.|GRP (glass reinforced plastic) for canoes and boat hulls; CRP (carbon reinforced plastic) for racing bike frames: lighter and stiffer, but costly.|Technical textiles: Kevlar in stab vests, fire-resistant fabric in firefighters' suits, conductive thread in touch-screen gloves.

title: Systems and mechanical devices
words: Systems approach — a product broken into input, process and output blocks, such as a sensor, a microcontroller and an LED|Sensor — an input that detects a change: an LDR's resistance falls as the light gets brighter, a thermistor's falls as it gets warmer|Microcontroller — a programmable chip that reads the inputs and switches outputs such as buzzers, speakers, lamps and LEDs|Types of motion — linear (in a straight line), reciprocating (back and forth in a straight line), rotary (round in a circle), oscillating (swinging in an arc)|Lever — a rigid bar that turns about a pivot, the fulcrum; first order has the fulcrum in the middle, second order the load, third order the effort|Linkage — connected parts that change the direction of motion or the size of a force: a bell crank turns it through 90°, a reverse motion linkage reverses it|Cam and follower — the turning cam pushes the follower up and down, changing rotary motion into reciprocating motion
formulas: Gear ratio — gear ratio = (teeth on driven gear) / (teeth on driver gear)|Output speed — output speed = (input speed) / (gear ratio)|Pulley velocity ratio — velocity ratio = (diameter of driven pulley) / (diameter of driver pulley)|Mechanical advantage — MA = load / effort|Moments about the pivot — effort × effort distance = load × load distance
points: Driver 20 teeth, driven 60 teeth: gear ratio = 60 / 20 = 3, written 3:1, so a 300 rpm motor turns the output at 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm.|Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions; an idler gear between them makes them turn the same way without changing the ratio.|A 200 N load 0.1 m from the pivot, effort 0.5 m away: effort = 200 × 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 40 N, so MA = 200 ÷ 40 = 5.|First order: scissors and a see-saw. Second order: a wheelbarrow and a nutcracker. Third order: tweezers and a fishing rod.|Night light: input, an LDR senses the dark; process, a microcontroller; output, an LED. A rack and pinion turns rotary into linear motion.

title: Materials and their properties
words: Papers and boards — paper is thin and light, board thicker and stiffer: cartridge paper, tracing paper, corrugated card, foil-lined board|Hardwood and softwood — hardwood comes from broadleaved trees and usually grows slowly: oak, beech, ash, mahogany, balsa; softwood comes from conifers and grows faster: pine, larch, spruce|Manufactured board — sheets of timber layers, particles or fibres glued together: plywood, chipboard, MDF|Ferrous and non-ferrous metals — ferrous metals contain iron and most will rust: low carbon steel, cast iron; non-ferrous contain none: aluminium, copper, tin, zinc|Alloy — a metal mixed with other elements to improve its properties: brass is copper and zinc; stainless steel is steel with chromium|Thermoforming and thermosetting polymers — a thermoforming polymer softens every time it is heated, such as acrylic; a thermosetting polymer sets for good, such as epoxy resin|Working properties — strength, hardness (resists scratching), toughness (absorbs impact), malleability (presses into shape), ductility (draws into wire), elasticity (springs back)
formulas: Density — density = mass / volume
points: Balsa is a hardwood yet very soft: hardwood means it comes from a broadleaved tree, not that it is hard.|Urea formaldehyde for an electric plug: a thermosetting polymer that is hard, rigid, an electrical insulator and will not soften when warm.|Polypropylene for a lunch box lid with a hinge: tough and flexible, so it can bend many times without breaking.|Fabrics: cotton, wool and silk are natural fibres; polyester and elastane are synthetic. Elastane blended with cotton gives jeans stretch.|An aluminium block 10 × 5 × 2 cm has a volume of 100 cm³ and a mass of 270 g: density = 270 ÷ 100 = 2.7 g per cm³.

title: Selecting and sourcing materials
words: Selection factors — functionality, aesthetics, environmental impact, availability, cost, and social, cultural and ethical factors|Tension and compression — a pulling force that stretches a material; a pushing force that squashes it|Bending, torsion and shear — a force that makes a material curve; a twisting force; two forces in opposite directions trying to slide one part past the other|Reinforcing — making a material stiffer or stronger by laminating, webbing, fabric interfacing, folding or corrugating|Ecological footprint — the damage a product does to the environment, from deforestation, mining, drilling and farming to energy use and waste|Six Rs — reduce, refuse, re-use, repair, recycle and rethink, to cut a product's impact on the environment|Primary processing — turning a raw material into a usable form: logs into planks, ore into metal, crude oil into polymer granules
points: A shelf fixed at one end and loaded at the other bends: its top surface is in tension and its bottom surface is in compression.|Corrugated card: a fluted layer glued between two flat liners makes thin card stiff enough for a box.|Timber is felled, converted (sawn into planks) and seasoned; aluminium is extracted from bauxite ore by electrolysis; most polymers come from crude oil.|Six Rs in use: a phone with a replaceable battery can be repaired; a refill pouch re-uses the soap bottle and reduces plastic.|Social footprint: Fairtrade cotton pays farmers a fair price; very cheap clothes may mean low pay and unsafe factories.

title: Treatments, stock and production
words: Annealing — heating a work-hardened metal so that it becomes softer and easier to shape again|Hardening and tempering — high carbon steel heated red hot and quenched becomes hard but brittle; reheating it gently (tempering) makes it tougher|Seasoning — drying timber to lower its moisture content, so it is stronger, more stable and less likely to warp|Stock form — the standard shape and size a material is bought in: sheet, rod, bar, tube, plank or a roll of fabric|Standard component — a ready-made part that is bought in, such as screws, nuts and bolts, hinges, zips and buttons|One-off and batch production — one-off: a single product made to order, often by hand; batch: a set number of identical products, then the set-up changes|Mass and continuous production — mass: very large numbers on a production line at a low cost each; continuous: running non-stop, 24 hours a day
formulas: Cost per product — cost per product = (total cost) / (number made)
points: Paper and board are sold by weight in gsm, printer paper being about 80 gsm; board thickness is also given in microns: 300 microns = 0.3 mm.|Low carbon steel has too little carbon to harden by quenching, so it is case hardened: carbon is added to the surface for a hard skin and a tough core.|Set-up £200 and materials £3 each: 50 clocks cost (200 + 150) / 50 = £7 each, but 100 clocks cost (200 + 300) / 100 = £5 each.|PSE (planed square edge) timber is a little smaller than its sawn size, because planing removes some of the wood.|One-off: a made-to-measure wedding dress. Batch: a bakery's bread. Mass: mobile phones. Continuous: steel and petrol.

title: Processes and finishes
words: Wasting — shaping by cutting material away: sawing, drilling, filing, turning, milling and laser cutting|Deforming and reforming — deforming bends or presses a material into shape without removing any; reforming melts it and sets it in a mould|Addition — joining or building up material: welding, gluing, stitching and 3D printing|Jig and template — a jig guides the tool so every copy is cut or drilled in the same place; a template is drawn round to mark out the same shape|CAD and CAM — computer-aided design draws and tests a design on screen; computer-aided manufacture makes it on a laser cutter, CNC router or 3D printer|Quality control — checking products during and after making to make sure they meet the specification|Surface finish — a treatment that protects a product from rust, rot, stains or wear (functional) or improves how it looks (aesthetic)
points: Vacuum forming deforms a heated HIPS sheet over a mould, which needs tapered sides and rounded corners so the sheet will come off.|Injection moulding reforms melted polymer granules in a steel mould; the mould is very expensive, so it suits mass production.|Metals: steel lamp posts are galvanised (dipped in molten zinc); bike frames are powder coated (powder sprayed on, then baked in an oven).|Timber: fence panels are tanalised, with preservative forced in under pressure, to stop rot; indoor furniture is varnished, oiled or waxed.|Paper: laminating protects, embossing raises a pattern, UV varnish adds gloss. Textiles: dyeing, printing, stain protection. Polymers: polishing, vinyl decals.

title: Designing principles
words: Design brief — a short statement of the problem, who the product is for and what it must do|Specification — a list of measurable points the product must meet, used later to evaluate it|Ergonomics and anthropometrics — designing a product to be comfortable, safe and easy to use; body measurements used to size it|User-centred design — the user's needs and wants shape every decision, and users are asked for feedback at each stage|Iterative design — design, make a prototype, test and evaluate it, then improve it and go round again|Design fixation — sticking to a first idea or an existing product, which stops new ideas|Orthographic projection — front, side and plan views of an object drawn to scale, usually in third angle, with dimensions in mm
formulas: Scale 1:n — real size = drawing size × n
points: Not "it should be small" but "it must be no bigger than 150 × 75 × 10 mm, so it fits in a pocket": a specification point you can test.|Size a handle to fit users from the 5th to the 95th percentile of hand width and it fits 90% of people.|A 1:5 drawing shows a 400 mm shelf as 400 ÷ 5 = 80 mm long; at 2:1 a 15 mm part is drawn 30 mm long.|Harry Beck's 1933 London Underground map: straight lines at 45° and 90° and evenly spaced stations, clarity before true distances.|Iterative design: James Dyson built thousands of prototypes before his bagless cyclone vacuum cleaner was right.

title: Making principles and the NEA
words: Prototype — a working model made to test a design against the specification and the client's needs before it is made for real|Tolerance — how far a size may vary from its target and still be accepted, written with ±, such as 50 ± 0.5 mm|Datum — a fixed edge, line or point that every measurement is taken from, so that errors do not add up|Nesting — fitting shapes close together on a sheet, like a jigsaw, so as little material as possible is wasted|Go and no-go gauge — a quick check: the part must fit the go end and must not fit the no-go end|Risk assessment — a list of the hazards of a process and the control measures that make it safe|NEA — non-exam assessment: a design-and-make project worth 50% of the GCSE, in response to a context set by AQA
formulas: Percentage waste — % waste = (area wasted) / (area of sheet) × 100|Tolerance limits — limits = target size ± tolerance
points: Twelve 10 × 12 cm parts from a 60 × 30 cm sheet: 1800 − 1440 = 360 cm² wasted, so 360 / 1800 × 100 = 20% waste.|A part dimensioned 50 ± 0.5 mm passes from 49.5 mm to 50.5 mm, so 50.4 mm is accepted and 50.7 mm is rejected.|Pillar drill: hazard, hair or a sleeve caught in the chuck; control, tie hair back, roll up sleeves, lower the guard and clamp the work.|NEA marks: investigating 10, brief and specification 10, generating ideas 20, developing ideas 20, realising ideas 20, analysing and evaluating 20.|The exam, 2 hours and 100 marks: core technical principles 20, specialist technical principles 30, designing and making principles 50.

title: GCSE Food Preparation and Nutrition
summary: The whole GCSE in eight short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Food Preparation and Nutrition (8585) specification, ending with the two non-exam assessment tasks.
subject: Food Preparation and Nutrition

title: Macronutrients and micronutrients
words: Macronutrient — a nutrient needed in large amounts: protein, fat and carbohydrate|Micronutrient — a nutrient needed in small amounts: vitamins and minerals|High biological value protein — contains all the essential amino acids, as in meat, fish, eggs, milk, soya and quinoa; low biological value protein lacks one or more|Protein complementation — eating low biological value proteins together so that each supplies the essential amino acids the other lacks|Saturated fat — no double bonds in its fatty acids; mainly from animal foods such as butter and lard, solid at room temperature; too much raises blood cholesterol|Unsaturated fat — one (mono) or more (poly) double bonds; found mainly in plant oils, nuts and oily fish, and liquid at room temperature|Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K, carried in fat and stored in the body; the B group and C are water-soluble, so most are not stored and are needed every day
points: Beans on toast: the wheat and the beans are each low biological value, but together they supply all the essential amino acids.|Vitamin D, from sunlight, oily fish and eggs, helps the body absorb calcium; too little causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.|Iron makes haemoglobin, which carries oxygen; too little causes anaemia. Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods such as lentils.|Fibre (NSP) holds water and keeps waste soft, preventing constipation; adults should aim for 30 g a day from wholegrains, pulses, fruit and vegetables.|Too much sodium, mostly from salt, raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke.

title: Nutritional needs and health
words: Eatwell Guide — the government model of a balanced diet: just over a third fruit and vegetables, just over a third starchy foods, then protein, dairy and a little oil|Energy values — fat gives 9 kcal per gram, protein 4 kcal per gram and carbohydrate 3.75 kcal per gram|Basal metabolic rate (BMR) — the energy the body needs at rest just to stay alive: breathing, heartbeat, keeping warm|Physical activity level (PAL) — a number showing how active a person is; BMR multiplied by PAL gives daily energy needs|Energy balance — energy taken in from food equals energy used; more in than out over time leads to weight gain|Obesity — a body mass index of 30 or more in an adult; it raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease and some cancers|Type 2 diabetes — the body does not make enough insulin or does not respond to it, so blood glucose stays too high
formulas: Energy from carbohydrate — kcal = grams of carbohydrate × 3.75|Energy from protein — kcal = grams of protein × 4|Energy from fat — kcal = grams of fat × 9|Daily energy requirement — energy = BMR × PAL|Share of energy from a nutrient — % of energy = (energy from the nutrient) / (total energy) × 100|Body mass index — BMI = (mass in kg) / (height in m)^2
points: A snack with 10 g fat, 5 g protein and 20 g carbohydrate: 10 × 9 + 5 × 4 + 20 × 3.75 = 90 + 20 + 75 = 185 kcal.|Fat in that snack: 90 / 185 × 100 ≈ 49% of its energy, more than the 35% advised for the diet as a whole.|BMR 1400 kcal and PAL 1.6: daily energy requirement = 1400 × 1.6 = 2240 kcal.|Life stages: folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of spina bifida; teenage girls need extra iron because of periods.|Coronary heart disease: saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which builds up and narrows the arteries; swap butter for an unsaturated spread.

title: Cooking and heat transfer
words: Reasons for cooking — to make food safe to eat, easier to digest, better in flavour, texture and look, and to keep it for longer|Conduction — heat passes through a solid from molecule to molecule, as from the hob through the pan into the food|Convection — heated liquid or air rises and cooler liquid or air sinks to take its place, setting up currents that carry heat round, as in a pan of water or an oven|Radiation — heat travels as infrared rays straight onto the surface of the food, as under a grill or over a barbecue|Water-based methods — blanching, boiling, simmering, poaching, steaming, stewing and braising|Fat-based methods — shallow frying, stir frying and deep frying; quick, and they brown the food, but they add fat|Dry methods — baking, roasting, grilling, toasting and dry frying
points: Boiling pasta: heat conducts through the base of the pan, then convection currents in the water carry it round the pan to the pasta.|Steaming broccoli keeps more vitamin C than boiling it, because the vitamin is water-soluble and the broccoli is not sitting in the water.|Grilling a burger lets the fat drip away, so it ends up lower in fat than the same burger shallow fried.|Stir frying cooks thin strips fast in a little oil, so vegetables stay crisp and colourful and lose fewer vitamins.|Microwaving: the microwaves make water molecules in the food vibrate, which heats it; stir halfway and leave it to stand so there are no cold spots.

title: Functional and chemical properties
words: Denaturation — heat, acid or whisking unfolds the structure of a protein, as when egg white is whisked or meat is marinated in lemon juice|Coagulation — denatured proteins join together and set, changing from a liquid to a solid, as when an egg is cooked; it cannot be reversed|Gluten — formed when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water; kneading makes it stretchy, so bread dough can hold gas|Gelatinisation — starch grains absorb liquid, swell and burst as they are heated, thickening the liquid, as in a white sauce|Dextrinisation and caramelisation — dry heat breaks starch down into brown dextrins, as on toast; heated sugar melts and browns into caramel|Shortening — fat coats the flour so that less gluten forms, giving a short, crumbly texture, as in shortcrust pastry and shortbread|Plasticity — a fat softens over a range of temperatures, so it can be spread, shaped or rubbed in
points: Mayonnaise: lecithin in the egg yolk is an emulsifier, holding the oil and the vinegar together so that they do not separate.|Whisking egg white denatures its protein and traps air as a foam; in a low oven the protein coagulates and the meringue sets.|Creaming butter and sugar traps air; baking powder, bicarbonate of soda plus an acid, gives off carbon dioxide. Both make a cake rise.|Bread: yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol in a warm, moist dough, and the stretchy gluten traps the gas, so the dough rises.|Choux pastry and Yorkshire puddings rise by steam: water in the mixture boils in a hot oven and pushes it up before it sets.

title: Food safety
words: Pathogenic bacteria — bacteria that cause food poisoning, such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, E. coli, Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus|Danger zone — 5 °C to 63 °C, the range in which bacteria multiply readily; they grow fastest at about 37 °C, body temperature|High-risk foods — moist, protein-rich, ready-to-eat foods that bacteria grow on easily, such as cooked meat, dairy foods, eggs, cooked rice and seafood|Cross-contamination — bacteria passing from raw food, hands, cloths or equipment onto food that is ready to eat|Use-by date — on high-risk foods; the food is not safe to eat after this date, even if it looks and smells fine|Best-before date — about quality, not safety; after it the food may be past its best but is still safe if stored correctly|Enzymic browning — enzymes in cut fruit and vegetables react with oxygen and turn them brown; an acid such as lemon juice slows it
points: Fridge 0 °C to 5 °C, freezer −18 °C or colder. Cook until the centre reaches 75 °C, checked with a clean probe, and keep hot food above 63 °C.|Bacteria need warmth, moisture, food and time: one bacterium dividing every 20 minutes becomes 512 after 3 hours (9 divisions).|Raw chicken and salad: separate colour-coded boards (red for raw meat, green for salad) and raw meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge.|Useful micro-organisms: yeast raises bread, moulds give blue cheese its veins, and bacteria turn milk into yogurt.|Defrost raw meat in the fridge, not on the worktop, and cook it within 24 hours; do not refreeze it raw.

title: Food choice
words: Factors affecting food choice — cost, season, availability, enjoyment, lifestyle, health, religion, culture, ethics and medical conditions|Food allergy — the immune system reacts to a food, such as nuts, eggs or shellfish; a severe reaction, anaphylaxis, can kill|Food intolerance — the body struggles to digest a food, causing symptoms such as bloating, as in lactose intolerance; the immune system is not involved|Cuisine — the typical ingredients, equipment, cooking methods and presentation of a country or region|Sensory evaluation — judging food by sight, smell, taste, touch and sound, on a tasting panel in a quiet place, with water between samples|Traffic light labelling — front-of-pack colours, red for high, amber for medium and green for low, for fat, saturates, sugars and salt|Marketing — the ways food is promoted to persuade people to buy it, such as advertising, meal deals and loyalty points
points: Religion: Muslims eat halal meat and no pork; Jewish people eat kosher food and do not mix meat with dairy; many Hindus do not eat beef.|Ethical choices: free-range eggs for animal welfare, Fairtrade bananas for a fair price to the grower, local food for fewer food miles.|A pre-packed label must list ingredients in descending order of weight, with the 14 allergens emphasised, plus a date mark, net quantity and nutrition.|Cuisines: British roast beef with Yorkshire pudding; Italian pasta with tomatoes, olive oil and basil; Indian curries spiced with cumin and turmeric.|Star profile: rate the crunch, sweetness and colour of each sample from 1 to 5, plot the scores on the spokes, and compare the shapes.

title: Food provenance
