words: Food provenance — where a food comes from: where it was grown, raised or caught, and how it was produced|Food miles — the distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten|Carbon footprint — the total greenhouse gases released in growing, processing, transporting and storing a food|Organic — grown without artificial fertilisers or most chemical pesticides, with high standards of animal welfare|Primary processing — changing a raw food so that it can be eaten or used, such as milling wheat into flour or pasteurising milk|Secondary processing — turning primary products into other foods, such as flour into bread or pasta, or milk into cheese|Fortification — adding nutrients to a food, such as the calcium, iron, thiamin and niacin added to white flour by law
points: Strawberries flown in from abroad in December have far more food miles than British strawberries bought in season in June.|Milk is pasteurised at 72 °C for 15 seconds, killing pathogenic bacteria; secondary processing then turns it into cheese or yogurt.|Cutting food waste: plan meals, store food correctly, use up leftovers, and remember a best-before date is about quality, not safety.|Genetically modified crops have had their genes changed, for example to resist pests; they can raise yields, but some consumers distrust them.|Sustainable fish: choose fish with the blue MSC label, caught in ways that leave enough fish in the sea to breed.

title: The two NEA tasks
words: Food investigation (Task 1) — a practical experiment into how and why an ingredient behaves as it does when it is prepared and cooked; 15% of the GCSE|Food preparation assessment (Task 2) — plan, then cook and serve three dishes as a final menu in one session of three hours at most; 35% of the GCSE|Hypothesis — a prediction, based on your research, of what you expect to happen and why|Fair test — change one variable and keep everything else the same, so any difference is caused by that variable|Technical skills — preparation and cooking skills, such as knife skills, making a sauce or shaping dough, shown in trial dishes|Time plan — the order of work for the final session, with timings, hygiene and safety points, and quality checks|Nutritional analysis — working out the energy and nutrients in a dish, often with software, and judging it against the task
points: Task 1: "How does the amount of baking powder affect the rise of a scone?" Change only the baking powder; keep the oven, time and other amounts the same.|Record results, not just opinions: the height of each scone in mm and a tasting panel's ratings, in a table with photographs.|Conclusion: "The scone with the most baking powder rose highest, which supports my hypothesis because more carbon dioxide was produced."|Task 2: trial dishes that show a range of technical skills, choose three for the final menu, and justify each choice against the task.|An evaluation names a strength, a weakness and an improvement: "The pastry edges were crisp but the base was soggy, so next time I would bake it blind."

title: GCSE Art and Design
summary: The whole GCSE in eight short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each, for the AQA GCSE Art and Design: Art, craft and design (8201) specification, ending with the portfolio and the externally set assignment.
subject: Art and Design

title: The assessment objectives
words: AO1 Develop — investigating sources such as artists and designers, and using what you learn from them to grow your own ideas|AO2 Refine — making work better by trying ideas out in suitable media, materials, techniques and processes and choosing the best|AO3 Record — capturing what you see, think and discover about your theme, in drawings, photographs and notes, all through the project|AO4 Present — producing a personal final response that achieves what you set out to do and uses the formal elements with understanding|Equal weighting — each objective is worth a quarter of the marks: 24 out of 96 in each component|Intentions — what you set out to show, say or explore; the work is judged against them
points: One project, all four: artist research (AO1), experiments in different media (AO2), drawings and photographs (AO3), a final piece (AO4).|The objectives overlap: a page of the same shell in pencil, ink and paint is recording (AO3) and experimenting (AO2) at once.|Weak AO2: one medium, tried once. Strong AO2: the idea tried in pencil, watercolour and lino, with a note on which worked best and why.|Each component gives 24 marks to each objective, 96 in all, so leaving one out throws away up to a quarter of the marks.

title: The formal elements
words: Line — a mark made by a moving point; thick or thin, smooth or broken, it can show an outline, called a contour|Tone — how light or dark something is; shading from highlight to shadow makes a flat drawing look solid|Colour — its hue is its name, such as red; a tint adds white and a shade adds black; warm colours seem to come forward and cool colours recede|Shape and form — a shape is flat, in two dimensions; a form is three-dimensional, or drawn to look it|Texture — how a surface feels (actual texture) or looks as though it would feel (visual texture)|Pattern — a line, shape or motif repeated in a regular way|Composition — how everything is arranged: the focal point, the balance, and the foreground, middle ground and background
points: Primary colours mix to make secondaries: red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, blue + red = purple.|Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. Side by side, each looks brighter.|Tone on a sphere: a highlight nearest the light, mid-tones, a dark core shadow where it turns away, and a cast shadow on the ground.|Rule of thirds: split the picture into a 3 × 3 grid and put the focal point where two lines cross, not in the middle.|In annotation: "Short, jagged lines and strong tonal contrast make the portrait feel tense."

title: Drawing and recording
words: Observational drawing — drawing from the real thing in front of you, looking more than you draw|Primary source — something you see first-hand, such as an object, a place or a person, including your own photographs|Secondary source — an image made by somebody else, such as a picture in a book or online|Mark-making — the range of marks a tool can make: hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, scribbling and smudging|Proportion — the size of one part compared with another part, and with the whole|Viewfinder — a card with a small window, used to choose and frame a composition|Thumbnail sketch — a small, quick drawing to try out an idea or a layout
points: Face proportions: the eyes sit about halfway down the head, and the gap between them is about one eye wide.|Grid method: a 2 cm grid on the photograph and a 4 cm grid on the paper doubles the size; copy one square at a time.|Sighting: hold a pencil at arm's length, one eye shut, and compare lengths, such as how many times the width fits into the height.|Record one subject three ways: a tonal pencil study of a shell, a close-up photograph of its ridges, and notes on its colours.|Annotation: "I used cross-hatching to build the dark tone under the rim, so the cup looks rounded."

title: Painting and printmaking
words: Watercolour — transparent paint thinned with water; work from light to dark and keep the white of the paper for highlights|Acrylic — water-based paint that dries quickly and is waterproof when dry; it can be used thick or thin|Impasto — paint laid on so thickly that the brush or knife marks stand up from the surface|Relief print — ink is rolled onto the raised surface of a block, such as lino; the parts cut away stay white|Intaglio print — ink is held in lines scratched or etched into a plate, as in drypoint and etching|Monoprint — a one-off print, such as drawing on paper laid over a rolled-out sheet of ink|Screen print — ink is pushed through a fine mesh with a squeegee; a stencil stops it where it should not print
points: A print is a mirror image of the block, so any letters must be cut back to front.|Reduction lino: cut, print the lightest colour, cut again, print the next, end with the darkest. The block is used up, so print every sheet at each stage.|Wet-on-wet watercolour gives soft, bleeding skies; wet-on-dry gives crisp edges for buildings and detail.|Van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889) uses thick impasto swirls, so the sky seems to move.|Safety: always cut lino away from the hand holding it, with the block held against a bench hook.

title: Sculpture, photography and mixed media
words: Additive sculpture — made by building up, such as modelling clay or joining card, wire and wood|Subtractive sculpture — made by taking material away, such as carving stone, wood or plaster|Maquette — a small model used to plan a larger sculpture|Armature — an inner frame, often of wire, that supports a modelled sculpture|Depth of field — how much of a photograph, from near to far, is in sharp focus|Shutter speed — how long the camera's shutter stays open; fast freezes movement and slow blurs it|Collage — a picture made by sticking down paper, fabric, photographs or other materials
points: Joining clay: score both surfaces, add slip (watery clay), press together and smooth the seam, or the join may crack as it dries or is fired.|Wedge clay before using it, to push out air bubbles that could make the piece crack or burst in the kiln.|A wide aperture, a small f-number such as f2.8, gives a shallow depth of field: the face sharp, the background blurred.|A slow shutter speed of a few seconds, with the camera on a tripod, turns car headlights at night into streaks of light.|Mixed media: collage torn newspaper onto card, glaze it with thin acrylic, then draw back into it with pen and ink.

title: Researching and annotating artists
words: Contextual source — the work of an artist, designer or craftsperson, or of a period or culture, that informs your own|Critical understanding — knowing how and why a work was made and what it means, not just describing it|Content, form, process, mood — four headings for analysing a work: what it shows, how the elements are used, how it was made, how it feels|Annotation — written notes beside your work that explain your choices, judge the results and say what comes next|Transcription — a close copy of part of an artist's work, made to learn how they did it|Art movement — artists sharing a style at the same time, such as Impressionism, Cubism or Pop Art
points: Content: "Monet painted the same haystacks at different times of day to show how the light changes their colour."|Form: "Matisse cut shapes from paper painted with gouache, so his colours are flat and his edges crisp."|Process: "Warhol screen-printed Marilyn Monroe's face again and again, like a product on a shelf."|Link: "Like Hokusai in The Great Wave, I will use bold outlines and flat colour in my lino print of the coast."|Weak: "I like it because it is colourful." Strong: name the element, its effect, and how you will use it.

title: Developing and refining ideas
words: Mind map — words and images round a theme, linked up to find a direction|Mood board — a collection of images, colours and materials that sets the look and feel of an idea|Experiment — trying an idea in a new medium, scale, colour or technique to see what works|Refine — improving the strongest experiment step by step and dropping what does not work|Final piece — the outcome that realises your intentions and pulls the project together|Evaluation — judging how well the work meets your intentions and what you would change
points: Development: a drawing of a shell becomes a lino block, then a repeat pattern, then a printed fabric; each step grows from the last.|Annotate a failure: "The watercolour was too pale to show the cracks, so next I will try black ink with a dry brush."|Try one composition three ways, in pencil, collage and paint, then pick one and say why.|Before the final piece, make a small full-colour study to test the colours and the layout.|Evaluation: "The print shows decay as I intended, but the background is too busy; I would simplify it."

title: Portfolio and set assignment
words: Component 1 portfolio — a sustained project and a selection of further work; no time limit, 96 marks, 60% of the GCSE|Sustained project — one project that shows the whole journey, from first ideas to realised intentions|Component 2 externally set assignment — one starting point chosen from an AQA paper released in January; 96 marks, 40% of the GCSE|Preparatory period — the weeks before the supervised time, spent researching, recording and developing ideas|Supervised time — 10 hours of unaided work under exam conditions, in which the final outcome is made|Moderation — the school marks both components and AQA checks the marking, usually on a visit|Two titles — the portfolio must draw on at least two of fine art, graphic communication, textile design, three-dimensional design and photography; the set assignment can use one
points: Prepare so well that the 10 hours are for making the final piece, not for finding the idea.|Preparatory work can be used during the supervised time, and it is marked together with the final piece.|Rehearse: a practice version before the 10 hours shows how long each stage takes and what could go wrong.|Between supervised sessions the work stays at school, kept secure, and it must be all your own.|Portfolio: pick the strongest further work to go with the sustained project, and check all four objectives are covered.

title: GCSE Music
summary: The whole GCSE in nine short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each for the elements, notation, the four areas of study, the listening exam, performing and composing, in the order of the AQA GCSE Music (8271) specification.
subject: Music

title: The elements of music
words: Melody — the tune: conjunct when it moves by step, disjunct when it leaps, shaped by devices such as sequence, repetition and ornaments|Harmony and tonality — the chords under the tune and the key: major, minor or modal, or atonal with no key at all|Rhythm, metre and tempo — the pattern of note lengths, how the beats group into bars (duple, triple or quadruple) and the speed|Texture — how the layers of sound fit together: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, or melody and accompaniment|Timbre — the tone colour of a voice or instrument, and the way it is played, such as pizzicato, muted or with distortion|Dynamics and articulation — how loud (pp to ff, crescendo, diminuendo) and how each note is played (staccato, legato, accented)|Structure — how the music is built from sections, such as binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo (ABACA), theme and variations, or verse and chorus
points: Monophonic: one line alone. Homophonic: the parts move together in chords. Polyphonic: two or more independent tunes at once.|Tempo: largo very slow, adagio slow, andante at a walking pace, moderato moderate, allegro fast, presto very fast. Accelerando speeds up, ritardando slows.|Cadences: perfect V–I sounds finished; imperfect ends on V and sounds unfinished; plagal IV–I is the "Amen"; interrupted V–vi is a surprise.|Answer one element at a time: "The melody is conjunct and in a minor key; the texture is homophonic; the dynamics stay mostly piano."

title: Reading notation
words: Stave — five lines and four spaces; the clef at the start fixes the pitch of every line and space|Treble clef — for higher parts; it curls round the second line up, which is the G above middle C|Bass clef — for lower parts; its two dots sit either side of the fourth line up, which is the F below middle C|Time signature — two numbers: the bottom one names a note (2 minim, 4 crotchet, 8 quaver) and the top one says how many fill a bar|Key signature — the sharps or flats at the start of every stave, which hold for the whole piece|Accidental — a sharp, flat or natural written beside a note, which lasts until the end of that bar|Interval — the distance between two notes, counted in letter names including both the bottom and the top note
points: Treble clef lines, bottom to top: E G B D F; spaces: F A C E. Bass clef lines: G B D F A; spaces: A C E G.|Semibreve 4 beats, minim 2, crotchet 1, quaver half a beat, semiquaver a quarter. A dot adds half the value again, so a dotted minim lasts 3.|3/4 is three crotchets a bar, simple triple, as in a waltz. 6/8 is six quavers in two dotted crotchets, compound duple, as in a jig.|C up to G is a 5th: C D E F G is five letter names. C up to E is a major 3rd; C up to E♭ is a minor 3rd.|One sharp, F♯: G major or its relative minor, E minor. One flat, B♭: F major or D minor. The relative minor starts three semitones lower.

title: Western classical, 1650–1910
words: Baroque — about 1600 to 1750: basso continuo, ornamented melodies, terraced dynamics and one mood held through a movement|Classical — about 1750 to 1820: balanced question-and-answer phrases, mostly homophonic textures, and the piano replacing the harpsichord|Romantic — about 1820 to 1910: bigger orchestras, chromatic harmony, extremes of dynamics, rubato, and music that tells a story or paints a scene|Basso continuo — the Baroque bass part, played by a low instrument such as a cello, with a harpsichord or organ filling in chords above it|Oratorio — a large-scale religious work for soloists, chorus and orchestra, performed without costumes, scenery or acting|Sonata form — exposition (two subjects in different keys), development, then recapitulation (both subjects in the tonic)|Requiem — music for the dead, usually a setting of the Catholic Mass for the dead, for soloists, choir and orchestra
points: Four strands: Handel's coronation anthems and oratorios; orchestral Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven; Chopin and Schumann's piano music; the late Romantic requiem.|This is the one area of study with a compulsory question in Section B, on your set study piece: know its key, structure, texture and instruments.|Classical piano: an Alberti bass breaks each chord into low, high, middle, high, so a C major chord becomes C G E G under the tune.|Sonata form in C major: first subject in C, second subject in G (the dominant), the development through several keys, then both subjects return in C.|Romantic piano: rubato pushes and pulls the tempo for expression, and the sustaining pedal blurs rich chromatic chords under a singing melody.

title: Popular music
words: Riff — a short repeated musical pattern, often played on guitar or bass|Hook — a short, catchy phrase that makes a song memorable, often in the chorus|Verse–chorus form — verses with new words alternate with a repeated chorus, often with an intro, a bridge or middle eight, and an outro|Power chord — a guitar chord of just the root and the fifth, often played with distortion in rock|Backbeat — the accent on beats 2 and 4 of a four-beat bar, usually played on the snare drum|Leitmotif — a short musical idea linked to a character, place or object, used in film and game music|Reprise — a song from earlier in a musical heard again later, often with changed words or a new mood
points: Four strands: Broadway musicals of the 1950s to 1990s, rock of the 1960s and 1970s, film and computer game music since the 1990s, and pop since the 1990s.|Rock line-up: lead and rhythm guitar, bass guitar, drum kit and vocals, with effects such as distortion and wah-wah, and guitar solos over the chords.|Game music loops seamlessly so it lasts as long as the player stays in a level, and changes mood when the action changes.|Musicals: a solo song shows one character's feelings, a duet shows two at once, and a big chorus number often opens or closes an act.|Model answer: "Synthesisers and a drum machine; the bass drum plays on every beat, four to the floor, and the hook repeats in the chorus."

title: Traditional music
words: 12-bar blues — twelve bars using chords I, IV and V, most often I I I I, IV IV I I, V IV I I|Blue note — a flattened 3rd, 5th or 7th note of the scale, which gives the blues its sound|Call and response — a phrase from one singer or player answered by another, or by a group|Improvisation — music made up as it is performed, often over a repeated chord pattern|Polyrhythm — two or more different rhythms played at the same time, common in African drumming|Clave — a repeating two-bar rhythm that holds Latin music such as salsa together, often played on claves, a pair of wooden sticks|Fusion — two or more styles combined, such as African or Caribbean music with Western pop, rock or folk
points: Four strands: blues from 1920 to 1950, fusion with African or Caribbean music, contemporary Latin music, and contemporary folk music of the British Isles.|12-bar blues in C: C C C C, F F C C, G F C C. The lyrics are often AAB: a line, the same line again, then an answering line.|Salsa: clave, congas, timbales, a syncopated piano montuno, punchy brass, and call and response between the lead singer and the chorus.|Folk: jigs in 6/8 and reels in 4/4 on fiddle, accordion, tin whistle or bodhrán, sometimes over a drone; ballads tell a story verse by verse.|Reggae from Jamaica: off-beat chords on guitar and keyboard (the skank), a heavy bass line, and the drums stressing beat 3 (the one drop).

title: Western classical since 1910
words: Minimalism — music built from short repeated patterns that change very gradually over a long time|Phase shifting — two parts repeat the same pattern at slightly different speeds, so they drift out of step and back again|Ostinato — a short musical pattern repeated many times|Dissonance — notes that clash; after 1910 they are often left unresolved|Bitonality — two keys heard at the same time|Pentatonic scale — a five-note scale, such as C D E G A, common in folk melodies|Irregular metre — uneven groups of beats or changing time signatures, such as five or seven quavers in a bar
points: Four strands: Copland's orchestral music; British music by Arnold, Britten, Maxwell Davies and Tavener; Kodály and Bartók; minimalism by Adams, Reich, Riley.|Copland: open fifths and wide-spaced chords for the American landscape, quoted folk and cowboy tunes, syncopated rhythms and bold brass.|Kodály and Bartók collected Hungarian folk songs: listen for folk modes, pentatonic tunes and irregular rhythms; Bartók is often percussive and dissonant.|Minimalism, model answer: "A steady pulse, ostinato cells layered one part at a time, and very slow harmonic change."|Tavener: slow, still music shaped by Orthodox church chant, with long held drones and simple modal melodies.

title: The listening exam
words: Unfamiliar music — short extracts you have not studied, chosen from all four areas of study|Study piece — a set work you studied in class; Section B asks about two of them|Dictation — writing down notes or rhythms you hear, by filling in a stave or a rhythm grid|Identify — name the feature with a musical word, such as pizzicato or perfect cadence|Describe — say what happens, in detail, using the language of the elements|Compare — say what is the same and what is different in two extracts or two sections
points: 1 hour 30 minutes, 96 marks, 40% of the GCSE. Section A, unfamiliar music: 68 marks, two questions on each area of study. Section B, study pieces: 28 marks.|Section B: the compulsory question on Western classical 1650–1910, then one question from the other three areas of study; 14 marks each.|Each extract is played a set number of times, printed on the paper: read the question first, then listen for the element it names.|Name it, then prove it: "The texture is homophonic, because the choir sings the words together in chords."|Rhythm dictation in 4/4: each bar must add up to four crotchet beats, such as crotchet, two quavers, minim: 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 + 2 = 4.

title: Performing (NEA)
words: Non-exam assessment — work done in school during the course, marked by your teacher and checked (moderated) by AQA|Solo performance — one piece in which you are the soloist, with or without an accompaniment|Ensemble performance — playing or singing with at least one other live performer, in a part that nobody else doubles|Level of demand — how difficult the piece is, which counts towards the mark|Intonation — playing or singing in tune|Interpretation — shaping the dynamics, phrasing and tempo to suit the style and mood of the piece|Production via technology — performing by recording, sequencing and layering tracks with music technology, instead of on one instrument or voice
points: Solo plus ensemble must last at least four minutes in total, with the ensemble at least one minute. Each is out of 36: 72 marks, 30% of the GCSE.|Both are recorded during the year you take the exam, on any instrument or voice, or produced with music technology.|Singing along to a backing track is not an ensemble: there must be at least two live performers, and your part must not be doubled.|Choose a piece you can play accurately and fluently: control, accuracy and expression earn marks as well as the level of demand.

title: Composing (NEA)
words: Composition to a brief — Composition 1, written in answer to one of the briefs AQA sets for the year you take the exam|Free composition — Composition 2, in any style and for any instruments or voices you choose|Lead sheet — the melody written out with chord symbols above it, and the lyrics if there are any|Motif — a short musical idea that a piece grows from|Sequence — a phrase repeated straight away at a higher or lower pitch|Modulation — changing key during a piece, often to a related key such as the dominant or the relative minor|Inversion — a melody turned upside down, so that each rising interval falls
points: Two pieces with at least three minutes of music between them, each out of 36: 72 marks, 30% of the GCSE.|Hand in a recording of each piece with a score, a lead sheet or a written account of how it was composed.|Motif C–E–G in C major: in sequence a step higher it is D–F–A; inverted it is C–A–F; augmented, every note lasts twice as long.|A four-chord song pattern: I–V–vi–IV, which in C major is C–G–Am–F. Close a section with a perfect cadence, G to C.|Ternary form for contrast: A in C major, B in A minor at a slower tempo, then A again with a new ending.

title: GCSE Drama
summary: The whole GCSE in eight short chapters: the key words and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Drama (8261) specification: Understanding drama, Devising drama and Texts in practice.
subject: Drama

title: Roles in the theatre
words: Playwright — writes the script: the dialogue and the stage directions|Director — decides the overall interpretation of the play and guides the actors and designers in rehearsal|Performer — brings a character to life on stage; an understudy learns a role in order to step in if the performer cannot go on|Designer — creates the set, costume, lighting, sound or puppets, working to the director's interpretation|Technician — rigs and operates the equipment, such as the lights and sound, during performances|Stage manager — organises the rehearsals and runs everything backstage during performances|Theatre manager — runs the building: front of house, the box office, the staff and the audience's safety
points: Who tells the actors where to move during a scene? The director, in rehearsal, not the stage manager.|The lighting designer plans the lighting states and cues; a technician rigs the lanterns and operates the desk each night.|The lead actor is ill on the night: the understudy, who has learnt the lines and moves, plays the part.|The audience is let in, seated and kept safe by the theatre manager and the front-of-house team.

title: Stages and stage positions
words: Proscenium arch — the audience faces the stage from one side, through a frame like a picture frame|End on — the audience faces the stage from one side, with no arch around it|Thrust — the stage juts out so that the audience sits on three sides of it|Traverse — the audience sits on two opposite sides, facing each other across a long acting area|Theatre in the round — the audience sits all the way round the stage|Promenade — the audience moves from place to place, following the action|Stage positions — named from the actor's view facing the audience: stage left is the actor's left, and upstage is furthest from the audience
points: Nine areas: upstage right, upstage centre, upstage left; centre right, centre stage, centre left; downstage right, downstage centre, downstage left.|Walking towards the audience is moving downstage; an actor who stays upstage of a partner makes the partner turn away from the audience.|In the round, keep moving and use low furniture, so no part of the audience watches a back for the whole scene.|A proscenium arch suits a detailed, realistic box set, because the whole audience looks at it from the front.|Thrust: tall scenery goes upstage, where it blocks nobody's view; a speech downstage brings the actor close to three sides.

title: Performance skills
words: Pitch — how high or low the voice is|Pace and pause — how quickly the lines are spoken, and the deliberate silences between them|Volume and projection — how loud the voice is, and making it carry to the back of the audience without shouting|Tone — the emotion or attitude in the voice, such as sarcastic, gentle or bitter|Posture and gait — how the body is held, and the way a character walks|Gesture and facial expression — movements of the hands, arms or head, and what the face shows, that reveal thoughts and feelings|Proxemics — the distance between characters on stage, which shows their relationship
points: Vocal: "I would lower my pitch and slow my pace on the threat, so the audience hears the danger under his calm."|Physical: "A hunched posture, a shuffling gait and no eye contact would show how ashamed and defeated she feels."|Proxemics: the two start far apart and edge closer with each line, so the audience sees the friendship being mended.|Weak: "I would speak loudly." Strong: "I would raise my volume on the last word, to show his anger finally breaking through."

title: Design skills
words: Set — the scenery, furniture and props that show where and when the action takes place|Composite set — several locations on stage at once, with the action moving between them|Costume — what a character wears, with hair, make-up and accessories, showing their age, status, personality and period|Lighting state — a fixed arrangement of lights for one moment; a cue changes it, as a snap or a slow fade|Profile spot and Fresnel — a profile spot gives a hard-edged beam and can take a gobo; a Fresnel gives a soft-edged beam|Gobo — a metal or glass stencil in a lantern that projects a pattern, such as leaves or a window frame|Diegetic sound — a sound the characters can hear, such as a doorbell; non-diegetic sound, such as mood music, is for the audience only
points: Lighting: a cold blue wash and one hard-edged spot on her face isolate her and show her loneliness.|Colour: an amber gel suggests warmth or sunset; a pale blue gel suggests night or cold.|Costume: a tailored dark suit and polished shoes show his wealth and power; frayed cuffs would show the money running out.|Sound: rain and distant thunder, faded up under the argument, build tension, then cut out at the door slam.|Set: a composite set puts two homes side by side, so the audience can compare the rich family with the poor one.

title: The set play
words: Set play — the one play studied in full for the written exam, with questions from a performer's and a designer's point of view|Extract — the section of the set play printed on the exam paper, which most of the questions are about|Context — the social, historical and cultural setting of the play, which a design or performance should reflect|Interpretation — the choices a performer or designer makes about how to bring a character or moment to life|Subtext — what a character really thinks or feels under the words they say|Stage directions — the playwright's notes on the setting, the action and how lines are spoken|Open book — a clean, unmarked copy of the set play may be taken into the exam
points: Performer: "On her refusal I would stand still and drop my volume, so her calm seems stronger than his shouting."|Space: "I would move from upstage centre to downstage left, away from him, so the gap shows their relationship breaking."|Context in costume: a play set in a Victorian home calls for long skirts, high collars and waistcoats to fix the period.|Design: "A bare stage with one wooden chair under a single cold spotlight shows how empty and alone he is now."

title: Reviewing live theatre
words: Production — one company's staging of a play, with its own interpretation, actors and design|Theatre makers — the actors, director and designers whose choices the review writes about|Describe — say exactly what was seen and heard at a precise moment|Analyse — explain how a choice was made and what it communicated to the audience|Evaluate — judge how well a choice worked, and why, with its effect on the audience|Atmosphere — the mood created for the audience, such as tense, joyful or eerie
points: "His voice cracked to a whisper on the final line, showing his grief; it was powerful because the whole audience fell silent."|Weak: "The set was good." Strong: "The tilted floor kept the actors off balance, like a family slowly falling apart."|Lighting: "A slow fade to one red spot on the dying king shrank the stage and made the moment feel intimate."|Name the character, the moment and the exact change: "the snap blackout after the gunshot", not "the lighting was effective".

title: Devising drama
words: Devising — a group creating its own original piece of drama, starting from a stimulus|Stimulus — the starting point, such as a photograph, poem, song, object or news headline|Practitioner — a theatre maker whose methods can shape the work, such as Stanislavski, Brecht or Frantic Assembly|Genre and style — the type of drama, such as comedy or tragedy, and the way it is staged, such as physical or verbatim theatre|Artistic intention — what the group wants the audience to think, feel or understand|Structure — how the scenes are ordered: linear from start to end, or non-linear with flashbacks|Devising log — the record of the process in three sections: response to a stimulus, development and collaboration, and analysis and evaluation
points: Stimulus to idea: a photograph of an empty swing becomes the story of a missing child, told backwards in flashbacks.|Stanislavski: the actor works out the given circumstances and the character's objective, so the character feels real.|Brecht: a character steps out to speak to the audience and a placard names the scene, so the audience thinks rather than just feels.|Frantic Assembly: a chair duet, a repeated sequence of touches and moves by two performers sitting side by side, shows a relationship without words.|Log: "Our still image of the empty swing worked because the long silence made the audience feel the family's loss."

title: Texts in practice
words: Texts in practice — performing, or designing for, two extracts from one play, which must not be the set play from the written exam|Statement of dramatic intentions — a short note for each extract saying what the student aims to communicate|Blocking — the planned moves and positions of the actors, set in rehearsal|Hot-seating — answering questions in role, to build a character's background and motives|Objective — what a character wants in a scene; the obstacle is what stands in the way|Realising intentions — making the planned choices work in front of an audience
points: Intention: "In extract 1 I want the audience to pity him, so I will keep my voice soft and my eyes down as he is accused."|Off-text improvisation: act out the moment just before the extract, so the first line arrives with real feeling behind it.|Cue learning: a partner reads the line before yours and you answer, then you run it again with the moves.|Extract 1 and extract 2 are each marked out of 20: 40 marks, which is 20% of the GCSE.

title: GCSE Media Studies
summary: The whole GCSE in ten short chapters: the key words, the key theorists and a few worked lines each, in the order of the Eduqas GCSE (9–1) Media Studies (C680QS) specification: the theoretical framework, the media forms and the production.
subject: Media Studies

title: Signs, codes and conventions
words: Semiotics — the study of signs; Barthes argued that texts make meaning through signification, and that familiar meanings come to seem natural, which he called myth|Denotation — what a sign literally shows: a red rose is a flower|Connotation — the ideas a sign suggests or is associated with: a red rose connotes love and romance|Anchorage — words, such as a caption or a tagline, that fix the meaning of an image so the audience reads it as intended; Barthes's term|Conventions — the familiar features audiences expect of a form or genre, such as a masthead across the top of a magazine cover|Mise-en-scène — everything placed in the frame: setting, props, costume, make-up, lighting, and the positions and body language of the people|Technical codes — camera shots, angles and movement, editing, lighting and sound
points: Camera angle: a low-angle shot looks up at a character, connoting power; a high-angle shot looks down, making them seem vulnerable.|Colour: red can connote danger, passion or excitement; white, purity or innocence; black, mystery, sophistication or threat.|Anchorage: a photo of a cheering crowd could mean many things until the caption "Fans celebrate the win" fixes it as joy.|Sound: diegetic sound belongs to the world on screen, such as dialogue; non-diegetic sound is added for the audience, such as the soundtrack.|Model sentence: "Low-key lighting and the shadowed face connote danger and secrecy, signalling the crime genre."

title: Narrative and genre
words: Narrative — the way a story is structured and told, and how its events are revealed to the audience|Equilibrium — Todorov's theory: narratives move from an equilibrium, through a disruption or disequilibrium, to a new equilibrium|Enigma code — a question or mystery that makes the audience want to find out more; Barthes's term|Action code — an action that signals what will happen next, such as a character drawing a gun; Barthes's term|Binary oppositions — pairs of opposites, such as good and evil or hero and villain, that create conflict and meaning|Genre — a type of media product, such as crime drama, sitcom or horror, recognised by its shared conventions|Repetition and difference — Neale's idea that genres repeat familiar conventions but also vary them, borrow from each other and change over time
points: Todorov, as often taught in five stages: equilibrium, disruption, recognition of the disruption, an attempt to repair it, and a new equilibrium.|Crime drama: a quiet town (equilibrium), a body is found (disruption), the detective investigates, the killer is caught (new equilibrium).|Endings carry values: a criminal caught and punished at the resolution reinforces the idea that crime does not pay.|Neale: a new superhero film repeats the costumed hero and the final battle, but adds difference, such as a comic, self-aware tone.|Hybrid genre: a horror comedy mixes the conventions of both genres, so it can appeal to two audiences at once.

title: Representation and identity
words: Representation — how the media present people, places, groups, events and issues; Hall saw it as the production of meaning through language, a system of signs|Mediation — the process by which the media select, construct and shape reality before it reaches the audience|Stereotype — a simplified view of a group; Hall argued that stereotyping reduces people to a few simple characteristics and tends to occur where power is unequal|Countertype — a representation that challenges a stereotype, such as a female engineer shown as the expert|Under-representation — a group appearing rarely, or only in a narrow range of roles|Misrepresentation — a group, place or event shown inaccurately or unfairly|Identity — Gauntlett argued that the media offer a wide range of ideas and role models, which audiences pick and mix from to build their own identities
points: Selection: a news photo of one protester throwing a bottle, not the thousands marching peacefully, represents the whole protest as violent.|Older adverts often showed women as housewives and men as breadwinners, reflecting the gender roles of their time.|Countertype: a father shown as the patient, skilled carer at home challenges the stereotype of the clueless dad.|Gauntlett: a pop star who mixes traditionally masculine and feminine styles gives fans ideas to use in shaping their own identity.|Model sentence: "The cover constructs a narrow ideal of beauty through a slim model and a cover line about weight loss."

title: Media industries
words: Conglomerate — a large company that owns many businesses, often across several media and other industries|Vertical integration — one company owns different stages of the same process, such as film production, distribution and exhibition|Horizontal integration — one company owns several businesses at the same stage, such as a group of radio stations|Convergence — media and technologies coming together, such as a phone that streams TV, plays games and shows the news|Public service broadcasting — programmes made to serve the whole public, not only for profit; the BBC's mission is to inform, educate and entertain|Regulation — rules and the bodies that enforce them: Ofcom for TV and radio, IPSO for most newspapers, BBFC for films, PEGI for games, ASA for adverts|Media concentration — ownership of most of the media by a few large companies; Curran and Seaton argue these firms chase profit and power, which narrows choice and holds back new ideas
points: Funding: the BBC is paid for mainly by the licence fee, so it shows no paid adverts in the UK; ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 rely mainly on advertising.|Vertical integration: a studio that makes a film, distributes it and streams it on its own service keeps the profit from every stage.|Curran and Seaton: "Because a few companies dominate, they back safe sequels and familiar stars rather than risky new ideas."|Curran and Seaton: ownership spread more widely, including small independent companies, makes room for bolder and more varied products.|Age ratings: BBFC film ratings include U, PG, 12A, 15 and 18; PEGI rates games 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18.

title: Media audiences
words: Target audience — the group a media product is aimed at, described by its demographics and psychographics|Demographics — dividing audiences by facts such as age, gender, ethnicity, income, occupation and where they live|Psychographics — dividing audiences by their values, attitudes, interests and lifestyles|Active and passive audiences — a passive audience absorbs the messages it is given; an active one chooses, questions and interprets them|Uses and gratifications — Blumler and Katz: audiences actively choose media to meet their needs, such as information, entertainment, personal identity, and integration and social interaction|Media effects — Bandura: audiences can learn attitudes and behaviour, including aggression, by watching and imitating models in the media|Reception theory — Hall: producers encode a preferred reading, and audiences decode it with a preferred, negotiated or oppositional reading
points: Social grade: ABC1 are managerial, professional and clerical workers; C2DE are manual and casual workers, state pensioners and the unemployed.|Uses and gratifications in a game: entertainment from play, social interaction with friends online, personal identity through a customised avatar.|Reception: a reader who agrees a front-page story matters but rejects the paper's angle on it is making a negotiated reading.|Bandura: young players who see violence rewarded may imitate it, one argument for age ratings such as PEGI 18.|Psychographics: a travel magazine aims at explorers, who seek new experiences; a luxury watch advert aims at aspirers, who want status.

title: Contexts of the media
words: Context — the circumstances in which a product is made and received, which shape what it means|Social context — the way people lived and what society saw as normal at the time, such as family life and gender roles|Cultural context — the arts, fashions, beliefs and lifestyles of a time or a group, such as a music scene|Historical context — the period and events when a product was made; older products reveal the values of their time|Political context — who held power, and the political events and debates of the time, such as an election|Economic context — how money shapes what is made: funding, sales, advertising income and competition|Ideology — a set of values and beliefs; a product can reinforce the dominant ideology of its time or challenge it
points: Historical: a 1950s advert shows a wife delighted by a new cooker, reflecting a time when a woman's role was widely seen as running the home.|Social: showing more same-sex couples on screen reflects changing attitudes and the law: same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2014.|Political: before a general election, a newspaper's front page may tell readers how to vote, revealing its political leaning.|Economic: as print sales fall, newspapers and magazines depend more on websites, apps, paywalls and online advertising.|Cultural: a music video copying the look of 1980s pop draws on nostalgia and the audience's shared cultural memory.

title: Advertising, film marketing, magazines
words: Slogan — a short, memorable phrase linked to a brand and repeated across its advertising|Tagline — the short phrase on a film poster that hints at the story, genre or tone|Billing block — the list of credits at the foot of a film poster, such as the director, the main cast and the studio|Distribution — releasing and marketing a film so that it reaches audiences; it comes between production and exhibition in cinemas or online|Masthead — the title of a magazine or newspaper, in a distinctive font across the top of the front cover|Cover lines — short phrases on a magazine cover that tell readers what is inside|Mode of address — the way a product speaks to its audience: formal or informal, or directly as "you"
points: Component 1, 1 hour 30 minutes, 40%: Section A tests media language and representation in print, including a comparison with an unseen product.|Film marketing: teaser trailers, posters, social media, star interviews and merchandise build awareness before release.|Synergy: a toy range and a fast-food tie-in promote the film, and the film promotes them, so each sells the others.|Magazine cover: the model's direct gaze and "you" in the cover lines create an informal, personal mode of address.|Charity advert: an emotive image of someone in need and a direct appeal, such as "Donate today", push the reader to act.

title: Newspapers, radio and video games
words: Tabloid — a popular newspaper style: big headlines, large images, short stories and an informal tone; red-tops have a red masthead|Broadsheet — a quality newspaper style: longer, more detailed reporting and a formal tone, though many are now printed in a smaller size|News values — what makes a story newsworthy, such as negativity, celebrity, closeness to the audience and the unexpected|Circulation — the number of copies of a newspaper or magazine sold or given away; a higher circulation earns higher advertising rates|Commercial radio — stations funded by advertising and sponsorship; BBC radio is funded by the licence fee and carries no adverts|Free-to-play — a game that costs nothing to download and makes money from in-game purchases|Participatory culture — audiences create and share their own content, such as game streams, fan art and online communities
points: Component 1, Section B tests media industries and audiences in newspapers, radio and video games, and industries only for film.|Front page conventions: masthead, splash headline, main image, standfirst, byline, and puffs and teasers for what is inside.|Two papers can show the same politician as a hero or as a failure, choosing words and images to suit their political leaning.|Radio audiences: apps, podcasts and smart speakers let listeners hear programmes on demand, reaching people who never tune in live.|Video games: new seasons, events and cosmetic items keep players returning and spending, while streams and esports build the fan community.

title: Television, music videos and online
words: Crime drama — a TV genre built around a crime and its investigation, usually led by a detective, with enigmas resolved by the end|Sitcom — situation comedy: regular characters in a familiar setting, short episodes, and comedy from their flaws and clashes|Scheduling — choosing when to broadcast a programme to reach its target audience, such as a family show in the early evening|Watershed — 9pm on UK free-to-air television, before which programmes unsuitable for children should not be shown|Streaming — watching or listening on demand over the internet, which lets audiences binge-watch whole series|Music video — a short film promoting a song, built from performance, narrative or concept, or a mix of them|Star persona — the public image of a musician, built through videos, social media, interviews and live shows
points: Component 2, 1 hour 30 minutes, 30%: Section A is television, Section B music videos and online media, across the whole framework.|Crime drama opening: a body, a police cordon and low-key lighting set up the enigma of who did it.|Industry: co-productions and sales to streaming services abroad help pay for expensive drama and take it to global audiences.|Music video: repeated close-ups of the artist's face and a signature look build the star persona and help sell the song.|Online: musicians post behind-the-scenes clips and reply to fans on social media, building a loyal community around the star.

title: Creating a media production
words: Non-exam assessment — Component 3, 30% of the GCSE: each student makes their own media product for a target audience, answering one of the briefs Eduqas sets|Brief — the task set for the production, giving details such as the form, the target audience and the industry context|Statement of aims and intentions — a short written plan, done before production, saying how the product will meet the brief and reach its audience|Research — studying existing products in the same form and genre to learn the codes and conventions to use|Flat plan — a sketch of a print page's layout, showing where the masthead, images and text will go|Storyboard — a sequence of drawn frames planning each shot of a video, with notes on camera, sound and timing|Original material — photographs, footage, artwork and writing the student has created themselves
points: Statement of aims: "My cover will target 16- to 24-year-old fans of indie music, so I will use an informal mode of address and a handwritten font."|A print brief might ask for a front cover and a double-page spread: masthead, cover lines, original photographs and one consistent house style.|Apply the framework: choose the representations to construct and the conventions to follow or subvert, and justify each choice by the audience.|A video brief: vary shot types, angles and settings, and use editing and sound to show control of technical codes.

title: GCSE Physical Education
summary: The whole GCSE in nine short chapters: the key words, the formulas and a few worked lines each, in the order of the AQA GCSE Physical Education (8582) specification, ending with the non-exam assessment.
subject: Physical Education

title: Bones, joints and muscles
words: Synovial joint — a freely moveable joint: cartilage on the bone ends, a joint capsule lined with synovial membrane, synovial fluid, bursae and ligaments|Ligaments and tendons — ligaments join bone to bone and keep a joint stable; tendons attach muscle to bone|Antagonistic pair — two muscles working together at a joint: the agonist contracts to cause the movement while the antagonist relaxes|Flexion and extension — flexion closes a joint, so the angle gets smaller; extension opens it, so the angle gets bigger|Abduction and adduction — abduction moves a limb away from the midline of the body; adduction moves it back towards the midline|Isotonic contraction — the muscle changes length as it contracts: concentric when it shortens, eccentric when it lengthens under tension|Isometric contraction — the muscle contracts but stays the same length, so the joint does not move, as when holding a plank
points: Skeleton: support, protection, movement, shape, mineral storage, blood cell production. The cranium protects the brain; the femur, a long bone, acts as a lever.|Hinge joints: elbow, knee and ankle. Ball and socket: hip and shoulder. Pivot: the neck (atlas and axis). Condyloid: the wrist.|Kicking: flexion then extension at the knee. Star jump: abduction then adduction at the shoulder and hip. Jump take-off: plantar flexion at the ankle.|Biceps and triceps at the elbow, quadriceps and hamstrings at the knee, hip flexors and gluteals at the hip, gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior at the ankle.|Bicep curl: lifting, the biceps is the agonist and contracts concentrically; lowering slowly, the biceps contracts eccentrically to control the weight.

title: Heart, lungs and energy
words: Cardiac output — the volume of blood pumped out of the heart each minute; stroke volume is the volume pumped in one beat, heart rate the beats per minute|Tidal volume — the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath; in exercise it rises, using up some of the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes|Gaseous exchange — at the alveoli oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, helped by a large surface area, walls one cell thick and many capillaries|Vascular shunting — in exercise the blood vessels to working muscles widen (vasodilation) and those to organs such as the stomach narrow (vasoconstriction)|Aerobic and anaerobic — aerobic exercise is with enough oxygen, for long steady work; anaerobic exercise is without enough oxygen, for short intense bursts|EPOC — excess post-exercise oxygen consumption: the extra oxygen taken in after exercise to recover, also called the oxygen debt|Effects of exercise — immediate: heart and breathing rates rise, sweating, red skin; short-term: tiredness, cramp, DOMS; long-term: lower resting heart rate, bigger heart and muscles
formulas: Cardiac output — cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate|Minute ventilation — minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate|Aerobic respiration — glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water|Anaerobic respiration — glucose → energy + lactic acid
points: At rest: stroke volume 70 ml, heart rate 72 bpm. Cardiac output = 70 × 72 = 5040 ml, about 5 litres per minute.|Exercise: tidal volume 0.5 to 2.5 litres and breathing rate 12 to 40 a minute, so minute ventilation goes from 0.5 × 12 = 6 to 2.5 × 40 = 100 litres a minute.|Deoxygenated: vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs. Oxygenated: pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta, body.|Breathing in: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the intercostal muscles lift the ribs up and out, so the chest gets bigger and air is drawn in.|A 100 m sprint is mainly anaerobic, so lactic acid builds up; a marathon is mainly aerobic. Recovery: a cool-down, ice baths, massage, carbohydrate and fluids.

title: Levers, planes and axes
words: Lever — a rigid bar (a bone) that turns about a fulcrum (a joint), with an effort from the muscles moving a load|First-class lever — the fulcrum is in the middle, between the effort and the load|Second-class lever — the load is in the middle, between the fulcrum and the effort|Third-class lever — the effort is in the middle, between the fulcrum and the load|Mechanical advantage — how well a lever moves a load with little effort: high when the effort arm is longer than the load arm, as in a second-class lever|Planes — imaginary flat surfaces through the body: sagittal (left and right halves), frontal (front and back halves), transverse (upper and lower halves)|Axes — imaginary lines the body turns about: frontal (side to side), sagittal (front to back), longitudinal (head to toe)
formulas: Mechanical advantage — mechanical advantage = (effort arm) / (load arm)
points: Extension at the neck: the fulcrum (top of the spine) is between the load (weight of the head) and the effort (neck muscles), so it is a first-class lever.|Rising onto the toes: the load (body weight) is between the fulcrum (ball of the foot) and the effort (gastrocnemius), so it is a second-class lever.|Bicep curl: the effort (biceps) is between the fulcrum (elbow) and the load (weight in the hand), so it is a third-class lever, like most levers in the body.|Elbow: effort arm 4 cm, load arm 32 cm, so mechanical advantage = 4/32 = 0.125. A big effort is needed, but the hand moves fast through a wide range.|Front somersault: sagittal plane, frontal axis. Cartwheel: frontal plane, sagittal axis. Full twist jump: transverse plane, longitudinal axis.

title: Fitness and training
words: Health and fitness — health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease; fitness is the ability to meet the demands of the environment|Components of fitness — agility, balance, cardiovascular endurance, coordination, flexibility, muscular endurance, power, reaction time, speed and strength|SPORT — the principles of training: specificity, progressive overload, reversibility and tedium|FITT — frequency, intensity, time and type: the ways to apply overload|Training methods — circuit, continuous, Fartlek, interval, plyometric, static stretching and weight training|Training seasons — pre-season builds fitness, the competition season maintains it, and post-season is rest and light activity|Altitude training — aerobic training where the air is thinner, so the body makes more red blood cells and carries more oxygen back at sea level
formulas: Maximum heart rate — MHR = 220 − age|Aerobic training zone — 60% to 80% of MHR|Anaerobic training zone — 80% to 90% of MHR
points: Tests: multi-stage fitness test (cardiovascular endurance), handgrip dynamometer (strength), sit-up test (muscular endurance), sit and reach (flexibility).|Illinois agility run (agility), 30 m sprint (speed), vertical jump (power), stork stand (balance), wall toss (coordination), ruler drop (reaction time).|Age 16: MHR = 220 − 16 = 204 bpm. Aerobic zone: 0.6 × 204 to 0.8 × 204 = 122 to 163 bpm. Anaerobic zone: 163 to 0.9 × 204 = 184 bpm.|Warm-up: pulse raiser, stretches, then skill practice, to raise heart rate and muscle temperature. Cool-down: light jog and stretches to help clear lactic acid.|Avoid injury: PAR-Q first, warm up, correct technique and kit, the right level, rest. Strength: heavy weights, few reps; muscular endurance: light, many reps.

title: Use of data
words: Quantitative data — data in numbers that can be measured, such as a sprint time or a heart rate|Qualitative data — descriptive data in words, such as how a performer felt, gathered by interview or observation|Bar chart — bars of equal width whose heights compare separate groups, such as the number of students taking part in each sport|Line graph — points joined by lines to show how one value changes over time, such as heart rate during a match|Trend — the general direction of data over time: rising, falling or staying level
formulas: Percentage change — percentage change = (new value − old value) / (old value) × 100|Mean — mean = (total of the values) / (number of values)
points: Sit and reach rises from 20 cm to 25 cm: percentage change = (25 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%, an improvement in flexibility.|Three 30 m sprints of 4.6, 4.4 and 4.5 seconds: mean = 13.5 ÷ 3 = 4.5 seconds.|A heart rate graph rises just before and at the start of exercise, levels off during steady exercise, then falls back towards resting during recovery.|Quantitative: a stopwatch, a fitness test or a heart rate monitor. Qualitative: an interview, or watching a match and noting how a player copes.

title: Sports psychology
words: Skill — a learned action that brings about a planned result with maximum certainty and the least time and energy; ability is inherited and stable|Open and closed skills — an open skill is affected by the environment, such as a pass in netball; a closed skill is not, such as a free throw in basketball|Basic and complex skills — a basic skill needs little thought or coordination, such as running; a complex skill needs much decision making and coordination, such as a pole vault|SMART targets — goals that are specific, measurable, accepted, realistic and time-bound|Guidance — visual (a demonstration), verbal (instructions), manual (the coach moves the body) and mechanical (equipment such as a float or harness)|Feedback — intrinsic (felt by the performer) or extrinsic (from a coach), positive or negative, knowledge of results or knowledge of performance|Arousal — a physical and mental state of alertness and readiness, varying from deep sleep to intense excitement
points: Sam aims to cut her 800 m time from 2:40 to 2:35 by July: a performance goal, measured against herself, not an outcome goal like winning the race.|Cricket: input, the batter sees the ball; decision making, play a pull shot; output, the shot; feedback, it goes for four.|Inverted-U: performance rises with arousal to an optimum, then falls. A golf putt needs low arousal, a rugby tackle high; deep breathing and imagery lower it.|Direct aggression is physical contact, such as a tackle; indirect aggression is aimed at an object, such as smashing a shuttlecock.|Introverts tend to prefer individual sports with fine skills (archery), extroverts team sports with gross skills (rugby). Intrinsic motivation lasts longer.

title: Socio-cultural influences
words: Commercialisation — managing and promoting sport to make a profit|Golden triangle — the link between sport, sponsorship and the media, each of which needs and feeds the other two|Sportsmanship — playing fairly within the written and unwritten rules, such as kicking the ball out so an injured player can be treated|Gamesmanship — bending the rules to gain an advantage without breaking them, such as time-wasting|Deviance — behaviour that goes against the morals and laws of sport, such as taking banned drugs or deliberately injuring an opponent|Performance-enhancing drugs — banned substances and methods used to improve performance: anabolic steroids, beta blockers, diuretics, stimulants, narcotic analgesics, EPO and blood doping|Hooliganism — violent or disorderly behaviour by spectators, such as fighting or damaging property
points: A girl with no local club, little spare money and few female role models on television is less likely to take part; a free club and visible role models help.|Television pays for the rights to show a sport, the viewers attract sponsors, and sponsorship money pays for wages, facilities and events.|Commercialisation brings money and coverage, but also kick-off times set for television and dearer tickets. Hawk-Eye and VAR help officials but can slow play.|Steroids build muscle but can damage the liver; beta blockers steady the hand in archery but can cause tiredness; EPO adds red blood cells but thickens blood.|Rivalry, alcohol, gang culture and frustration fuel hooliganism; segregated fans, all-seater stadia, alcohol bans, CCTV, police and banning orders reduce it.

title: Health, well-being and diet
words: Physical health — the heart, lungs and other body systems working well, with a lower risk of illnesses such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes|Emotional health — coping with stress and controlling emotions; exercise releases feel-good chemicals such as serotonin and builds self-esteem|Social health — friendship, a sense of belonging and the chance to cooperate and work as a team|Sedentary lifestyle — a lifestyle with little, irregular or no physical activity|Obesity — being extremely overfat, in adults a BMI of 30 or more; it limits stamina, flexibility, agility and speed|Somatotype — body type: ectomorph (tall and thin), mesomorph (muscular, wide shoulders, narrow hips) or endomorph (pear-shaped, wide hips, more fat)|Dehydration — losing more water than is taken in: the blood thickens, heart rate and body temperature rise, and reactions slow
formulas: Body mass index — BMI = mass / height^2, with mass in kg and height in m
points: Sam has a mass of 72 kg and is 1.80 m tall: BMI = 72 ÷ 1.80² = 72 ÷ 3.24 = 22.2, inside the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9.|A sedentary lifestyle raises the risk of weight gain, obesity, heart disease, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, and of poor sleep and low self-esteem.|Ectomorphs suit high jump and long-distance running; mesomorphs suit sprinting and gymnastics; endomorphs suit sumo wrestling and shot put.|Carbohydrate: the main energy source. Protein: builds and repairs muscle. Fat: energy at low intensity. Vitamins and minerals: healthy body. Fibre: digestion.|An average man needs about 2500 kcal a day and a woman about 2000, more if they are active. Take in more energy than is used and weight goes up.

title: The non-exam assessment
words: Practical performance — three activities from the approved list, one team, one individual and a third of either, assessed as a player or performer|Skills in progressive drills — the core skills of each activity, performed in practices that become more demanding|Full context — performing each activity in a competitive or formal setting, such as a match|Analysis and evaluation — finding the strengths and weaknesses of your own performance in one activity, then justifying an action plan to improve it
points: Papers 1 and 2: 1 hour 15 minutes, 78 marks and 30% each. NEA: 100 marks and 40% of the GCSE.|NEA marks: 25 per activity (10 for drills, 15 for full context) and 25 for the written or spoken analysis (15) and evaluation (10).|Analysis: "my cardiovascular endurance is weak, as I fade in the last 15 minutes of a match." Action plan: Fartlek training three times a week for six weeks.
